On directed questioning she recalls being scratched on the left forearm by an unfamiliar kitten about three weeks before onset, with a small papule at the scratch site that healed. Household exposure to cats was confirmed.

explanation: Regional tender axillary lymphadenitis after a kitten scratch, sterile routine cultures from node aspirate, and ultrasound evidence of central necrosis point to infection with the cat-associated fastidious organism that causes localized lymphadenopathy. Lack of response to a beta-lactam and the temporal relationship to the scratch support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 56-year-old man presented with three weeks of low-grade fevers, fatigue, night sweats and progressive exertional dyspnoea. On examination he was febrile 38.3°C, heart rate 96/min, and had a new holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex with palpable splenomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin.

He has known degenerative mitral valve prolapse diagnosed five years earlier and otherwise good health. Two weeks before symptom onset he underwent an uncomplicated extraction of an infected lower molar; he denied intravenous drug use and had no prior valve surgery.

Blood tests showed WBC 11.5 × 10^9/L and CRP 78 mg/L. Three separate blood culture sets became positive within 48 hours for Gram-positive cocci in chains; colonies on blood agar produced a greenish zone consistent with alpha-haemolysis and were resistant to optochin.
Transoesophageal echocardiography identified an 8 mm mobile vegetation on the posterior mitral leaflet with new moderate mitral regurgitation and no periannular complication.

High-dose intravenous benzylpenicillin was started and fevers subsided within 48 hours; repeat blood cultures after 72 hours of therapy were sterile. The laboratory final report described a penicillin-susceptible, alpha-haemolytic, optochin-resistant oral-flora organism and the patient completed six weeks of targeted therapy with clinical cure.

explanation: Subacute native mitral valve endocarditis following a recent dental extraction with multiple blood cultures yielding alpha-haemolytic, optochin-resistant Gram-positive cocci in chains that are penicillin-sensitive indicates viridans streptococci as the most likely pathogen.

hints.text: A 49-year-old previously independent man presented 9 days after a motorway collision with fever and a painful draining wound over his left tibia. He is on the orthopaedic ward, temperature 38.9°C, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 105/66 mmHg, and the external-fixator site has greyish purulent discharge and surrounding erythema extending several centimetres.

At the referring hospital he underwent irrigation and external fixation of an open tibial fracture, required intubation for 4 days for pulmonary contusion, and received intravenous cefuroxime for 48 hours then piperacillin-tazobactam for a presumed ventilator-associated chest infection. He has no chronic liver or renal disease, no diabetes, and no recent travel outside the region.

White blood cell count 16.5 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 182 mg/L. A wound swab Gram stain showed pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacillary organisms in heavy growth. Two sets of blood cultures were drawn and are pending.

CT of the lower leg demonstrates a fluid collection tracking along the external-fixator tract with cortical irregularity of the tibial diaphysis and periosteal reaction consistent with early contiguous osteomyelitis around the pin sites. There is no radiographic evidence of intrathoracic infection.

Definitive cultures from the wound and one blood culture grew an oxidase-negative, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative coccobacillus. Antimicrobial susceptibility showed resistance to cephalosporins, carbapenems, fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides, with retained susceptibility only to polymyxin and tigecycline. The same organism was recovered from the dressing trolley and ward sink at the referring hospital.

explanation: Nosocomial multidrug-resistant Gram-negative coccobacilli causing wound and bloodstream infection after trauma and ICU care, plus recovery from hospital surfaces, indicate a healthcare-associated environmental organism. The resistance profile and propensity to persist on dry surfaces support a diagnosis of Acinetobacter baumannii infection.

hints.text: A 54-year-old man presents to the cardiology clinic with nine months of progressive exertional dyspnoea and two episodes of syncope this month. He also reports orthopnea and reduced exercise tolerance; on examination his pulse is 42 beats per minute, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, jugular venous pressure is elevated, and there is a laterally displaced apex beat with bibasilar crackles.

He has no history of hypertension or diabetes and denies prior myocardial infarction. Three years ago he received a permanent pacemaker for complete atrioventricular block, and over the last two years he has developed progressive dysphagia to solids with nocturnal regurgitation and weight loss of 4 kg.

Full blood count normal with white cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L and haemoglobin 132 g/L. BNP is 910 ng/L, high-sensitivity troponin is within reference range, and serology returned strongly positive for parasite-specific IgG by two independent assays; blood PCR intermittently detected parasite DNA.

Transthoracic echocardiography shows a markedly dilated left ventricle, left ventricular ejection fraction 28%, and a thin-walled apical aneurysmal segment with an attached mural thrombus. Chest radiograph confirms cardiomegaly and ECG (prior to pacemaker) demonstrated complete heart block and right bundle-branch conduction delay.

He was born and raised in a rural highland community in Bolivia and lived in a mud-adobe house with cracked walls and thatch roofing until emigrating 24 years ago. As a child he recalled frequent nocturnal insect bites to the face and several older relatives died of progressive heart failure in middle age.

explanation: Chronic infection with Trypanosoma cruzi explains the combination of non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy with a classic left ventricular apical aneurysm, conduction system disease requiring a pacemaker, chronic oesophageal dysphagia from enteric nervous system damage, and positive parasite serology/PCR in a patient from rural Bolivia. Ischaemic disease is less likely given the clinical history and lack of coronary risk factors. The exposure history and family clustering support chronic acquisition in childhood.

hints.text: A 46-year-old man presented to the ambulatory clinic with a 6-week history of progressive left submandibular swelling and intermittent purulent drainage. The mass is firm, mildly tender, and has produced two small cutaneous sinuses over the past 2 weeks; he reports difficulty opening his mouth and has lost 3 kg since symptoms began.

His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes with recent HbA1c 8.2% and a 20 pack-year smoking history. He had a short 5-day course of oral cephalexin prescribed by his general practitioner without improvement, takes no immunosuppressive medication, and denies recent travel or animal bites.

Blood tests showed WBC 12.6 × 10^9/L and CRP 48 mg/L, random plasma glucose 12.1 mmol/L. An aspirate from one sinus was sent for culture; aerobic swab grew mixed oral streptococci, Gram stain of the purulent fluid demonstrated many neutrophils and no acid-fast bacilli, and routine aerobic cultures remained sterile at 48 hours.

Contrast CT of the neck demonstrated a multiloculated low-density collection in the left submandibular and submental spaces that tracked across fascial planes with multiple cutaneous sinus tracts and focal cortical erosion of the adjacent mandible.

On return visit the sinuses discharged thick yellowish granular material; the patient then recalled a difficult lower molar extraction about 10 weeks before symptom onset. The granules were submitted for anaerobic culture and after prolonged incubation yielded a slow-growing filamentous gram-positive anaerobe with susceptibility to penicillin.

explanation: A chronic, slowly progressive cervicofacial mass that crosses fascial planes and produces cutaneous sinuses after recent dental manipulation suggests infection by an oral anaerobic filamentous organism. The presence of yellow granular discharge and isolation of a slow-growing filamentous gram-positive anaerobe sensitive to penicillin supports that diagnosis in this patient.

hints.text: A 49-year-old man presents to clinic with a 6-week history of progressive fatigue and reduced urine output following a kidney transplant. He reports one episode of visible haematuria, has lost appetite, and on examination his blood pressure is 150/92 mmHg with mild tenderness over the right iliac fossa at the transplant site.

End-stage kidney disease from hypertensive nephrosclerosis. He received a deceased-donor renal transplant 9 months ago and is on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone. He had a steroid-treated acute cellular rejection episode 3 months ago but no recent urinary tract instrumentation.

Serum creatinine has risen from a baseline of 90 µmol/L to 210 µmol/L. Urinalysis shows 15–20 RBC/HPF and 10–15 WBC/HPF with negative routine bacterial culture. Tacrolimus trough is within target range.

Doppler ultrasound of the graft shows preserved arterial flow and no hydronephrosis. There is no perinephric fluid collection and kidney size is slightly reduced compared with immediate post-transplant imaging.

Quantitative plasma viral DNA assay reports 6.4 × 10^4 copies/mL. Urine cytology shows epithelial cells with large basophilic intranuclear inclusions and renal allograft biopsy demonstrates tubulointerstitial nephritis with viral inclusion-positive nuclei on SV40 immunostain.

explanation: Reactivation of a polyomavirus that targets renal tubular epithelium explains rising creatinine, sterile pyuria, haematuria and positive urine cytology after transplant. High plasma viral DNA and SV40 positive inclusions on graft biopsy confirm the diagnosis of BK virus nephropathy, which is managed primarily by reducing immunosuppression.

hints.text: A 47-year-old man presented to the emergency department with three weeks of low-grade fevers, progressive fatigue, and exertional dyspnea. He reported a 5 kg weight loss and night sweats; on examination temperature was 38.1°C, he had pallor, a new early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border and a palpable spleen 2 cm below the costal margin.

He has a history of alcohol dependence and has been sleeping intermittently in crowded shelters and rough sleeping over the past six months. He denied intravenous drug use and had no prosthetic cardiac material; he had poor dentition but no recent dental procedures and a rapid HIV test on admission was negative.

Haematology and inflammatory markers showed haemoglobin 86 g/L, white cell count 8.6 × 10^9/L, platelets 160 × 10^9/L, CRP 98 mg/L and ESR 68 mm/h. Three separate sets of routine aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures incubated for five days remained negative.

Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 12 mm mobile vegetation on the aortic valve with cusp perforation and moderate to severe regurgitation, prompting urgent surgery. Contrast CT of the abdomen showed two small wedge-shaped splenic infarcts consistent with embolic phenomena.

Social work inspection of his belongings documented numerous body lice on clothing and recent lice bites; he had months of incomplete access to laundry and showers. Microbiology of the excised valve tissue returned PCR positivity for DNA from a fastidious intracellular gram-negative bacillus known to be transmitted by body lice.

explanation: The combination of subacute culture-negative endocarditis with valve destruction, embolic splenic infarcts, chronic anaemia, prolonged exposure to body lice and PCR confirmation from valve tissue is most consistent with infection by Bartonella quintana. Routine blood cultures are often negative and diagnosis frequently requires molecular testing of tissue in this epidemiological context.

hints.text: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 36 hours of fever, progressive lethargy, and increasing breathlessness. He reported fever and rigors followed by confusion and reduced urine output earlier that morning, on arrival he was febrile at 38.9°C, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Examination showed cool, slightly mottled distal extremities and a 2 cm tender, erythematous area with a dark crust on the dorsal left forearm.

Medical history included type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and long-standing heavy alcohol use without known cirrhosis; he had no prior splenectomy and no recent hospital admissions. He was independent at baseline and works outdoors; he denied recent travel, dental procedures, or intravenous drug use.

Initial blood tests showed WBC 3.4 × 10^9/L, platelet count 35 × 10^9/L, creatinine 210 μmol/L, lactate 5.6 mmol/L and INR 2.1. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive at about 48 hours; Gram stain demonstrated slender fusiform Gram-negative rods and growth on blood agar was slow and required enriched media.

Ultrasound of the left forearm demonstrated diffuse subcutaneous thickening and hyperaemia consistent with cellulitis but no discrete abscess. Chest radiograph showed no focal lobar consolidation and transthoracic echocardiography revealed no valvular vegetations.

On focused questioning the patient recalled being bitten on the left forearm by a neighbour's dog two days before symptom onset; the bite broke the skin but he cleaned it at home and did not seek medical attention.

explanation: Severe sepsis with rapid onset after a dog bite, thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy, and growth of a slow-growing, fusiform Gram-negative rod from blood cultures point to the organism that commonly follows canine bites. The combination of alcohol use and fulminant bacteremia supports that diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to primary care with 3 months of progressive fatigue and intermittent crampy abdominal discomfort. She reports loose stools two to three times weekly and has lost 3 kg since symptoms began. On examination she is pale with conjunctival pallor and heart rate 98/min. Neurological exam is normal and there is no jaundice.

She is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications, and has no history of gastrointestinal surgery. She does not drink alcohol regularly and is not on strict vegetarian diet. She travelled to northern Europe for two weeks about five months ago for a family event but did not volunteer dietary details at that time.

Haemoglobin 82 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 108 fL, white blood cell count 5.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 280 × 10^9/L. Peripheral smear shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum cobalamin 90 pmol/L, folate normal, intrinsic factor antibody negative, methylmalonic acid reported as elevated.

Abdominal ultrasound performed for persistent abdominal symptoms shows a long, curvilinear, mobile echogenic structure within the lumen of the proximal small intestine, without bowel wall thickening or free fluid.

On directed re-questioning she recalls eating raw marinated freshwater fish at a lakeside festival during the northern Europe trip. She also reports noticing a single long, pale, ribbon-like segment in a stool sample about six weeks ago.

explanation: Macrocytic anaemia with low serum cobalamin and elevated methylmalonic acid indicates true B12 deficiency. Imaging demonstrating a long intraluminal mobile linear structure plus history of ingesting raw freshwater fish and passage of a ribbon-like stool segment points to an adult intestinal platyhelminth that consumes cobalamin. These findings most strongly support Diphyllobothrium latum infection rather than dietary deficiency or autoimmune pernicious anaemia.

hints.text: A 38-year-old male livestock farmer presented to the regional hospital with 4 days of high fever, severe myalgia and diffuse abdominal pain. He reported progressive lethargy and two episodes of dark vomitus; on arrival he was febrile 39.4°C, tachycardic 112 bpm, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, and mildly confused but cooperative.

He is previously well with no chronic illness and takes no regular medication. Over the prior two weeks he had been tending a small flock of sheep, several of which recently aborted; he had not travelled outside the province and had no recent hospital admissions until this illness.

Initial blood tests showed leukopenia 2.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 19 × 10^9/L, hemoglobin 110 g/L, AST 1 200 U/L and ALT 850 U/L. Coagulation was abnormal with INR 2.1, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L and D-dimer 8.0 mg/L FEU. Blood film and malaria rapid test were negative.
Focused abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly with a liver span of 17 cm and a moderate volume of free intraperitoneal fluid without focal collection. Chest radiograph was unremarkable.

On further questioning he recalled removing an attached tick from his forearm three days before his fever began and had assisted in slaughtering one of the aborting ewes five days before symptoms. A ward nurse who cared for him later developed fever and conjunctival injection. Real-time RT-PCR on serum returned positive for a high-consequence segmented negative-sense RNA virus known to circulate in parts of Africa, the Balkans, the Middle East and Central and South Asia.

explanation: The patient has an acute febrile illness progressing to marked thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and coagulopathy with capillary leak. Recent tick exposure and handling of viremic livestock in an endemic region, secondary illness in a healthcare worker, and a positive RT-PCR for a segmented negative-sense RNA virus together point to a tick-borne viral haemorrhagic fever as the most likely diagnosis in this case.

hints.text: A 38-year-old woman presents to the hepatology clinic with six months of intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort and progressive pruritus. Symptoms worsen after meals and she reports increasing fatigue and two episodes of pale, clay-coloured stools; on examination she is afebrile, jaundiced with scleral icterus, and has a palpable liver edge 3 cm below the right costal margin.

She has no prior hepatobiliary surgery and no known chronic liver disease. Over the past five years she has had several shorter episodes of right upper quadrant pain that were treated empirically with short courses of antibiotics and improved, but the current symptoms have been more persistent.

Complete blood count shows WBC 10.6 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.72 × 10^9/L. Liver tests show a cholestatic pattern: alkaline phosphatase 420 U/L, GGT 360 U/L, total bilirubin 42 μmol/L, ALT 68 U/L. Concentration stool microscopy demonstrates numerous small ovoid operculated eggs measuring about 28 μm in length.

Transabdominal ultrasound reveals diffuse dilation of intrahepatic bile ducts with relative sparing of the common bile duct and no gallstones. MR cholangiopancreatography confirms peripheral intrahepatic biliary dilatation with mild periductal thickening and no obstructing calculus or mass.

On focused dietary history she reports a lifelong habit of eating thinly sliced raw freshwater fish at family gatherings in her home region, with servings several times per month until recently; the fish was never frozen before consumption and was sourced from local rivers.

explanation: Cholestatic liver tests, peripheral eosinophilia, imaging showing intrahepatic bile duct dilation, and finding of operculated eggs in stool point to a trematode infecting the biliary tree. The history of frequent ingestion of raw freshwater fish from an endemic area supports the diagnosis of Clonorchis sinensis causing chronic biliary infection.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents 4 days after a hand injury with increasing pain, swelling, and reduced flexion of the right little finger. Temperature 38.2°C. Exam shows a 1-cm dorsal puncture wound over the fifth MCP, surrounding erythema, and tenderness along the extensor sheath.
He smokes 15 cigarettes daily and reports chronic gum bleeding and multiple untreated dental caries. No diabetes, no immunosuppressive therapy, and no recent animal bites or intravenous drug use.

WBC 12.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 82 mg/L. Purulent aspiration sent for culture grew small, slow-forming colonies after 48 h that produced agar pitting. Isolates were susceptible to ampicillin-sulbactam and resistant to clindamycin.

Contrast CT of the hand shows fluid collection 1.2 cm adjacent to the fifth MCP with extension into the extensor tendon sheath and surrounding soft tissue edema. No cortical bone destruction identified.

On re-questioning he admits he punched another person's mouth during a bar fight and felt a tooth penetrate his knuckle. The timeline, inoculation by a human tooth, and culture pattern suggest an oral-saliva source.

explanation: A penetrating clenched-fist tooth injury with progressive deep hand space infection focuses the differential on organisms from human saliva.

hints.text: A 29-year-old amateur runner presents with a 5-month history of an intensely pruritic rash in his groin and progressive thickening of the right great toenail. He reports difficulty wearing tight shorts and intermittent maceration between the toes; examination shows well-demarcated erythematous scaly plaques along both inguinal folds and a yellow, crumbly onycholytic right hallux nail.

Symptoms began after a minor rash that his primary care clinician treated with a mid-potency topical corticosteroid, which produced temporary palliation followed by spread toward the medial thigh. He has no diabetes, takes no immunosuppressants, and has been in good general health; he has tried over-the-counter topical antifungal cream intermittently without sustained benefit.
Potassium hydroxide preparations of skin scrapings and nail clippings reveal abundant septate, branching hyphae. Routine fungal culture was set up from both skin and nail specimens.

Plain radiograph of the distal phalanx shows no bony erosion or periosteal reaction. High-frequency ultrasound of the nail unit demonstrates subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis with a thickened nail plate but no evidence of deep soft-tissue extension.

Environmental swabs of the patient’s athletic socks and a foam gym mat grew the same filamentous fungus seen on culture. Microscopy of the culture showed abundant smooth-walled, club-shaped multicelled macroconidia and a notable absence of small single-celled microconidia.

explanation: The combined presentation of chronic groin and interdigital involvement with onychomycosis suggests a dermatophyte infection. Culture morphology showing numerous smooth, club-shaped multicelled macroconidia without microconidia identifies Epidermophyton floccosum. The clinical distribution and environmental recovery from clothing and mats support the diagnosis in this patient.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with a 5-day history of increased vaginal discharge and a mild low pelvic ache. She is afebrile, ambulatory, and on speculum examination there is a thin, pale discharge coating the vaginal walls; the cervix appears normal and there is no cervical motion tenderness.

She completed a 7-day course of oral amoxicillin for sinusitis two weeks ago and reports occasional vaginal douching. She is not pregnant, uses condoms inconsistently with a single recent new partner, and has no history of recurrent yeast infections.

Vaginal pH is 5.2. Wet mount microscopy shows many vaginal epithelial cells with numerous small bacteria adherent to their surfaces and only a scant number of neutrophils. A saline preparation shows no motile protozoa and a potassium hydroxide test later becomes notably odorous.

Transvaginal ultrasound performed because of persistent discomfort shows normal uterine and adnexal anatomy with no fluid collections to suggest abscess. There is no sonographic evidence of pelvic inflammatory disease.
The patient was treated with a standard 7-day course of oral nitroimidazole and reported marked symptomatic improvement within 48 hours with restoration of normal-appearing discharge by one week.

explanation: The combination of thin malodorous discharge, elevated vaginal pH, epithelial cells coated with small bacteria on wet mount and clinical response to nitroimidazole is most consistent with overgrowth of an anaerobic coccobacillary vaginal organism causing bacterial vaginosis. The responsible organism in this clinical context is Gardnerella vaginalis.

hints.text: A 22-year-old previously well university student presents to the emergency department with 6 days of sore throat followed by 48 hours of pleuritic chest pain and increasing breathlessness. He is febrile at 39.0°C, heart rate 118 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, and reports new left-sided neck discomfort that limits rotation of his head.

He says the throat pain began after a weekend away and was initially treated at home with ibuprofen. On day 3 he saw a primary care clinician and received a 5-day course of oral amoxicillin with only brief symptomatic improvement; there is no intravenous drug use, no recent dental extraction, and no chronic illness.

Admission blood tests show white cell count 18 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 210 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive in the anaerobic bottles at 48 hours and Gram stain showed pleomorphic Gram-negative bacilli.

Contrast CT pulmonary angiography demonstrates multiple bilateral peripheral nodules, several with central cavitation, consistent with septic emboli. Contrast CT of the neck shows a filling defect in the left internal jugular vein consistent with an acute thrombosis.

Thrombus aspirate and repeated blood cultures grew a non-spore-forming obligate anaerobic pleomorphic Gram-negative bacillus that was also recovered from a tonsillar swab, linking the bloodstream infection to the oropharynx; the isolate was indole positive and susceptible to metronidazole in vitro.

explanation: Young adult with antecedent pharyngitis who developed internal jugular vein thrombosis and septic pulmonary emboli, together with isolation of an obligate anaerobic pleomorphic Gram-negative bacillus from blood and thrombus, points to Fusobacterium necrophorum. The clinical course and in vitro metronidazole susceptibility support that organism as the cause of this septic thrombophlebitis originating from the oropharynx.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents with 10 days of progressive jaundice, dark urine, anorexia and right upper-quadrant discomfort. He is afebrile, heart rate 96/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg; examination shows scleral icterus, tender hepatomegaly 3 cm below the costal margin and reduced grip strength from fatigue.

He has lived in the same city for 2 years after emigrating from a country in the eastern Mediterranean. Eight years ago he was told he was a long-term carrier of a surface-antigen–positive viral hepatitis after a transfusion; he had mild, stable transaminase elevations and no prior antiviral therapy.

Serum ALT 2 600 U/L, AST 1 900 U/L, total bilirubin 180 μmol/L, INR 2.0, platelets 130 × 10^9/L. Routine serology confirms persistent serum surface antigen positivity from the chronic carrier state. PCR on serum detects high-level RNA of a small circular, single-stranded negative-sense RNA virus.

Abdominal ultrasound shows an enlarged liver with coarse echotexture and no biliary dilatation or focal lesion. Previous ultrasound two years ago documented only mild hepatic coarseness without portal hypertension features.

On reinterview he reports recent unprotected sex and a single episode of shared-needle use while travelling back to his country of origin 8 weeks before symptom onset. The clinical picture is consistent with superinfection of his chronic surface-antigen–positive hepatitis by a defective RNA virus transmitted parenterally that requires the helper virus surface antigen to assemble.

explanation: Acute severe hepatitis on a background of a chronic surface-antigen–positive carrier state with detection of a small circular negative-sense RNA in serum indicates infection by a defective hepatitis agent that depends on the helper virus surface antigen. The clinical course, high transaminases, coagulopathy and recent parenteral exposure make superinfection the likely cause of this decompensation.

hints.text: A 39-year-old park ranger presents with 6 days of fever and malaise. He has a painful ulcer on the left forearm and a firm tender left axillary lymph node, temperature 38.9°C.
Previously healthy, no immunosuppression. Symptoms began after he sustained a small forearm abrasion while working outdoors; no recent travel or cat contact.
Leucocytosis 14.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 128 mg/L. Blood cultures sterile at 48 hours. Gram stain of node aspirate shows faint, pleomorphic coccobacilli.
CT of the left axilla shows a 3.0 cm necrotic lymph node with surrounding soft-tissue oedema and no discrete drainable fluid collection.
One week before onset he skinned a wild rabbit he found injured, handling it with the same forearm that had the abrasion.

explanation: An ulcer at an inoculation site with regional necrotic adenopathy, faint Gram-variable coccobacilli on aspirate, sterile routine blood cultures and recent rabbit handling point to tularemia caused by Francisella tularensis.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to a primary care clinic with a 6-month history of progressive fatigue and exertional breathlessness. She also reports intermittent crampy abdominal discomfort and a three-week history of a dry, nonproductive cough; on examination she is pale, pulse 110 min⁻¹, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, and there is mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without organomegaly.

She emigrated from a rural district of northern India 4 months ago and has no chronic medical conditions. Menstrual periods are regular and not heavy, she is vegetarian, she briefly took oral iron prescribed by a community clinic but noted little improvement, and she has no history of peptic ulcer disease or recent NSAID use.

Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 72 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 68 fL, white cell count 8.6 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.3 × 10^9/L (15%); ferritin 9 μg/L and transferrin saturation 6%. A faecal occult blood test is positive and peripheral smear shows microcytic, hypochromic red cells.

Chest radiograph obtained for cough shows a small, patchy peripheral infiltrate in the left lower zone with no consolidation elsewhere; a repeat film two weeks later shows partial clearing and a new small peripheral opacity in the right mid zone.

On further questioning she describes working barefoot in flooded rice paddies until her recent migration and recalls frequent pruritic papules on the dorsum of her feet after field work; household sanitation in her home village relied on open defecation and night soil was used on market vegetables that she often ate raw.

explanation: Chronic iron-deficiency anaemia with eosinophilia, migrating pulmonary infiltrates and a history of barefoot exposure in an Old World rural setting support infection by a soil-transmitted blood-feeding nematode acquired through skin contact or contaminated produce. The combination of substantial blood loss, pruritic percutaneous exposure and origin in northern India makes Ancylostoma duodenale the most likely pathogen in this case.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presents to neurology with eight months of progressive stiffness and weakness in both legs, worsening gait and frequent falls. She reports urinary urgency and occasional constipation. On examination she has spastic paraparesis with 3/5 hip flexor strength, increased tone in both lower limbs, brisk deep tendon reflexes, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Cranial nerve and upper limb exams are normal. Temperature and other vital signs are within normal limits.

Symptoms began insidiously and progressed despite a two-week course of high-dose oral corticosteroids prescribed by a general practitioner for presumed inflammatory myelopathy. She recalls a chronic, itchy, scaly rash across the torso for about two years that she attributed to 'eczema'. Past medical history is notable only for treated hypertension. She has no known family history of neurologic disease.

Cerebrospinal fluid shows 24 × 10^6/L mononuclear cells, protein 1.1 g/L, and glucose 3.5 mmol/L. Oligoclonal bands are absent. HIV testing is negative, vitamin B12 and thyroid function are within reference ranges. Routine blood counts and chemistry are unremarkable.

MRI of the spine demonstrates segmental atrophy of the thoracic spinal cord, greatest in the mid-thoracic region, without focal compressive lesion or contrast-enhancing plaque. Brain MRI shows a few small non-specific white matter foci but no periventricular demyelinating lesions typical of multiple sclerosis.

The patient was born and breastfed in Jamaica and emigrated in her twenties. Serum and CSF testing returned reactive antibodies to a human T-cell tropic retrovirus endemic to some Caribbean regions, with confirmatory serology performed on both compartments.

explanation: Progressive spastic paraparesis with thoracic cord atrophy, CSF lymphocytic inflammation, absence of oligoclonal bands, chronic rash, and reactive serum and CSF antibodies to a T-cell tropic retrovirus in a person from a high-prevalence area point to a virus-associated chronic myelopathy. These findings favour infection-related myelopathy over multiple sclerosis or compressive causes and are diagnostic when supported by positive serology in both serum and CSF.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously healthy man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of fever, myalgia and progressive shortness of breath that began acutely the previous evening. On arrival he is febrile 38.9°C, tachypnoeic at 28/min, tachycardic 110/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation 88% on room air; chest examination reveals diffuse inspiratory crackles and he is short of breath at rest.

He describes a 3-day prodrome of nausea and intermittent abdominal pain before the respiratory symptoms started, and reports no chronic medical conditions or regular medications. Twelve days before presentation he spent a long weekend renovating an unoccupied lakeside hunting lodge, doing a day of heavy dry-sweeping and clearing insulation, but he has not travelled overseas and has no known sick contacts.

Blood tests show leucocytosis 17.0 × 10^9/L, haemoconcentration with haematocrit 0.56 L/L, thrombocytopenia 58 × 10^9/L, serum creatinine 110 μmol/L and C-reactive protein 120 mg/L. Lactate is 3.4 mmol/L and arterial blood gas on room air shows PaO2 8.0 kPa (consistent with hypoxaemia).

Chest radiograph shows bilateral interstitial and patchy alveolar opacities; CT pulmonary angiography excludes embolus and demonstrates diffuse bilateral ground-glass change with small bilateral pleural effusions. Transthoracic echocardiography shows normal left ventricular systolic function and no volume-overload cardiomyopathy.

On further questioning he acknowledges that while clearing the lodge he swept out two small storage rooms that contained numerous dried rodent droppings and nests within the insulation, producing heavy dust exposure and aerosolisation of material approximately 12 days before symptom onset.

explanation: The combination of a febrile prodrome followed by rapid development of noncardiogenic pulmonary oedema, haemoconcentration with marked thrombocytopenia, and normal cardiac function points to a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome. The recent history of heavy dust exposure while cleaning a rodent-infested lodge 1 to 3 weeks before illness provides the likely route and incubation consistent with this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented with a three-week history of progressive right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Symptoms began with clumsiness of his right hand and evolved to difficulty ambulating, he denies fever or headache. On examination he is afebrile, alert and oriented, with right facial weakness and right upper and lower limb weakness graded 4/5, and a right pronator drift.

He has a 10-year history of relapsing neurological episodes diagnosed as multiple sclerosis and has been receiving outpatient disease-modifying therapy for the past 18 months. No recent systemic infections, no known HIV, and no recent corticosteroid pulses within the prior three months.

Blood work shows lymphopenia with lymphocytes 0.6 × 10^9/L and otherwise normal full blood count and biochemistry. Lumbar puncture: opening pressure normal, CSF white cells 3 × 10^6/L (predominantly lymphocytes), protein 0.9 g/L, glucose normal, Gram stain and bacterial culture negative, oligoclonal bands absent.

MRI brain shows multiple asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the left frontal and parietal subcortical white matter, lesions are non-enhancing after gadolinium and show minimal mass effect. Compared with an MRI from six months earlier the lesions are new and confluent rather than ovoid and periventricular.

On further questioning the patient reports regular infusions of a monoclonal antibody therapy for his disease, started 18 months ago with the last infusion three weeks before symptom onset. CSF nucleic acid testing returned positive for the viral DNA most commonly linked to progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, viral load 1.2 × 10^5 copies/mL.

explanation: Subacute focal neurological deficits in an immunomodulated patient with asymmetric, non-enhancing white matter lesions and a CSF viral DNA signal indicate progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The clinical context and positive CSF nucleic acid test identify JC virus as the causative agent.

hints.text: A 14-year-old previously well girl presents to the school health clinic with 36 hours of abrupt onset fever, prominent myalgias, sore throat and dry cough. She is febrile at 39.4°C, pulse 110 beats/min, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, and reports profound fatigue that prevented her attending classes today.

Her younger brother developed a similar febrile respiratory illness two days before her symptoms began. She has mild persistent asthma treated with low-dose inhaled corticosteroid, did not receive the seasonal respiratory vaccine this year, and has had no travel or animal exposures.

Complete blood count shows leukocytes 3.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 1.9 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 0.8 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 15 mg/L. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for multiplex respiratory PCR.
Frontal chest radiograph shows no focal lobar consolidation and only mild peribronchial cuffing. Lung auscultation is at her usual baseline with no new wheeze.

Oral neuraminidase inhibitor was started within 36 hours of symptom onset, she defervesced within 24 hours and myalgias improved markedly by 48 hours. The multiplex PCR later returned positive for a segmented negative-sense RNA respiratory virus encoding haemagglutinin and neuraminidase, with subtyping negative for the A-specific target and positive for the human non-A seasonal lineage.

explanation: Abrupt high fever, severe myalgia, leukopenia and rapid onset in a school cluster point to a seasonal influenza illness. Prompt clinical response to a neuraminidase inhibitor and PCR demonstrating a segmented negative-sense RNA virus with HA and NA genes and a non-A human lineage confirms Influenza B virus infection in this patient.

hints.text: A 32-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation presented to the maternity unit with five days of progressive jaundice, anorexia, nausea and right upper-quadrant pain. She had fever to 38.2°C on arrival, icteric sclerae, tender hepatomegaly on palpation and reported reduced fetal movements over the preceding 12 hours.

She had been healthy before pregnancy, no known chronic liver disease, took only prenatal vitamins and iron, and denied alcohol or unprescribed medication use. Antenatal course had been unremarkable with normal blood pressure and urine tests at previous visits; she reported no recent blood transfusion or sexual exposure of concern.

Serum testing showed ALT 1 430 U/L, AST 1 110 U/L, total bilirubin 85 µmol/L, albumin 28 g/L and INR 1.9. Platelets were 190 × 10^9/L and white cell count 10.1 × 10^9/L. Routine viral serologies and molecular tests had been sent but results were pending.

Right upper-quadrant ultrasound demonstrated a mildly enlarged liver (craniocaudal span 17 cm) with homogeneous echotexture and no biliary ductal dilation or gallstones. Doppler flow in the portal and hepatic veins was normal and the fetal scan showed preserved biometry and fetal heart activity.

On directed questioning she reported spending three weeks visiting relatives in a rural region of South Asia six weeks earlier, where she drank unfiltered well and river water and used local street vendors for meals. Several contacts in the village had developed acute jaundice during the recent rainy season.

explanation: This pregnant patient has acute icteric hepatitis with marked transaminase elevation and coagulopathy, normal platelet count, and no biliary obstruction. Recent travel with consumption of untreated water in an endemic region and a small community outbreak point to an enterically transmitted, single-stranded RNA hepatitis virus that carries increased risk of severe maternal disease in late pregnancy.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to a regional hospital with 9 days of fever, progressive malaise, and diffuse muscle aches. He now reports sore throat with odynophagia and two days of vomiting that left him unable to eat; on arrival he is febrile at 39.1 °C and hypotensive with blood pressure 88/56 mmHg.

He is previously healthy with no chronic illnesses and is HIV negative. He had been treated as an outpatient first for presumed malaria with oral antimalarial therapy and then received a single dose of parenteral ceftriaxone before transfer, but his symptoms and weakness progressed over the week before admission.

CBC shows white blood cell count 2.1 × 10^9/L and platelet count 48 × 10^9/L. Chemistry reveals creatinine 210 μmol/L and urea 18 mmol/L. Liver tests show AST 640 U/L and ALT 220 U/L. Malaria thick film and rapid dengue antigen were negative. Coagulation testing shows INR 1.7 and aPTT prolonged. Urinalysis has 3+ protein and microscopic hematuria.

Chest radiograph shows small bilateral pleural effusions and patchy interstitial opacities at the lung bases. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates mild hepatomegaly and a small volume of ascites. No focal intracranial abnormality on non-contrast head CT performed after a transient episode of confusion.

On focused questioning the patient reports he returned 11 days before symptom onset from a three-week stay in a rural district of Sierra Leone where he slept in mud-brick houses with visible rodent droppings and ate locally stored grain. Two other household members had recent febrile illnesses, one died at home, and the national reference laboratory later reported a positive PCR for a West African rodent-borne viral haemorrhagic fever agent.

explanation: The combination of a 1–3 week incubation, recent rural West African travel with rodent exposure, progressive febrile illness with mucosal involvement, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, marked AST elevation, renal impairment and household clustering points to infection with Lassa virus. The reference laboratory PCR result for a rodent-borne viral haemorrhagic agent confirms the diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 49-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 days of fever, progressive bifrontal headache, photophobia, and new confusion. On arrival his temperature was 38.5°C, heart rate 102/min, Glasgow Coma Scale 14, and he had nuchal rigidity without focal limb weakness.

He received a deceased-donor kidney transplant 21 days earlier and is taking tacrolimus and mycophenolate. The early postoperative course was uncomplicated and he had no recent travel. Donor information at the time of transplant was limited to cause of death reported as intracerebral haemorrhage.

Lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 22 cm H2O, CSF white cell count 160 × 10^6/L with 90% lymphocytes, protein 1.2 g/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L with serum glucose 5.4 mmol/L. CSF PCRs were negative for herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus, enterovirus, cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus. Peripheral blood showed leukopenia 2.0 × 10^9/L and platelets 120 × 10^9/L, ALT 145 U/L.

Contrast MRI brain demonstrated diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and patchy T2 hyperintensity in both temporal lobes without frank diffusion restriction. Susceptibility-weighted images revealed multiple small punctate foci consistent with microhaemorrhages.

When donor records were reviewed the donor's family described keeping several wild house mice in cages at home for a personal project and an unexplained febrile illness in the donor the week before death. Metagenomic RNA sequencing from the donor serum and the recipient CSF returned identical viral RNA sequences that matched isolates obtained from those house mouse specimens, and the recipient developed a new serum IgM response to the same rodent-borne agent.

explanation: The combination of post-transplant lymphocytic meningoencephalitis, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with negative routine viral PCRs, MRI showing meningeal enhancement and microhaemorrhages, and identical viral RNA sequences traced to house mice in the donor points to Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus transmitted via the organ donor. The timeline and acute serologic conversion in the recipient support donor-derived infection rather than community acquisition.

hints.text: A 56-year-old man presents with three months of progressive right lower-leg swelling and painless skin nodules. He reports trouble walking more than a few hundred metres because of leg discomfort. On exam there are multiple 0.5–2.0 cm purple-brown papules and nodules over the anterior shin and moderate pitting oedema. Temperature 36.8°C.

Medical history notable for deceased-donor renal transplant 14 months ago for diabetic nephropathy. Current immunosuppression includes tacrolimus and prednisone. Graft function stable. Last HIV test one year ago was negative. No prior cutaneous lesions reported.

Born and raised in southern Italy, visits family there every 2 years; last visit six months ago. Retired construction foreman, no history of intravenous drug use. Sexual history is monogamous with wife. No recent new topical exposures or insect bites.

Doppler ultrasound of the leg shows no deep venous thrombosis. MRI of the lower leg demonstrates multiple subcutaneous enhancing nodules tracking along fascia without bone involvement. Contrast CT chest shows small bilateral peribronchovascular nodules and a tiny left pleural effusion.

Punch biopsy of a shin nodule reveals spindle-cell proliferation forming irregular vascular slits with extravasated erythrocytes. Immunohistochemistry is positive in lesional spindle cells for a latent viral nuclear antigen. PCR of the lesion detects viral DNA concordant with the virus that causes Kaposi sarcoma.

explanation: Progressive violaceous cutaneous nodules in an immunosuppressed transplant recipient from a Mediterranean region, with spindle-cell vascular histology and positive latent viral antigen, indicate Kaposi sarcoma caused by human herpesvirus 8. The combination of transplant immunosuppression, compatible imaging suggesting visceral involvement, and lesion PCR/IHC confirms the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 6 days of fever, dry cough and progressive dyspnoea. He was tachypnoeic at 28 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 89% on room air, temperature 38.6°C, and had bilateral inspiratory crackles; he reported marked functional decline and could not walk more than 20 metres without stopping.

He has type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease stage 3. Ten days before symptom onset he returned from a two-week business trip to the Arabian Peninsula during which he spent several hours visiting a relative admitted to a busy urban hospital emergency department.

Blood tests showed WBC 3.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.7 × 10^9/L, CRP 150 mg/L and creatinine 180 μmol/L (baseline 120 μmol/L). Blood cultures and routine sputum culture were sterile. Multiplex PCR for influenza A and B, RSV and a panel of common respiratory viruses was negative.

Chest CT demonstrated bilateral multilobar ground-glass change and patchy consolidation, greatest in the lower lobes, with small bilateral pleural effusions. There was no lobar cavitation and a CT pulmonary angiogram excluded pulmonary embolus.

A lower respiratory tract sample was positive by RT-PCR for a novel zoonotic single-stranded RNA respiratory virus first reported from the Arabian Peninsula and epidemiologically linked to dromedary camel contact and hospital clusters causing severe pneumonia often complicated by acute kidney injury.

explanation: Severe community-acquired pneumonia after travel to the Arabian Peninsula with nosocomial exposure, lymphopenia, rising creatinine and an RT-PCR positive lower respiratory sample for a novel zoonotic RNA respiratory virus points to Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus. His diabetes and chronic kidney disease increase risk for severe disease and renal complications, which fits this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presented to an infectious diseases clinic with four months of episodic migratory subcutaneous swellings and intermittent pruritus. The swellings arose on forearms and lower legs, each lasted hours to a few days, and at presentation a 3 cm mobile, mildly tender subcutaneous nodule was palpable over the right forearm; temperature 37.2°C and other vital signs were normal.

She had returned eight months earlier after living for three years in a rural part of central Africa where she worked on a cocoa plantation. She recalled numerous daytime insect bites while outdoors and had participated in a community anthelmintic campaign during her last year there, receiving a single oral dose of medication and developing a transient febrile reaction for 48 hours thereafter; she has no chronic medical problems and takes no immunosuppressive drugs.

Full blood count showed leukocytes 9.6 × 10^9/L with marked eosinophilia of 3.2 × 10^9/L and haemoglobin 128 g/L. Liver and renal function tests were within reference ranges and C-reactive protein was 6 mg/L.

High-frequency ultrasound of the forearm nodule identified a 2.5 cm tubular hypoechoic structure in the subcutaneous plane that displayed intermittent linear movement during real-time scanning. No abscess cavity or foreign-body artefact was present.

One week later she reported a distinct event: while gardening she felt a slender threadlike object cross the surface of her right eye and took a photograph that shows a translucent motile filament beneath the bulbar conjunctiva; she again noted that during her years on the plantation she had frequent daytime 'horse fly' bites.

explanation: Episodic migratory subcutaneous swellings with marked eosinophilia, a motile tubular structure on ultrasound, and a contemporaneous photograph of a translucent motile filament beneath the conjunctiva after daytime biting exposure in central Africa are most consistent with Loa loa infection. The history of a systemic reaction after a community anthelmintic dose raises concern for high microfilarial burden.

hints.text: A 34-year-old previously healthy male field biologist presented to a regional hospital on day 6 of illness with high fever, severe myalgia, profuse watery diarrhoea and repeated vomiting. On arrival he was febrile at 39.3°C, hypotensive with blood pressure 88/56 mmHg, tachycardic 112 beats per minute, markedly lethargic and producing only small volumes of dark urine despite oral rehydration attempts.

He reported onset of fever nine days after beginning a three-week work assignment in a remote river valley in Central Africa where he conducted wildlife surveys. He has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications, had self-treated with antimalarials and oral antibiotics prescribed at a village clinic without improvement, and there was no history of hospital procedures or transfusions before symptom onset.

Initial laboratory studies showed haemoglobin 112 g/L, white cell count 1.8 × 10^9/L, platelet count 38 × 10^9/L, creatinine 210 µmol/L, AST 1 340 U/L, ALT 630 U/L. Coagulation testing demonstrated INR 2.3 and fibrinogen 0.8 g/L. Thick and thin malaria films and routine bacterial blood cultures were negative.

Focused abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly, splenomegaly and a moderate amount of free intraperitoneal fluid. Chest radiograph showed small bilateral pleural effusions without lobar consolidation, consistent with a capillary leak physiology rather than primary bacterial pneumonia.

Further public-health interviewing revealed he entered a limestone cave containing a large colony of fruit bats about 12 days before his symptoms began and assisted staff at a local wildlife rescue where several recently imported monkeys had died from an undiagnosed febrile illness. Two colleagues who entered the same cave developed fevers shortly after his return.

explanation: Severe febrile gastroenteritis progressing to hypotension with marked thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, coagulopathy and capillary leak after travel to a bat- and primate-exposure setting is most consistent with infection by Marburg virus. The exposure history and negative bacterial and malaria tests support a viral haemorrhagic fever. diagnosis is confirmed by specific PCR or direct detection of the virus.

hints.text: A 10-month-old previously well infant presented to the emergency department after a first-time generalized tonic-clonic seizure that lasted approximately three minutes. The child had four days of high fever at home with a peak of 40.0°C, was drowsy but arousable on arrival, heart rate 150/min, capillary refill <2 s and no neck stiffness.

The infant attends a group day care. Parents report an older sibling had a brief febrile illness with a mild rash last week. There is no past history of seizures, no known immunodeficiency, vaccinations are up to date, and there has been no travel or sick animal exposures.

Blood tests showed WBC 7.8 × 10^9/L with relative lymphocytosis, CRP 6 mg/L, ALT and AST within reference range. Lumbar puncture yielded CSF with 5 × 10^6/L white cells, predominantly lymphocytes, protein 0.25 g/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L. A multiplex PCR of CSF detected a single viral DNA target with a CSF load of 2.3 × 10^5 copies/mL and a corresponding blood viral load of 1.8 × 10^6 copies/mL.

MRI brain performed the day after admission showed no focal diffusion restriction or haemorrhage and preserved signal in the medial temporal lobes and limbic structures. No meningeal enhancement was seen.

Fever resolved with supportive care by hospital day 5 and within 12–24 hours of defervescence the infant developed a blanching macular rash beginning on the trunk and spreading to the neck and proximal limbs. The rash faded over 48 hours without specific therapy and the child returned to baseline neurologic status.

explanation: The combination of a high fever in an infant complicated by febrile seizure, lymphocytic CSF with a high viral DNA load in blood and CSF, and the characteristic trunk-first blanching rash appearing after defervescence points to primary infection with Human herpesvirus 6. The age, transient rash after fever breaks, and association with febrile seizures support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 days of fever, severe myalgias concentrated in both calves, frontal headache, and progressive dark urine. He reported worsening fatigue and oliguria, had temperature 38.6°C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, and on examination had marked tenderness of the calf muscles and visible jaundice of the sclerae; he was ambulatory but noted difficulty climbing stairs because of the pain.

He was previously well, with no chronic liver or kidney disease and no regular medications. Symptoms began after a week of outdoor work during seasonal rains, with an interval of slight improvement on day 3 followed by recurrence of fever and new yellowing of the eyes on day 4. He denied recent travel abroad, transfusions, or risky sexual contacts, and had taken a short course of ibuprofen before coming in.

Laboratory tests showed white blood cell count 16.0 × 10^9/L, platelet count 95 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 125 µmol/L with predominantly conjugated fraction, AST 120 U/L, ALT 85 U/L, creatinine 320 µmol/L, and CRP 120 mg/L. Urinalysis demonstrated 2+ protein, microscopic haematuria and numerous granular casts. Blood cultures were pending and rapid malaria test was negative.

Chest radiograph demonstrated patchy bilateral air‑space opacities more pronounced at the bases without lobar consolidation. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatomegaly with normal biliary ducts and mildly enlarged kidneys with increased cortical echogenicity.

On targeted questioning the patient recalled wading barefoot through flooded rice paddies and village drains about 10 days before symptom onset, and he had several minor skin abrasions then. He also reported frequent rodent sightings around his house and recent heavy local flooding that contaminated fields and household courtyards.

explanation: The combination of acute febrile illness with severe calf myalgia, jaundice out of proportion to transaminases, acute kidney injury, pulmonary infiltrates and recent wading through contaminated floodwater with rodent exposure points to infection by Leptospira interrogans. The laboratory pattern and exposure history together make this diagnosis more likely than viral hepatitis, malaria, or common bacterial sepsis.

hints.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought to clinic with a 3-week history of a single enlarging itchy patch on the scalp. The lesion measures about 4 cm, is erythematous and scaly with focal crusting, and several hairs are broken close to the scalp; temperature is 36.8°C and there are no systemic symptoms.

He is otherwise well with no chronic illness and receives routine childhood vaccinations. Parents report they tried a topical antibacterial shampoo and a corticosteroid cream prescribed by a primary care clinician with no improvement; there has been increasing hair fragility and the child has begun to avoid combing the affected area.

Scalp scrapings examined with a potassium hydroxide preparation show branching septate hyphae within hair shafts. Fungal culture incubated at 25°C produced a fluffy, white colony with a pale yellow reverse and, after 7 days, numerous large, thick-walled multicellular spindle-shaped macroconidia were observed. Full blood count was normal with a white cell count 7.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein <5 mg/L.

Dermoscopy of the plaque reveals broken hairs and multiple 'black dot' stubs at follicular ostia with perifollicular scaling. Clinical photography documents an annular alopecic plaque with hair shafts fractured at the skin surface rather than intact hair loss.

Parents report they rescued a litter of stray kittens about 6 weeks before onset. One kitten had patchy scaly alopecia and was taken to a veterinarian; the child frequently cuddles and sleeps with the household cat.

explanation: This is tinea capitis in a child with broken hairs and perifollicular scaling. Culture morphology showing abundant large multicellular macroconidia indicates a Microsporum-type dermatophyte, and recent close contact with symptomatic kittens makes a zoonotic species from cats the most likely cause. Together these findings point to the pathogen most commonly transmitted from domestic cats and kittens.

hints.text: A 67-year-old man with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease presented with 4 days of increasing cough, purulent green sputum and worsening dyspnoea. He reported low-grade fever and new orthopnoea. On arrival temperature 38.1°C, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air. Examination showed diffuse expiratory wheeze and coarse crackles without focal bronchial breath sounds.

He has a 50 pack-year smoking history and moderate airflow obstruction with FEV1 45% predicted, maintained on inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting bronchodilator. Two weeks before presentation he had a self-limited viral upper respiratory illness. He received a short course of oral amoxicillin for sinusitis three months ago and has no recent hospital admissions or indwelling devices.

Blood tests showed WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 11.0 × 10^9/L and CRP 82 mg/L. Sputum was sent for microbiology and the Gram stain was initially reported as 'mixed flora'. Blood cultures were negative.

Chest radiograph demonstrated hyperinflation and peribronchial cuffing consistent with an exacerbation of chronic bronchitic change. There was no lobar consolidation or pleural effusion to suggest focal pneumonia.

He was started on oral amoxicillin for presumed bacterial exacerbation but remained febrile and dyspnoeic after 48 hours. Therapy was changed to oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and he had clear clinical improvement within 48 hours. Subsequent sputum culture grew an oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting, beta-lactamase producing gram-negative diplococcus.

explanation: An older smoker with COPD developed a bacterial bronchitic exacerbation. The clinical setting, lack of lobar consolidation and rapid response to amoxicillin-clavulanate support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of productive cough, pleuritic right-sided chest pain and low grade fevers, and a 4 kg weight loss. He became more short of breath over the last week and now tires when climbing a single flight of stairs. On arrival temperature was 38.1°C, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, and chest examination showed reduced breath sounds with coarse crackles at the right upper lung field.

He has been taking prednisone 15 mg daily for six months for polymyalgia rheumatica and had a brief course of oral prednisolone pulses earlier in the year. He is a former smoker, tends a small vegetable garden and reports occasionally inhaling dust while digging compost. He has no recent travel, no known tuberculosis contacts, and no history of HIV diagnosis.

Outpatient therapy with two different courses of oral beta-lactam antibiotics produced no clinical improvement, so he was admitted and given intravenous ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin for presumed complicated community-acquired pneumonia. After 72 hours of inpatient therapy his fever persisted and his cough worsened. Admission blood tests showed white cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 120 mg/L.

Contrast chest CT showed a 4.0 cm cavitary lesion with irregular thick wall in the right upper lobe and several smaller adjacent nodules. Brain MRI performed for new onset intermittent left hand weakness demonstrated a 1.5 cm ring enhancing lesion in the right precentral gyrus with surrounding vasogenic oedema.

Bronchoscopy with protected brush and subsequent culture grew slow forming chalky colonies after five days on blood agar. Direct microscopy of the colonies showed branching filamentous, gram-variable organisms that were weakly acid-fast on a modified stain. Blood cultures remained negative.

explanation: Subacute pulmonary illness in a patient on chronic corticosteroids with cavitation and simultaneous brain abscess points to a disseminating filamentous bacterial infection. The slow-growing chalky colonies and branching, weakly acid-fast filamentous organisms on modified stain are characteristic of an aerobic actinomycete that causes pulmonary disease with central nervous system spread in immunosuppressed hosts.

hints.text: A 67-year-old previously independent woman presented to the respiratory clinic with a 6-month history of productive cough, intermittent low-grade fevers and a 5 kg weight loss. She describes progressive exertional dyspnoea, now limited to walking 200 m, temperature 37.5°C, oxygen saturation 95% on room air and bibasilar crackles on chest auscultation.

She has a history of bronchiectasis diagnosed 18 months earlier after recurrent chest infections and has not received treatment for tuberculosis. She is HIV negative, not diabetic, a lifelong never-smoker, takes no systemic immunosuppressants and reports no recent travel or known tuberculosis contacts.

Three expectorated sputum specimens were sent for analysis; one smear showed acid-fast bacilli while a nucleic-acid-amplification test for tuberculosis was negative. Bloods showed WBC 8.6 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 129 g/L and CRP 18 mg/L.

High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrated multifocal cylindrical bronchiectasis with tree-in-bud nodularity and small nodular consolidations predominating in the right middle lobe and lingula, without large cavitation.

Liquid culture grew a slow-growing, non-pigmented acid-fast organism over 2–3 weeks; the team commenced azithromycin plus ethambutol and the patient experienced symptomatic improvement with sputum cultures converting to negative after four months.

explanation: Chronic nodular bronchiectatic disease in an older, slender woman with AFB-positive but TB NAAT-negative sputum, slow-growing environmental acid-fast growth and clinical response to a macrolide-ethambutol regimen is most consistent with pulmonary infection due to Mycobacterium avium complex.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously healthy man presented to a sexual health clinic with 5 days of fever, myalgia, and progressive painful lesions around the anus and proximal penis. He describes firm tender papules that have evolved into shallow painful ulcers; left inguinal node is 2 cm and tender. Temperature 38.2°C and he reports difficulty sitting because of local pain.

He reports receptive anal intercourse with a new partner during a multi-day international music festival 12 days before symptom onset. He has no chronic medical conditions, is not taking immunosuppressive therapy, and his last HIV test 18 months ago was negative.

PCR from a lesion swab was negative for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2. Syphilis serology was non-reactive. Full blood count showed WBC 6.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 3.4 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 2.0 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 14 mg/L.

Contrast CT pelvis performed because of severe rectal pain showed circumferential rectal wall thickening with mild perirectal fat stranding consistent with proctitis. There was no drainable abscess or gas-forming collection.

Two recent sexual contacts developed similar anogenital lesions after the same festival. National reference laboratory sequencing of lesion samples from those contacts matched a single strain responsible for recent international clusters of human-to-human transmission of an ulcerative anogenital viral infection; public health informed the patient his lesion sample was confirmed to contain that same virus.

explanation: Painful anogenital lesions with tender regional lymphadenopathy and proctitis after recent sexual contact, plus negative HSV and syphilis testing, point toward the outbreak-associated zoonotic viral infection presenting in sexual networks. Sequencing linking the patient to recent international clusters confirms infection with Mpox virus.

hints.text: A 42-year-old man presents to outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of progressive productive cough, low-grade fevers, drenching night sweats and an 8 kg weight loss. He also reports a slowly enlarging, painless ulcer on the right buccal mucosa for 3 weeks. He is a non-smoker, afebrile at evaluation, respiratory rate 18/min and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Examination shows multiple firm cervical lymph nodes to 2 cm and a 2.0 cm irregular oral mucosal ulcer with a granular base.

He was born and raised in a rural area of a Latin American country and now lives in a regional city where he works in construction but returns to his family's small coffee farm every few months. He has no known immunodeficiency, is not on long term corticosteroids or immunosuppressants, and reports no recent hospitalisations. There is no history of tuberculosis treatment and no significant alcohol use.

Blood tests show haemoglobin 110 g/L, white cell count 12.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, platelet count 320 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 48 mg/L. Three induced sputum samples are negative for acid-fast bacilli on smear and PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis is negative. HIV antibody test is negative.

Chest CT demonstrates bilateral, multifocal nodular infiltrates with several thin-walled cavitary lesions predominantly in the middle and lower lobes, and enlarged hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes up to 2.5 cm. No pleural effusion is present. Panoramic dental radiograph shows subtle loss of alveolar bone adjacent to the ulcerated buccal mucosa.

He recalls decades of childhood work turning soil on the family coffee plantation and reports occasional hunting of small mammals in nearby forest patches. Incisional biopsy of the buccal ulcer was performed; silver stain of the tissue shows multiple round yeasts with several narrow-based buds arranged around a central mother cell producing a mariner's wheel appearance.

explanation: Chronic pulmonary nodules with cavitation, mucocutaneous ulceration, rural agricultural soil exposure and biopsy demonstrating multiple budding yeasts in a mariner's wheel pattern are diagnostic of Paracoccidioides brasiliensis infection. The negative mycobacterial studies and absence of immunosuppression support a primary systemic dimorphic fungal infection mimicking tuberculosis or malignancy.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 36 hours of progressive pain and swelling of his right index finger and dorsal hand. He had fever to 38.6°C, heart rate 100/min, a tense erythematous swelling over the radial aspect of the hand extending from the base of the index finger to the wrist, and markedly reduced active flexion of the index finger.

He has type 2 diabetes mellitus with recent HbA1c 8.4% and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. His primary care physician started oral flucloxacillin 24 hours earlier for presumed cellulitis but symptoms progressed despite the antibiotic.

Blood tests showed white blood cell count 16.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 220 mg/L. Gram stain of purulent material obtained at bedside revealed small gram-negative coccobacillary organisms; blood cultures were drawn and a wound culture was sent.

Point-of-care ultrasound of the hand demonstrated a 15 mm anechoic collection tracking along the flexor tendon sheath of the index finger with surrounding hyperemia, findings consistent with pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis and a loculated hand-space abscess.

On further questioning the patient recalled being bitten on the hand by one of his indoor cats three days before presentation; operative specimens grew small, grey, rapidly appearing colonies on blood agar within 24 hours that were susceptible to penicillin and ampicillin.

explanation: Rapid-onset hand cellulitis with flexor tenosynovitis after a cat bite, wound Gram stain showing small gram-negative coccobacilli, and growth of rapidly appearing, penicillin-susceptible colonies point to Pasteurella multocida.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents to the respiratory clinic with a 3-month history of a persistent productive cough and two episodes of small-volume hemoptysis. She reports intermittent pleuritic left-sided chest pain and a 3 kg weight loss over that time, is afebrile on exam, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, and has coarse crackles localized to the left lower chest.

She was previously healthy, does not smoke, and is not taking immunosuppressive medications. Over the preceding 3 months she received two courses of oral antibiotics for presumed community-acquired pneumonia without clinical improvement, and a flexible bronchoscopy done three weeks ago showed inflamed mucosa with an eosinophil-rich bronchoalveolar lavage but no growth on routine bacterial or mycobacterial culture.

Complete blood count shows leukocytes 9.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.6 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein is 18 mg/L. Repeated sputum acid-fast bacilli smears and mycobacterial cultures are negative. Initial stool ova and parasite examinations were reported as negative.

High-resolution CT of the chest demonstrates a 3.0 cm thin-walled cavitary lesion in the posterior segment of the left lower lobe, adjacent patchy consolidation, a small left pleural effusion, and a subtle linear subpleural tract extending toward the pleura.

On reinterrogation she recalls eating a communal dish of raw freshwater crab at a family wedding in rural Southeast Asia four months before onset. A concentrated sputum specimen sent to the parasitology laboratory contained ovoid operculated eggs measuring approximately 80 µm, consistent with a trematode that migrates to the lung.

explanation: Chronic cough with episodic hemoptysis, peripheral eosinophilia, a peripheral cavitary subpleural lesion with a pleural tract, recent ingestion of raw freshwater crab in an endemic region, and operculated eggs in sputum together indicate pulmonary infection with Paragonimus westermani. The combination of epidemiology, imaging, eosinophilia, and demonstration of eggs in sputum establishes the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presented to clinic with a 3-month history of progressive left-sided neck swelling and intermittent seropurulent drainage. She reported low-grade fevers and a 5-kg weight loss; on examination there was a 4-cm firm, partly fluctuant mass in the left level II–III region with overlying erythema and a small sinus tract discharging purulent material.

Her past medical history included rheumatoid arthritis treated with methotrexate and low-dose prednisone for two years. She had no known contact with persons treated for pulmonary tuberculosis, no recent travel, and a negative HIV test performed one month earlier. Several courses of oral broad-spectrum antibiotics produced no durable improvement.

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 115 g/L, white cell count 9.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L and ESR 58 mm/h. Fine-needle aspirate of the node yielded purulent fluid; routine bacterial cultures were sterile, Ziehl-Neelsen staining showed rare acid-fast bacilli, and nucleic acid amplification for the tuberculosis complex was negative. Mycobacterial culture incubated on specific media became positive after several weeks.

Contrast CT of the neck demonstrated a multiloculated necrotic lymph node with peripheral enhancement and a small contiguous tract to the skin. A chest radiograph was normal without parenchymal lesions or cavitation.

After failed percutaneous drainage and empiric antibiotics, the node was surgically excised. Species-level testing by 16S rRNA and hsp65 sequencing matched a slow-growing scotochromogenic nontuberculous mycobacterial reference sequence most often recovered from cervicofacial lymphadenitis; in vitro testing showed susceptibility to a macrolide and to ethambutol and variable activity of rifamycins. The patient began tailored therapy after excision with clinical improvement over subsequent weeks.

explanation: The combination of chronic unilateral cervicofacial lymphadenitis with draining sinus, lack of response to standard.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with 6 months of intensely pruritic papular rash and several firm subcutaneous nodules on both forearms and upper chest. Over the past 6 weeks she has developed gradual, painless blurring of vision in the right eye. She is afebrile and a 3 cm mobile nodule is palpable over the left forearm.

She was born and continues to live in a riverside village in West Africa and works as a cassava farmer. She reports years of wading in fast-flowing stretches of the river. She has no history of mass antiparasitic treatment and is HIV negative by recent testing.

Full blood count: WBC 8.6 × 10^9/L, eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L. Skin snips taken from nodular sites placed in saline yielded thin motile microfilariae on light microscopy. Peripheral blood smear showed no malaria parasites.

Slit-lamp exam of the right eye demonstrates punctate corneal opacities and mild anterior chamber inflammation. Fundoscopy shows focal chorioretinal atrophy and early optic disc pallor in the affected eye. Orbital ultrasound excludes an intraocular mass.

She describes frequent bites from small black flies when wading the river. Excision of a forearm nodule revealed adult filarial worms on histology, and repeat skin snip PCR detected DNA from a riverine-transmitted filarial species. Single-dose oral ivermectin produced prompt loss of motile microfilariae on subsequent snips.

explanation: Chronic pruritic papular dermatitis with subcutaneous nodules, skin snip microfilariae, ocular inflammation with chorioretinal atrophy, and a history of riverine black fly exposure point to a riverine-transmitted filarial infection with adults in subcutaneous nodules. Rapid fall in skin microfilariae after ivermectin supports the filarial diagnosis. The combined clinical, parasitologic, histologic, and exposure findings localise the pathogen.

hints.text: A 32-year-old man residing in a city shelter presents with three weeks of severe generalized itching that is worse at night and has disrupted his sleep. Examination shows numerous excoriated erythematous papules concentrated over the upper torso, lower back, and lateral thighs, with multiple crusted erosions but relative sparing of the scalp and face. Temperature 37.9°C, heart rate 96/min, he reports progressive fatigue from poor sleep.

He has schizoaffective disorder and limited access to laundry. Over the past month he has been sharing bedding with several other shelter residents and reports wearing the same undershirts and cuffed trousers for many days because he could not find a laundromat. He denies recent international travel and has no household pets.

Laboratory tests show WBC 8.9 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.7 × 10^9/L and CRP 15 mg/L. Bacterial swab of an excoriated lesion grew Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to flucloxacillin. Skin scrapings examined for dermal mites were negative.

Dermatoscopic photograph of the affected skin shows a cluster of small erythematous papules each with a subtle central punctum and surrounding excoriation. A separate photograph of the inside lining of his jacket demonstrates multiple dark specks concentrated along seam lines, seen at low magnification as discrete focal points against the fabric.

Public health staff inspected the patient’s soiled undershirt and found numerous tiny wingless insects clinging to the inner seams and dozens of oval eggs firmly cemented to textile fibres around the waistband and collar. Several other shelter residents reported similar itching after sharing blankets.

explanation: The combination of intense pruritus with excoriated papules on the trunk and thighs, negative skin scrapings for dermal mites, and finding of small wingless blood-feeding insects and cemented oval eggs on clothing seams points to infestation of clothing rather than scalp or skin burrowing.
