These features are diagnostic for body louse infestation. Secondary bacterial colonisation explains the Staphylococcus aureus from excoriations.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presents with a 6-week history of non-bloody watery diarrhoea and a 7 kg weight loss. He reports up to eight loose stools per day including nocturnal episodes and progressive fatigue, and arrives with orthostatic symptoms; supine blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, standing 100/60 mmHg with pulse rising from 86 to 112/min. Abdominal examination shows mild, diffuse tenderness without peritonism and he is afebrile.

He received a deceased-donor kidney transplant 10 months ago and is maintained on tacrolimus and mycophenolate. He had biopsy-proven acute rejection treated with high-dose corticosteroids three months ago. He denies recent travel, no recent antibiotics, no known sick contacts, and an HIV test four months earlier was negative.

Three separate stool bacterial cultures and routine ova and parasite wet mounts were negative. Stool PCR panel for common enteric viruses was negative. Haemoglobin 110 g/L, white cell count 5.8 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L, serum creatinine 160 μmol/L at baseline. A concentrated stool specimen was forwarded for specialised staining and electron microscopy.

CT enterography shows mild, segmental jejunal wall thickening with a few small mesenteric lymph nodes. There is no colonic wall thickening, no free fluid, and no biliary dilatation. Flexible sigmoidoscopy performed in hospital showed grossly normal mucosa.

Modified trichrome stain of the concentrated stool reveals numerous 1.0–2.0 μm oval intracytoplasmic bodies that stain bright red and lie along the brush border of enterocytes. Transmission electron microscopy of stool demonstrates a thick-walled spore containing a coiled polar filament projecting from one end. These findings confirm infection by a small, obligate intracellular, spore-forming parasite.

explanation: An immunosuppressed renal transplant recipient with chronic watery diarrhoea, negative routine stool studies, and jejunal involvement suggests an opportunistic enteric pathogen. Identification of 1–2 μm intracytoplasmic spores on modified trichrome and a coiled polar filament on electron microscopy establishes intestinal microsporidiosis. The clinical picture and those specific microscopy findings make this the most likely diagnosis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to a sexual health clinic with a 6-week history of multiple small skin lesions on the pubic region and proximal inner thighs. He complained of mild pruritus but denied pain, fever, or systemic symptoms. On examination there were about 12 firm, flesh-coloured, dome-shaped papules measuring 2–5 mm clustered along the pubic hairline and upper scrotum. Temperature was 36.8°C and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

He reported a new sexual partner approximately 3 months earlier and occasional unprotected intercourse since then. He has no chronic medical problems, takes no regular medications, and denies topical steroid use. He had no known history of atopic dermatitis or previous genital warts.

Blood tests showed WBC 6.4 × 10^9/L, lymphocytes 1.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 3 mg/L. A point-of-care fourth-generation HIV test was negative. Nucleic acid amplification tests for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae from a urethral swab were negative.

Dermoscopy of a representative papule demonstrated a central pale amorphous core with multiple tiny peripheral vessels forming a crown-like pattern and absence of surface scales. The lesion did not show pigment network or arborizing vessels.

After gentle curettage a curd-like white core was extruded from several lesions. Light microscopy of the expressed material stained with standard cytologic stain revealed large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies within keratinocytes.

explanation: The combination of clustered dome-shaped papules in the pubic region after new sexual contact, dermoscopic central core with crown vessels, and extrusion of curd-like material with large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions points to molluscum contagiosum virus infection. Normal inflammatory markers and negative STI screens support a localized cutaneous viral process in an immunocompetent host.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to a sexual health clinic with 3 weeks of intense pruritus localized to the groin and proximal thighs, worse at night. He reports disturbed sleep. Examination shows multiple excoriated papules and focal erythema concentrated at the base of the pubic hair and along the inguinal creases.

He self-treated with over-the-counter antifungal cream and intermittent topical corticosteroid without improvement. He is otherwise well and HIV-negative by recent testing. He recently moved into a shared dormitory and uses communal towels and bedding.

Skin scrapings aimed at detecting burrowing mites were negative and potassium hydroxide preparation showed no fungal elements. Bacterial swab grew only commensal skin flora. Full blood count was within reference range with white cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 0.4 × 10^9/L.

Dermatoscopy of the affected area demonstrates multiple translucent, ovoid structures firmly attached to individual hair shafts. Bedside light microscopy of gently plucked hairs shows empty ovoid shells adherent to shafts that cannot be slid off.

Partner screening revealed a small, wingless arthropod about 1.5–2 mm long with a broad flattened body and stout front legs grasping coarse hairs, plus firmly adherent oval eggs on hairs. Both patients improved only after topical pediculicidal treatment and laundering of bedding and towels.

explanation: Nocturnal pruritus focused at the base of coarse terminal hair, failure of. Negative scrapings for burrowing mites help exclude scabies.

hints.text: A 35-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 days of high fever, drenching sweats and progressive headache. He reported two episodes of vomiting and new confusion on the day of presentation; temperature was 39.5°C, pulse 112/min, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg. On examination he was pale and jaundiced, with a palpable spleen 3 cm below the left costal margin and mild bilateral lower limb weakness that limited ambulation.

He had been well previously with no chronic illness and no history of transfusion. Two weeks earlier he returned from a 10-day trip to rural Southeast Asia where he spent time in villages and at forest edges, and he recalled multiple mosquito bites despite using repellents. He had taken chemoprophylaxis intermittently and had not traveled elsewhere recently.

Full blood count showed haemoglobin 95 g/L, white cell count 3.8 × 10^9/L and platelets 58 × 10^9/L. Serum creatinine was 160 μmol/L, total bilirubin 65 μmol/L and ALT 85 U/L. Thick and thin blood films demonstrated intraerythrocytic ring forms and trophozoites with parasitaemia estimated at 2.8%; a point-of-care malaria antigen test returned negative.
Focused abdominal ultrasound performed at bedside confirmed splenomegaly with a longitudinal spleen length of 16 cm and mild hepatomegaly. Chest radiograph showed no consolidation or effusion.

On detailed questioning he described spending three nights at a long-house on the forest edge in Malaysian Borneo where macaques were commonly seen at dusk and he had multiple unprotected nocturnal mosquito exposures. Local public-health services later reported recent zoonotic malaria cases in that district.

explanation: The combination of intraerythrocytic parasitaemia with a negative rapid antigen test, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly and recent forest-edge exposure with macaques in Malaysian Borneo points to zoonotic malaria caused by Plasmodium knowlesi. The degree of parasitaemia and early kidney injury explain the patient's systemic features and risk for severe disease.

hints.text: A 29-year-old male volunteer presents to the clinic with a 6-day history of intermittent fevers, drenching sweats, myalgia and headache. He reports rigors and two episodes of lightheadedness; on arrival temperature is 39.1°C, pulse 110/min, blood pressure 115/70 mmHg, and examination shows pale conjunctivae and a spleen palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin.

He returned 10 weeks ago from a four-month aid assignment in rural Sierra Leone where he slept without air conditioning and had frequent mosquito exposure. He took malaria prophylaxis intermittently, and while abroad he had a brief febrile illness treated empirically at a local clinic without laboratory confirmation.

Laboratory tests show haemoglobin 92 g/L, white cell count 3.9 × 10^9/L, platelets 78 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 36 μmol/L and ALT 68 U/L. A peripheral blood film demonstrates intraerythrocytic parasites with a low-level parasitaemia of 0.4%. A rapid antigen panel is positive for a pan-malarial target and negative for a falciparum-specific target.

Abdominal ultrasound performed to evaluate left upper quadrant discomfort shows splenomegaly with a longitudinal splenic span of 13.5 cm and mild homogeneous hepatomegaly. There are no focal hepatic lesions or fluid collections.

He was treated with an appropriate blood schizonticide and became afebrile with clearance of parasitaemia, but returned 7 months later with the same pattern of febrile paroxysms and low-level parasitaemia. After administration of a hypnozoitocidal agent in addition to blood-stage therapy he had no further relapses during 12 months of follow-up.

explanation: Recent travel to West Africa, low-density parasitaemia with a pan-malarial positive but falciparum-specific negative antigen, splenomegaly, and recurrence months later that resolved only after adding a hypnozoitocidal agent point to a relapsing, hypnozoite-forming malaria species. These features best fit infection with Plasmodium ovale in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to clinic with a 6-week history of intermittent fevers, drenching night sweats, diffuse myalgia and progressive fatigue. Fevers have been documented to 39.1°C with intervening afebrile days; on examination he is pale and has a spleen palpable 4 cm below the left costal margin.

He emigrated from Sierra Leone five months ago and spent three weeks there 14 months prior to presentation visiting relatives. He recalls heavy mosquito exposure and a brief febrile illness while in the village that was treated locally with oral tablets of uncertain type; he denies chronic medical conditions and is not immunosuppressed.

Haemoglobin 88 g/L, leukocytes 3.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 95 × 10^9/L. Serum albumin 22 g/L and urine albumin creatinine ratio 310 mg/mmol consistent with nephrotic-range proteinuria. Thick and thin blood films performed on three occasions showed low-density parasitaemia.

Abdominal ultrasound confirms moderate, homogeneous splenomegaly without focal hepatic lesions. Renal ultrasound shows normal size and cortical thickness without obstruction. Chest radiograph is unremarkable.

The patient describes a striking pattern of fevers that recur with peaks approximately every third day separated by near-complete symptom-free intervals. Review at the reference laboratory noted thin-film forms with trophozoites traversing erythrocytes in a band-like configuration and schizonts containing four merozoites. After supervised treatment with chloroquine his fevers and parasitaemia cleared and proteinuria began to improve.

explanation: Chronic low-density parasitaemia with a 72-hour fever periodicity, splenomegaly and nephrotic-range proteinuria that improved after chloroquine point to Plasmodium malariae. The band-form trophozoites and four-merozoite schizonts on thin film are characteristic morphological findings that support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency clinic on day 5 of illness with high fever, severe frontal headache, diffuse myalgias and increasing confusion. He is a newly arrived resident of a crowded displacement camp and on exam was febrile to 39.8°C, tachycardic at 110 beats/min, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg and intermittently disoriented; there was a faint maculopapular rash over the trunk and proximal limbs but no nuchal rigidity.

He reported progressive symptoms beginning after an upper‑respiratory prodrome; three relatives in the same shelter developed similar febrile illnesses over the prior two weeks and one neighbour had died at home. He has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications and reports infrequent access to laundry or clean clothing since arrival.

Initial blood tests showed leukopenia 3.2 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 85 × 10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L, ALT 142 U/L and AST 190 U/L with mild hyponatraemia Na+ 129 mmol/L. Blood cultures and a malaria rapid test were negative; lumbar puncture was performed and cerebrospinal fluid showed 8 × 10^6/L white cells with normal glucose and protein.
Non-contrast CT of the head was unremarkable for acute intracranial process. Chest radiograph showed no focal consolidation and no evidence of cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

On re-questioning he described weeks of intense body itch and scratching, habitual sleeping in communal cots with shared outer garments, and visible small insects and 'eggs' in the seams of clothes used by many camp residents. Local public health had reported an outbreak of febrile illness among people living in the same shelter.

explanation: The combination of high fever with headache, confusion, a trunk-predominant maculopapular rash, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis in the setting of overcrowding and body lice infestation points to epidemic louse-borne rickettsial infection caused by Rickettsia prowazekii. The epidemiologic cluster and rapid clinical suspicion support empiric doxycycline while confirmatory serology or PCR is obtained.

hints.text: A 68-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 72 hours of fever, rigors, left flank pain and worsening dysuria. She was febrile at 38.9°C, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, and had left costovertebral angle tenderness on examination with reduced oral intake over the past two days.

Her past medical history includes neurogenic bladder after a lumbar fracture, managed with an indwelling urinary catheter for the last five months, and recurrent nephrolithiasis with one prior ureteroscopy three years ago. She reported recent catheter exchanges at a community clinic and several previous urinary tract infections treated with short antibiotic courses.

Blood tests showed white cell count 16 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 120 mg/L. Urine dip was strongly alkaline at pH 8.8 with positive leukocyte esterase and many leucocytes; urine culture grew a large colony of oxidase-negative, motile Gram-negative bacilli that produced urease on biochemical testing.

Non-contrast CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder demonstrated a large staghorn calculus occupying the left renal pelvis and calyces with partial hydronephrosis and perinephric inflammatory stranding. The calculus appeared dense and branching along the collecting system.

Percutaneous nephrolithotomy retrieved friable crystalline material and the indwelling catheter had visible encrustation. Cultures from the stone fragment and the catheter tip yielded the same urease-producing, rapidly motile Gram-negative bacillus as the urine.

explanation: This is a complicated urinary tract infection in a patient with a long-term indwelling catheter and staghorn calculi. The combination of markedly alkaline urine, urease activity on culture, motile oxidase-negative Gram-negative bacilli, and struvite-like staghorn stones points to an enteric urease-producing organism that commonly colonizes catheters and forms infection stones.

hints.text: A 27-year-old man presents with three months of progressive abdominal swelling and early satiety. He had one episode of hematemesis last week requiring emergency endoscopy, is afebrile, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, and examination shows a firm, non-tender liver edge, splenomegaly to 16 cm and shifting dullness consistent with ascites.

He emigrated from East Asia as a child and otherwise has no hazardous alcohol use, no prior blood transfusions, and no known chronic viral hepatitis. He reports intermittent watery diarrhoea and vague abdominal cramps in his late teens that resolved spontaneously and no history of intravenous drug use.

Full blood count shows WBC 8.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.6 × 10^9/L and platelets 82 × 10^9/L. Liver synthetic tests are preserved with albumin 41 g/L and INR 1.0, ALT 28 U/L, AST 32 U/L. Stool microscopy demonstrates numerous ovoid golden-brown ova about 70–100 µm in diameter, multiple per high-power field, each with a small lateral appendage.

Abdominal ultrasound shows symmetrical periportal thickening and increased echogenicity along portal tracts with a dilated portal vein (16 mm), markedly enlarged spleen, and small-volume ascites. Liver surface and overall echotexture are otherwise preserved without nodularity.

On direct questioning he recalls frequent childhood bathing and wading in rice paddies and irrigation channels in the Yangtze River delta, where local physicians had reported ‘‘river fever’’ in neighbours; family members had similar remittent gastrointestinal complaints when he was a boy.

explanation: Young patient with non-cirrhotic portal hypertension, preserved synthetic function, peripheral eosinophilia, periportal fibrosis on ultrasound, and abundant small ovoid eggs in stool after childhood freshwater exposure in East Asia indicates infection by a trematode transmitted through freshwater snails. The heavy egg burden and endemic location point to the East Asian intestinal schistosome species as the most likely cause of his hepatosplenic disease.

hints.text: A 35-year-old man presents to the emergency clinic on day 7 of illness with high fever, severe frontal headache, diffuse myalgias and a new faint, non‑pruritic maculopapular rash on his trunk. He reports progressive fatigue and lightheadedness; on exam he is febrile 39.2°C, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, and mildly confused but oriented. Lung and cardiac exams are unremarkable and there is no obvious eschar or localized tender lymphadenopathy.

He is normally healthy and works loading shipping containers at a coastal warehouse. Over the prior two weeks he cleaned an old storage unit that had rodent droppings. He denies recent travel abroad, tick bites, sexual exposures, or sick contacts. He owns a cat that sleeps in the storage unit occasionally.

Initial blood tests show white blood cell count 3.8 × 10^9/L, platelet count 110 × 10^9/L, sodium 131 mmol/L, ALT 120 U/L and AST 98 U/L. C-reactive protein is 56 mg/L. Blood cultures are sterile at 48 hours, malaria smear and dengue NS1 antigen are negative.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates mild hepatomegaly (midline craniocaudal span 16 cm) and a spleen of 13 cm without focal lesions. Chest radiograph shows no focal consolidation.

Municipal environmental inspection documented heavy rat activity in his building and fleas on stray animals around the warehouse; the patient recalled several recent flea bites. Convalescent serology by indirect immunofluorescence showed a fourfold rise in antibody titre to an organism commonly transmitted by rat fleas.

explanation: Subacute febrile illness with headache, trunk maculopapular rash, thrombocytopenia, hyponatraemia and mild transaminitis in the context of rodent exposure points to flea‑borne typhus. The epidemiologic finding of rat infestation with rising convalescent antibody titre to a flea‑transmitted agent supports that diagnosis and explains the rapid clinical course despite negative blood cultures.

hints.text: A 56-year-old woman is evaluated on postoperative day 4 for fever and new-onset rigors. She reports 48 hours of increasing suprapubic pain and cloudy urine; temperature 38.9°C, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, and focal suprapubic tenderness on palpation.

She underwent an uncomplicated total abdominal hysterectomy 4 days earlier and has an indwelling urinary catheter that has not yet been removed. Past history includes type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and she received a single perioperative dose of a first-generation cephalosporin.

Blood count shows leukocytosis of 16.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 120 mg/L. Urinalysis reveals many pyuria and bacteria; urine Gram stain shows Gram-negative bacilli and preliminary urine culture after 24 hours grew >10^5 CFU/mL of a non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod.
Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis performed to exclude complications shows stranding of the left renal perinephric fat consistent with acute pyelonephritis without drainable collection.

She remained febrile after 48 hours of empirical cefuroxime and the urinary isolate proved resistant to ampicillin and cefazolin but susceptible to gentamicin and ciprofloxacin. The microbiology laboratory noted that colonies on blood agar at 48 hours had a distinctive red pigment.

explanation: The isolate's resistance profile together with the recovery of red-pigmented colonies supports the specific bacterial cause in this case. Treatment should be guided by susceptibilities and removal or replacement of the urinary catheter.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presented to clinic with a 3-week history of low-grade fevers, increasing fatigue, exertional dyspnea and a 3 kg weight loss. On examination temperature was 38.0°C, heart rate 96/min, he had pale conjunctiva and a new soft systolic murmur at the cardiac apex, and he reported two episodes of dark stools in the previous month.

He has well controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension, no history of intravenous drug use and no prosthetic heart valves. He was found to have iron deficiency anaemia two months earlier but had not yet undergone investigation with colonoscopy.

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 88 g/L, white cell count 12.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 98 mg/L. Multiple sets of blood cultures became positive; Gram stain showed Gram-positive cocci in chains. The isolate hydrolysed bile esculin and was negative for pyrrolidonyl arylamidase, and had a low penicillin MIC.
Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a mobile 7 mm vegetation on the posterior mitral leaflet with new moderate mitral regurgitation and no perivalvular abscess.
Colonoscopy performed during the admission identified a fungating mass in the sigmoid colon; biopsy confirmed invasive adenocarcinoma.

explanation: The patient has native-valve endocarditis proven by vegetation and persistently positive blood cultures with a chain-forming, bile-esculin hydrolysing, PYR-negative Gram-positive coccus that is penicillin susceptible. The newly discovered colorectal adenocarcinoma in the setting of this bloodstream isolate strongly supports the pathogen that links streptococcal-type bacteraemia and endocarditis with colonic neoplasia.

hints.text: A 34-year-old previously healthy man presented to an outpatient clinic with a 4-month history of intermittent crampy abdominal pain, abdominal bloating, and unintentional 6-kg weight loss. He also reported new nocturnal perianal pruritus, and on examination vital signs were normal with faint perianal excoriations but no abdominal guarding or organomegaly.

He works as a cook in a busy metropolitan restaurant and prepares traditional dishes that sometimes include raw or briefly seared meats. He has no chronic medical conditions, is not immunosuppressed, had no recent foreign travel in the past year, and recalls self-treating episodic diarrhoea months ago with an over-the-counter antiparasitic preparation without sustained improvement.

Complete blood count showed haemoglobin 98 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 70 fL, white blood cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.2 × 10^9/L. Ferritin was 10 µg/L and C-reactive protein was within reference range. Initial stool bacterial culture was negative and routine fecal microscopy reported no cysts or trophozoites on the first sample.

Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis performed for persistent symptoms demonstrated a long, linear intraluminal soft-tissue density extending from the ascending colon into the rectosigmoid colon without surrounding wall thickening or fat stranding. Multiplanar reconstructions suggested a continuous ribbonlike structure occupying the lumen over several tens of centimetres.

On directed questioning he admitted to frequent consumption of a regional raw beef dish over the past year and this morning reported passing a long, white, ribbonlike segment in his stool that he described as motile and approximately 20–30 cm in length.

explanation: Chronic mild gastrointestinal symptoms with iron deficiency and eosinophilia raise parasitic infection. Imaging showing a long intraluminal ribbonlike structure plus the history of eating raw beef and passage of long motile proglottid segments indicates an adult beef tapeworm infection, caused by Taenia saginata. The motile long segments and bovine exposure support this species rather than a pork-associated tapeworm.

hints.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the outpatient clinic with three weeks of evening fevers, persistent dry cough and intermittent right upper quadrant abdominal discomfort. Symptoms began insidiously and parents report reduced appetite and a 1 kg weight loss. On examination temperature is 38.2°C, there is scattered wheeze on chest auscultation and the liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Growth and developmental milestones are otherwise appropriate for age.

The child has no chronic illness, takes no regular medications and has received routine childhood immunisations. He was treated briefly with oral amoxicillin for presumed lower respiratory infection and given an inhaled bronchodilator for presumed reactive airways disease without clinical improvement. Family report no recent travel outside the country and no household members with similar symptoms.

Complete blood count shows WBC 18.7 × 10^9/L with marked eosinophilia 5.2 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 126 g/L and platelets 320 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 8 mg/L. Total IgE elevated at 1 600 kU/L. Three separate stool ova and parasite examinations are negative.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates multiple 0.5–2.0 cm well circumscribed hypoechoic nodules scattered throughout both hepatic lobes. Chest radiograph shows fleeting patchy perihilar airspace opacities compared with film performed two weeks earlier.

History elicited that the family adopted two young puppies six weeks before illness onset. The child spends daily time playing in a local sandpit where dogs are often allowed to defecate and the parents admit he occasionally puts sand in his mouth.

explanation: Subacute fever, cough and hepatomegaly with pronounced peripheral eosinophilia, very high IgE and multiple hepatic hypoechoic lesions in a child with recent puppy contact and geophagia are most consistent with visceral larva migrans due to Toxocara canis. Negative stool examinations support a tissue-migrating helminth rather than an intestinal infection.

hints.text: A 36-year-old man presented to an urban infectious diseases clinic with 3 weeks of fever, progressive non-productive cough, and a 6 kg weight loss. On examination temperature was 38.5°C, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, there were multiple 2–4 mm erythematous papules on the trunk and face, palpable cervical lymph nodes about 2 cm, and the liver edge was 3 cm below the costal margin.

He was diagnosed with HIV infection 5 months earlier but never started antiretroviral therapy and reported recent oral thrush and night sweats. Two weeks before presentation his CD4 count was 38 × 10^6/L and plasma HIV RNA was 150 000 copies/mL. He was born in Vietnam and relocated to the city 18 months ago with no further travel since.

Contrast CT of the chest showed multiple bilateral ill-defined pulmonary nodules 5–15 mm with a peribronchovascular distribution, patchy ground-glass opacity, small bilateral pleural effusions, and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated splenomegaly to 14 cm.

He received empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and a 10-day trial of antituberculous therapy without clinical improvement. Intravenous amphotericin B was started on hospital day 12 and within 5 days fever resolved, oxygen requirement fell, and the skin papules softened and became fewer.

Blood cultures and skin biopsy cultures became positive after 5 days and grew a thermally dimorphic fungus. Histology of a papule showed numerous small intracellular yeast-like cells within macrophages with a central transverse septum on PAS stain. Sabouraud agar incubated at 25°C produced a green colony with a red diffusible pigment.

explanation: Advanced immunosuppression with systemic febrile illness, pulmonary nodules, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and papular skin lesions suggested a disseminated opportunistic infection. The recovery of a dimorphic fungus that produces a red diffusible pigment and shows intracellular yeast with a transverse septum in tissue establishes the specific diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 28-year-old male laboratory archivist presents with a 6-day history of high fever, severe headache and profound malaise followed 48 hours later by an evolving skin eruption. On arrival he is febrile to 39.4 °C, pulse 110/min, and exam shows multiple firm pustular lesions concentrated on the face and forearms, several of which are painful and limit active use of his right hand.

He is previously healthy, on no regular medications, and reports no recent travel or new sexual contacts. He has no visible vaccination scar and says his job involves retrieval of decades-old clinical samples and authenticated viral stocks from a national archive; he sustained a small tear in a glove while handling sealed material seven days before symptom onset.

Full blood count shows WBC 3.8 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.8 × 10^9/L. Pustule swab PCR detected very high copies of a large linear double-stranded DNA virus, bacterial cultures are negative, and electron microscopy of lesion fluid demonstrates large brick-shaped viral particles with complex internal structure.

Close-up clinical photographs show dozens of deep-seated, round pustules with central umbilication. The lesions are all in the same developmental stage and are most dense on the face and distal extremities, including the palms, with relatively fewer lesions on the trunk.

Public health review confirmed the archived material he handled was an authenticated mid-20th century human viral stock from the national repository of a human-only pathogen that was the target of historic global eradication efforts; whole-genome sequencing from his lesion matched the archived human outbreak sequences.

explanation: The combination of a febrile prodrome, deep-seated pustules all in the same stage with centrifugal distribution including palms, the absence of another pathogen on culture, EM showing large brick-shaped virions, and direct exposure to an archived eradicated human virus supports infection with variola virus. The occupational breach of an authenticated archival stock explains the route of acquisition.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 36 hours of progressive right lower leg pain, swelling, and several tense dark blisters. He reported fever and rigors since the evening before arrival. On examination his temperature was 38.9°C, heart rate 110 min‑1, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg. The right lower leg was markedly tender with dusky erythema extending beyond the visible margins and multiple flaccid bullae. He was unable to bear weight on the affected limb.

Past medical history included alcohol related cirrhosis, Child B, and type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. He denied chronic immunosuppressive therapy or recent hospital admissions. He recalled a superficial scratch to the ankle while gardening about 48 hours before symptom onset but no major trauma. He had not started any new medications.

Blood tests showed white cell count 18.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 16.0 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 312 mg/L, lactate 5.8 mmol/L. Liver tests were abnormal with bilirubin 58 µmol/L and INR 1.8. Blood cultures flagged positive after about 10 hours and Gram stain of the blood culture revealed curved gram-negative rods.

CT of the leg with contrast demonstrated diffuse subcutaneous oedema and marked fascial thickening with fluid tracking along fascial planes, but no detectable gas. Findings were reported as compatible with an aggressive necrotising soft tissue infection, prompting urgent surgical consultation.

On further questioning the patient said he had eaten raw oysters at a coastal meal and had stood ankle‑deep in seawater two days before becoming unwell. Definitive culture later grew a rapidly growing, halophilic, oxidase‑positive, motile gram‑negative curved bacillus that was susceptible to doxycycline and a third-generation cephalosporin.

explanation: A patient with cirrhosis developed fulminant soft tissue infection with hypotension, haemorrhagic bullae, and rapid Gram‑negative bacteraemia. The combination of recent raw oyster and seawater exposure, curved oxidase‑positive gram‑negative rods from blood culture, and necrotising fasciitis strongly supports Vibrio vulnificus as the cause.

hints.text: A 72-year-old man presented in early August with 4 days of fever and progressive confusion. Over the preceding 24 hours he developed new weakness of his right arm that left him unable to lift a cup, and his right biceps reflex was reduced. Temperature 38.4°C, heart rate 96/min, GCS 14. There was no rash and no neck stiffness on initial examination.

He has well controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He lives alone on the edge of a small river and spends evenings doing gardening and repairing fishing gear. He has not travelled recently and takes no immunosuppressive medications. Symptoms began with headache and malaise before neurologic decline.

Blood WBC 7.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 6 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L. Lumbar puncture opening pressure 18 cm H2O. CSF WBC 140 × 10^6/L with 80% lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, CSF glucose 3.9 mmol/L with paired serum glucose 7.8 mmol/L. Bacterial cultures sterile. PCR for herpes simplex virus and enterovirus negative.

Non-contrast CT head was unremarkable. MRI cervical spine showed a focal T2 hyperintense signal localized to the right anterior horn region at C4–C6 with mild cord swelling. Brain MRI showed subtle T2 changes in the basal ganglia.

Local public health reported increased detection of a mosquito-borne neurotropic arbovirus in sentinel birds and mosquito traps over the same fortnight. CSF and serum IgM directed against that locally circulating arbovirus returned positive, with PCR for the virus negative on blood.

explanation: An older adult with febrile meningoencephalitis, asymmetric flaccid motor weakness and diminished reflexes, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein, MRI showing anterior horn cell involvement, and regionally positive CSF IgM to a mosquito-borne arbovirus indicate neuroinvasive infection by West Nile virus. The combination of encephalopathy and poliomyelitis-like anterior horn pathology plus local arboviral activity supports this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 72-year-old man presented in late August with four days of fever, progressive confusion and headache. He lives in an inner-city apartment and had two falls at home; on arrival temperature was 38.3 C, he was disoriented to time and had new mild left-sided weakness with Glasgow Coma Scale 13.

He has well controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension, no recent travel and no immunosuppressive therapy. He reports doing evening gardening for several weeks and noted multiple mosquito bites in the fortnight before illness onset, but had no known animal exposures or febrile contacts.

Peripheral blood shows WBC 11.6 × 10^9/L and CRP 35 mg/L. Lumbar puncture yielded clear CSF with opening pressure 18 cm H2O, WBC 120 × 10^6/L (90% lymphocytes), protein 1.0 g/L, glucose 3.3 mmol/L with serum glucose 6.2 mmol/L. CSF bacterial cultures were negative and PCR for herpes simplex and enterovirus was negative.

Brain MRI with contrast performed on day 3 of admission showed bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the thalami and basal ganglia with mild restricted diffusion and no large territorial infarct. No leptomeningeal enhancement was present.

Local public health mosquito surveillance detected a North American Culex-transmitted flavivirus in pooled mosquitoes that week. Convalescent serum demonstrated a fourfold rise in neutralizing antibody titre by plaque reduction neutralization testing against the virus historically linked to urban Culex outbreaks in the Mississippi and Ohio valleys, and county health laboratory reported matching PRNT results from the patient.

explanation: An older adult with late-summer febrile neuroinvasive illness, lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis and bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia MRI signal suggests a mosquito-borne flavivirus. Louis encephalitis virus as the cause.

hints.text: A 39-year-old man presented to a regional hospital with 48 hours of fever, rigors and a rapidly painful swollen right groin. He is a farm worker and now has difficulty walking because of a 6 cm tender, erythematous, fluctuant inguinal mass, temperature 39.6 °C and heart rate 116 min-1.

He has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and no recent travel. Five days before presentation he noticed a small painless spot on his right thigh after sleeping in an uninsulated barn; he self-treated with oral amoxicillin for 48 hours without improvement.

Admission blood tests showed WBC 18.5 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, CRP 220 mg/L, creatinine 150 µmol/L and lactate 3.2 mmol/L. Blood cultures and an aspirate from the groin mass were submitted; Gram stain results from the aspirate were not yet reported.

Contrast CT of the pelvis demonstrated a 6.2 cm necrotic right inguinal lymph node with central low attenuation and extensive surrounding fat stranding. Interventional radiology performed ultrasound-guided drainage and sent purulent fluid for culture.

Local public health notified clinicians of a recent die-off of rats in the village and neighbours reported flea infestations in outbuildings. Culture from the drained fluid produced small non-lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey within 48 hours and Gram stain of colonies showed bipolar-staining gram-negative coccobacilli with a safety-pin appearance; isolate was oxidase negative and susceptible to gentamicin and ciprofloxacin.

explanation: The combination of acute febrile illness with a tender necrotic inguinal bubo, recent rodent die-off with flea exposure, and culture showing bipolar-staining non-lactose fermenting gram-negative coccobacilli is diagnostic for plague due to Yersinia pestis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 days of fever, severe myalgia, frontal headache and progressive dark urine. He was febrile at 39.1°C, pulse 82 bpm, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg; examination showed scleral icterus, mild right upper quadrant tenderness and no rash.

He returned 8 days earlier from a two-week trip to a tropical region in Africa during which he slept in basic accommodation and reported frequent mosquito bites. He has no known chronic liver disease, takes no regular medications, drinks alcohol only occasionally and did not receive any pre-travel immunisations.

Laboratory tests showed leucopenia 3.1 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 60 × 10^9/L, AST 1,350 U/L, ALT 620 U/L, total bilirubin 95 μmol/L and INR 2.3; serum creatinine 180 μmol/L. Blood films for malaria and routine blood cultures were negative; an arboviral RT-PCR panel was requested.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly (liver span 18 cm), homogeneous decreased echogenicity and a small volume of free fluid, with a normal common bile duct and no biliary obstruction.

While in-country he spent two days at a forested primate sanctuary where several monkeys were observed to die suddenly. On hospital day 2 he developed coffee-ground vomiting and melaena; serum RT-PCR returned positive for the travel-associated mosquito-borne haemorrhagic febrile virus that the clinic tests for.

explanation: Recent travel with heavy mosquito exposure and lack of pre-travel immunisation raise concern for a travel-acquired arboviral illness. Marked hepatic injury with AST>ALT, jaundice, coagulopathy and progression to gastrointestinal bleeding support the diagnosis of the specific mosquito-borne haemorrhagic febrile virus linked to primate die-offs. Positive RT-PCR for the travel-associated virus confirms the diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 33-year-old previously healthy man presents with 4 days of low-grade fever, a diffuse non-pruritic maculopapular rash and mild aching of the hands. He also notes bilateral conjunctival redness and new distal tingling in his feet that progressed over 48 hours to difficulty climbing stairs. Temperature 37.8°C, heart rate 96/min, proximal lower‑limb strength 4/5 on hip flexion, otherwise no cranial nerve deficit.

Symptoms began 10 days after a 2‑week trip to coastal Central America. He recalls an acute febrile rash illness that largely resolved over 4 days before the paresthesia and weakness developed. There was no diarrhoea, no recent vaccination, no antibiotic use, and no prior neurologic disease. He reports being sexually active and monogamous.

Full blood count shows WBC 3.8 × 10^9/L and platelets 210 × 10^9/L. CSF demonstrates protein 1.3 g/L with 4 × 10^6/L white cells. Serum IgM for two locally circulating arboviruses is negative. Reverse transcription PCR for viral RNA was negative in serum but positive in a urine specimen collected 11 days after symptom onset.
MRI lumbosacral spine with gadolinium shows enhancement of anterior nerve roots of the cauda equina consistent with a polyradiculoneuropathy. There is no spinal cord signal abnormality.

On further questioning he admits unprotected intercourse with a partner who had returned from northeast Brazil three weeks before his symptoms. Local public health had recently reported clusters of rash illness and an increase in congenital central nervous system malformations linked to a mosquito‑borne arbovirus.

explanation: The sequence of a brief febrile maculopapular rash with conjunctivitis followed by an ascending polyradiculoneuropathy, albuminocytologic dissociation, MRI nerve‑root enhancement and urine RT‑PCR positivity in the setting of relevant travel/exposure is most consistent with Zika virus infection leading to postinfectious Guillain‑Barré syndrome.

hints.text: A 21-year-old university rower presents with 5 days of sore throat, fever up to 39.0°C, and increasing redness of both eyes. On arrival she is febrile, has bilateral conjunctival injection without thick purulent discharge, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and marked oropharyngeal erythema that makes swallowing solids uncomfortable.
She is previously well and not immunocompromised. She lives in shared campus housing and has been training twice daily; she reports no recent antibiotic use, no travel, and no new sexual partners.

Blood test shows WBC 11.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 7.6 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 2.8 × 10^9/L. Rapid strep antigen and heterophile antibody test are negative. A multiplex respiratory PCR returned positive for a single respiratory virus; typing is pending. Conjunctival swab was sent for viral testing.
Ultrasound of the neck shows multiple enlarged reactive cervical lymph nodes, largest 18 mm, with preserved fatty hilum and no fluid collection. Chest radiograph is clear.

Three teammates from the rowing crew developed similar febrile sore throat and conjunctivitis this week. Conjunctival swabs from two teammates and the patient were PCR positive for a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA respiratory virus known to cause pharyngitis and conjunctivitis outbreaks in close-contact groups and swimmers; recent pool maintenance records documented lapses in chlorination.

explanation: The combination of fever, pharyngitis with tender cervical nodes and bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis in a clustered outbreak among swimmers points to adenoviral pharyngoconjunctival infection. Negative strep and heterophile tests with PCR detection of a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA respiratory virus support that diagnosis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents with a 9-month history of progressive right lower limb swelling and increasing difficulty wearing his work boots. He describes intermittent low-grade fevers and episodic sharp pain along the inner thigh that precede worsening of the swelling. On examination the right lower leg shows non-pitting oedema with thickened, hyperkeratotic skin and mild erythema; a 2 cm firm tender right inguinal node is palpable. Temperature is 37.8°C and he ambulates with a mild limp.

He grew up in a coastal, rural province of West Africa and worked in rice paddies until age 18 before emigrating ten years ago. He has no history of chronic skin infections, no prior limb surgery or trauma, and no known immunosuppression. Symptoms began several years after leaving the region and have progressed despite locally applied emollients and intermittent courses of oral antibiotics.

Full blood count shows leukocytes 8.9 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.6 × 10^9/L. CRP is 14 mg/L. Two daytime thick blood films were reported as negative for parasites and bacterial cultures from a superficial skin swab grew skin commensals only.

Doppler ultrasound of the affected limb demonstrates preserved deep venous flow but prominent subcutaneous soft-tissue thickening and multiple dilated superficial lymphatic channels in the medial calf. No fluid collection or venous thrombosis is identified. The radiologist notes that the lymphatic channels are markedly enlarged compared with the contralateral limb.

A nocturnal peripheral blood specimen collected at 23:30 for parasitological study showed motile, sheathed larvae approximately 250–300 µm in length; careful microscopy documented that somatic nuclei do not extend to the tip of the tail. A circulating antigen assay directed at lymphatic nematode antigens returned positive.

explanation: Chronic unilateral lower-limb lymphoedema after residence in an endemic tropical area, peripheral eosinophilia, ultrasound evidence of dilated lymphatics, nocturnal circulating sheathed larvae with terminal tail morphology and a positive circulating antigen together indicate lymphatic filariasis caused by Wuchereria bancrofti.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man, 10 weeks after allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplant, presents with 48 hours of fever to 39.2°C, dry cough and new onset gross haematuria. He is tachypnoeic with respiratory rate 24/min and oxygen saturation 90% on room air, has diffuse crackles on chest auscultation and suprapubic tenderness on palpation.
Transplant was performed for acute myeloid leukaemia. He remains on tacrolimus and mycophenolate, and received a short prednisone taper two weeks earlier for grade II acute graft versus host disease.

Full blood count shows WBC 1.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 0.6 × 10^9/L. Serum creatinine is 210 µmol/L from a baseline of 85 µmol/L. ALT 145 U/L. Urinalysis 3+ blood with microscopy 50 erythrocytes per high-power field and no growth on routine bacterial culture. BK virus PCR is negative; a multiplex viral PCR sent on admission is pending.

Chest CT demonstrates multifocal bilateral peribronchovascular consolidation with small centrilobular nodules and no cavitation. Bladder ultrasound shows diffuse bladder wall thickening and intraluminal echoes consistent with clot.

Two weeks before symptom onset his three-year-old daughter returned from daycare with abrupt fever, sore throat and red eyes. The daycare reported a late-summer cluster of pharyngitis with conjunctivitis among several children and staff.

explanation: An allogeneic HSCT recipient with pneumonia and sterile haemorrhagic cystitis after household contact with a cluster of pharyngoconjunctival illness points to adenoviral infection. Negative BK PCR and the combination of respiratory and urinary tract involvement in a severely immunocompromised host support this diagnosis. Confirmatory testing is by targeted viral PCR from respiratory secretions, blood or urine.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to the clinic with three months of progressive exertional dyspnoea and fatigue. He reports dizziness on standing and has become unable to complete his manual work; on examination he is pale with conjunctival pallor and a heart rate of 102 beats/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg.

He emigrated 10 months ago from a rural region where he worked seasonally, and he started a new job in the city six months ago. He has no history of overt gastrointestinal bleeding, denies regular NSAID use, and says oral iron tablets produced minimal improvement despite several weeks of therapy; he recalls an episode of a mild, itchy rash on his feet a few months before his fatigue began.

Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 64 fL, red cell distribution width 18%, reticulocyte count low. Ferritin 8 µg/L, transferrin saturation 6%, eosinophils 0.9 × 10^9/L. Two separate fecal occult blood tests are negative.
Chest radiograph obtained because of transient cough episodes shows patchy bilateral perihilar and peripheral airspace opacities that were not present on a radiograph taken a year earlier.

On directed questioning he describes frequent childhood and early adult walking barefoot through irrigated fields and contact with wet soil. Concentration stool microscopy performed at the clinic demonstrates numerous thin-walled ovoid eggs consistent with a blood-feeding intestinal nematode whose larvae penetrate skin.

explanation: Severe iron-deficiency anemia with low ferritin and microcytosis that responds poorly to oral iron, peripheral eosinophilia, transient pulmonary infiltrates, a history of barefoot exposure to irrigated soil, and stool microscopy showing thin-walled ovoid eggs point to infection with Ancylostoma duodenale. The organism's skin-penetrating larvae and adult intestinal blood feeding explain the chronic iron loss and the respiratory findings.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man inpatient for induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia developed new fever and productive cough on day 6 of admission. Over 48 hours he became more breathless, temperature 39.1°C, respiratory rate 24/min, oxygen saturation 89% on room air, with bilateral coarse crackles and reduced air entry at the right base on examination.

He has a tunneled central venous catheter for chemotherapy and severe mucositis. Earlier in this admission he received five days of meropenem and amikacin for suspected neutropenic sepsis, and his absolute neutrophil count has remained below 0.2 × 10^9/L.

Two sets of blood cultures and an endotracheal aspirate flagged positive at about 36 hours. Gram stain showed slender gram-negative rods. Automated biochemical testing reported a non-fermenting gram-negative bacillus with low-confidence identification. Admission bloods: WBC 0.6 × 10^9/L, ANC 0.12 × 10^9/L, CRP 156 mg/L.

Contrast CT chest demonstrated multifocal patchy consolidations with small cavitating nodules, predominantly in both lower lobes, and peribronchial thickening on the right. No pleural effusion or gross pulmonary embolus was seen. The catheter tip projected over the region of the right atrium without surrounding fluid collection.

Initial therapy with meropenem and aminoglycoside produced no clinical improvement and blood cultures persisted positive. The isolate proved resistant to carbapenems, piperacillin-tazobactam and aminoglycosides, and susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and minocycline. After catheter removal and targeted therapy with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole the patient defervesced and subsequent blood cultures cleared.

explanation: An immunocompromised patient with recent broad-spectrum carbapenem exposure and a central line developed bloodstream and pulmonary infection with a non-fermenting gram-negative bacillus that was resistant to carbapenems and aminoglycosides but responded to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Those features point to the identified non-fermenter in this clinical scenario.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to a district hospital with five days of intermittent colicky periumbilical pain, progressive abdominal distension, nausea, and reduced stool output. She had no fever, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and abdominal examination showed mild generalized distension with hyperactive bowel sounds and diffuse tenderness without rebound.

She has no history of abdominal surgery, is otherwise healthy, and works in a childcare setting. Two weeks before presentation she visited relatives in a rural area with limited sanitation; three days before symptom worsening she took a single over-the-counter anthelmintic tablet obtained locally for intermittent perianal itching.

Complete blood count showed leucocytosis 12.0 × 10^9/L with marked eosinophilia 3.2 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein was 28 mg/L and serum electrolytes were within reference ranges. An initial stool microscopy was requested and pending at the time of imaging.

Abdominal radiograph showed multiple small-bowel air fluid levels consistent with subacute obstruction. A right upper quadrant ultrasound demonstrated several long, linear, parallel echogenic structures within the jejunal lumen that moved faintly with bowel peristalsis, producing a 'striped' appearance.

On day 3 of admission the patient passed a single motile, cream-coloured cylindrical worm in her stool. The specimen measured about 15 to 20 cm and was photographed by the hospital laboratory before disposal.

explanation: The combination of recent rural exposure, peripheral eosinophilia, ultrasound evidence of long intraluminal tubular structures, and passage of a large adult cylindrical nematode point to an intestinal infection with a large soil-transmitted nematode. The single-dose anthelmintic preceded clinical worsening, which can precipitate aggregation or migration of adult worms and lead to subacute small-bowel obstruction in this setting.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back that began abruptly 24 hours ago. She had a prior hospital admission for acute pancreatitis six weeks earlier; today T 37.8°C, heart rate 96/min, blood pressure 120/76 mmHg, and marked epigastric tenderness without peritoneal signs.

She denies alcohol use and is not taking medications known to cause pancreatitis. Two months ago she spent three weeks visiting relatives in a rural agricultural region in South Asia, where she drank well water and frequently ate uncooked leafy vegetables; there is no known family history of gallstones.

Serum lipase 3 200 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 82 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L, total bilirubin 28 μmol/L. White blood cell count 12.4 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.4 × 10^9/L. Fasting triglycerides 1.1 mmol/L and CRP 18 mg/L.

Transabdominal ultrasound demonstrates a common bile duct dilated to 11 mm and a gallbladder without calculi. Real-time sonography shows a 6 to 8 cm linear echogenic tubular structure within the distal extrahepatic bile duct that shifts slightly with respiration and probe pressure and lacks posterior acoustic shadowing.

During endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography a motile, pale cylindrical organism approximately 20 cm long was retrieved from the ampullary orifice and photographed before disposal. Relatives in the village reported seeing similar long white worms on harvested vegetables and in children's stools during her visit.

explanation: Recurrent pancreatitis with biliary dilatation after travel to a rural area, peripheral eosinophilia, and removal of a single long motile, non-segmented cylindrical worm from the ampulla identify infection with Ascaris lumbricoides. Adult worm migration into the biliary tree explains the episodic obstructive picture and pancreatitis in this patient.

hints.text: A 36-year-old woman presented to the respiratory clinic with three weeks of progressive cough, thick brown sputum and increased wheeze. She reported reduced exercise tolerance and intermittent low-grade fevers, and examination showed diffuse expiratory wheeze and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.

She has had atopic asthma since childhood with frequent exacerbations requiring several short courses of oral corticosteroids over the past year. She uses inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting bronchodilator intermittently, has allergic rhinitis, and is a non-smoker with no known immunodeficiency.
Blood count showed eosinophils 1.6 × 10^9/L. Total IgE was markedly elevated at 2 200 kU/L and specific IgE to a thermotolerant mould extract was strongly positive.
Chest CT performed for persistent symptoms demonstrated central bronchiectasis and mucus plugging predominantly in the upper lobes, with patchy fleeting alveolar opacities on serial radiographs.

Bronchoscopy with lavage produced thick mucoid secretions. Culture grew green velvety colonies and microscopy showed septate hyphae with acute-angle branching and characteristic conidiophore structures. Oral azole therapy and a corticosteroid taper produced symptomatic improvement and a falling total IgE over four weeks.

explanation: Long-standing atopic asthma with very high total IgE, peripheral eosinophilia and central bronchiectasis indicates allergic bronchopulmonary involvement by a thermotolerant mould. Culture and microscopy from the bronchoscopy specimen demonstrating septate acute-angle branching hyphae with conidiophores and green colonies identify Aspergillus fumigatus as the culprit.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 7 days of fevers, drenching sweats, progressive fatigue and dark-coloured urine. He reports increasing exertional dyspnoea and lightheadedness; on examination he is febrile to 38.6°C, tachycardic at 112/min, markedly jaundiced and pale, and ambulates with mild breathlessness on minimal exertion.

He has a history of splenectomy after a motor vehicle collision two years ago and well controlled type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. He has not travelled abroad in the last year and had no recent hospital admissions or blood transfusions.
Point of care chest radiograph is without focal consolidation. Abdominal ultrasound confirms absence of spleen and shows mild hepatomegaly without biliary dilatation or gallstones.
He lives in a wooded, semi-rural area of the northeastern seaboard and reports removing an engorged tick from his calf about 10 days before symptom onset while clearing undergrowth in late spring.

Laboratory studies show haemoglobin 82 g/L, platelet count 78 × 10^9/L, white cell count 6.4 × 10^9/L. Evidence of intravascular haemolysis includes total bilirubin 55 μmol/L, LDH 920 U/L, haptoglobin < 0.1 g/L and reticulocyte count 150 × 10^9/L. Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Giemsa-stained peripheral blood smear demonstrates intraerythrocytic ring forms and tetrads forming a Maltese cross pattern, parasitaemia estimated at 6%.

explanation: The patient has Coombs-negative intravascular haemolysis with jaundice and dark urine developing days after a tick exposure in an endemic region. Prior splenectomy increases risk of severe erythrocytic parasitic infection. The peripheral smear finding of intraerythrocytic tetrads with significant parasitaemia is diagnostic of infection with Babesia microti.

hints.text: A 74-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 6 days of fever, drenching sweats, generalized weakness and dark brown urine. He is febrile at 38.6°C, heart rate 105/min, and examination shows scleral icterus and pallor without focal respiratory findings.

He had a splenectomy after a motor vehicle collision 35 years ago and otherwise is well controlled on lisinopril for hypertension. He denies recent transfusions, is not taking immunosuppressive medications, and reports progressive limitation of daily walking because of fatigue.

Blood tests show hemoglobin 85 g/L, platelet count 95 × 10^9/L, white cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L. Hemolysis panel demonstrates total bilirubin 63 µmol/L with indirect predominance, lactate dehydrogenase 720 U/L, haptoglobin <0.1 g/L, reticulocytosis 150 × 10^9/L, and a negative direct antiglobulin test. Blood cultures are sterile after 48 hours.
Abdominal ultrasound confirms absence of splenic tissue consistent with prior splenectomy and mild hepatomegaly. There is no biliary ductal dilatation to explain the jaundice.

Ten days before symptom onset he removed an engorged tick from his calf after working in his yard on the Rhode Island coast; a thin blood film performed in hospital shows small ring-shaped intraerythrocytic forms and occasional tetrad arrangements, and a nucleic-acid test on whole blood is positive for a protozoan parasite that infects red cells.

explanation: An asplenic older patient with febrile hemolytic anemia, negative direct antiglobulin test, and intraerythrocytic ring forms including tetrads after a tick bite points to a red cell protozoal infection. The exposure in an endemic area and positive blood nucleic-acid test support the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 46-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of an enlarging lesion on the dorsal aspect of his right forearm. He first noticed a small blister that became an ulcer with central dark necrosis and surrounding tense swelling that limits wrist extension, temperature 38.2°C and pulse 110/min, and tender ipsilateral axillary lymphadenopathy.

He is employed in a small workshop that makes drum heads and occasionally handles unprocessed animal hides without gloves. He denies recent antibiotic use, has well controlled type 2 diabetes, and has not travelled outside the region in the past month.

Blood tests show leukocytosis 22.0 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 180 mg/L. Gram stain of an exudate smear from the lesion shows large Gram-positive bacilli and preliminary cultures on blood agar yielded rapidly growing non-haemolytic colonies within 24 hours.
Ultrasound of the forearm demonstrates extensive subcutaneous oedema tracking proximally without a discrete fluid collection or abscess. Plain radiograph shows soft tissue swelling without gas.

Public health investigation found several recent shipments of untreated goat hides to the workshop. The isolate from the lesion is non-motile, forms non-haemolytic, mucoid colonies, shows a polypeptide capsule on capsule stain, and PCR detected genes encoding a tripartite toxin and capsule biosynthesis consistent with the organism linked to contaminated animal products.

explanation: Marked oedema out of proportion to the skin lesion, a history of handling raw animal hides, and growth of large non-motile Gram-positive bacilli with a polypeptide capsule and toxin genes point to cutaneous infection with the organism associated with contaminated animal products. Imaging showing oedema without abscess supports a toxin-mediated soft tissue process rather than purulent cellulitis.

hints.text: A 38-year-old male presented to the emergency department with five days of fever, progressive shortness of breath and increasing chest discomfort. He also noted a small painless papule on his left forearm that appeared three days earlier; on arrival T 38.8°C, HR 120/min, BP 95/60 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 92% on room air, and the papule had a 1.5 cm oedematous base with a central dark crust.

He is a current smoker with no diabetes or known immunodeficiency and was well until this illness. He had taken oral amoxicillin prescribed by his general practitioner after the forearm lesion appeared but symptoms progressed. He reports no recent travel outside the region and no known sick contacts.

Blood tests showed leukocytosis 18.5 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and CRP 220 mg/L. Lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Blood cultures became positive, and Gram stain from blood showed large gram-positive bacilli; colonies on blood agar were markedly non-haemolytic and had a mucoid appearance.

Contrast chest CT demonstrated marked mediastinal widening with confluent mediastinal soft-tissue stranding and bilateral pleural effusions, greater on the left. No cavitary pulmonary infiltrates were present.

Occupational history obtained on day two revealed he opens and sorts bales of imported untreated animal hides and goat hair at a small tannery. He recalls opening a sealed bale three days before his symptoms began and disturbing a dusty cloud of material that contacted his forearms.

explanation: The combination of a painless necrotic skin lesion with prominent local oedema, systemic sepsis with large non-haemolytic encapsulated gram-positive bacilli in blood culture, and mediastinal widening after exposure to raw animal hides points to Bacillus anthracis infection. The occupational exposure to untreated hides plus the imaging and microbiology support inhalational dissemination with concurrent cutaneous entry leading to severe illness.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presented to the respiratory clinic with a three-week history of progressive cough, intermittent low-grade fever, and two episodes of streaky haemoptysis. He has lost 4 kg and becomes breathless on exertion. On examination he is thin, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, with decreased breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right upper chest.

His past pulmonary history includes treated pulmonary tuberculosis 18 years earlier and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He is a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history and uses inhaled corticosteroid therapy. He reports no recent chemotherapy, organ transplant, or known immunodeficiency.

Blood tests show haemoglobin 110 g/L, white cell count 9.6 × 10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 48 mg/L. Three sputum acid-fast bacilli smears and nucleic acid amplification tests for mycobacteria were negative. A serum precipitin assay returned strongly positive against a filamentous environmental mould.

Contrast CT of the chest demonstrates a 3.5 cm rounded intracavitary mass within a thick-walled right upper-lobe cavity. The lesion is surrounded by an air crescent and shifts position between supine and upright imaging, consistent with a mobile intracavitary mycetoma.

He tends a large home compost heap and reports turning decaying plant material without respiratory protection several times weekly in the months before symptom onset. Family members noted dense greenish mould on the compost surface.

explanation: An intracavitary mobile mycetoma in a patient with an old tuberculous cavity and positive serum precipitin to a filamentous environmental mould indicates fungal colonisation producing an aspergilloma. The history of frequent exposure to decaying vegetation and compost points to an environmental mould acquired from plant material, with Aspergillus fumigatus the most likely species.

hints.text: A 36-year-old previously well man presents to a regional clinic with a 3-week history of productive cough, intermittent fevers, night sweats and a 5 kg weight loss. He also developed a single painful ulcerated skin lesion on the left forearm over the past 2 weeks. On exam temperature 38.6°C, pulse 102/min and breath sounds reduced with coarse crackles over the right upper chest. The forearm lesion is 2.5 cm, verrucous with raised heaped-up border and central crust.

He is a park ranger who spends most days maintaining trails and clearing fallen timber along a large inland river system. Two weeks before symptoms began he assisted colleagues in dismantling a beaver lodge and disturbed moist riverbank soil. He has no known immunosuppression, is HIV negative on prior testing, takes no regular medications and has never had tuberculosis.

Full blood count shows WBC 12.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance. C-reactive protein 58 mg/L. Sputum bacterial cultures and AFB smear are negative. Punch biopsy of the forearm lesion showed mixed granulomatous inflammation with multinucleate giant cells and organisms on fungal stains; specimen was sent for culture.

Chest radiograph followed by CT shows dense consolidation of the right upper lobe with a 2.5 cm cavitary focus and adjacent satellite nodules, without pleural effusion. No miliary pattern is present and mediastinal nodes are mildly enlarged.

Culture from both sputum and skin biopsy incubated at 25°C grew a mould whereas subculture at 37°C produced large thick-walled yeast forms that demonstrate broad-based budding. The organism was recovered after several days from material taken near the riverbank where he dismantled the beaver lodge.

explanation: The combination of subacute lobar pneumonia with cavitation, a verrucous cutaneous lesion, recent disruption of riverbank soil in an endemic inland river region, and conversion of the isolate to thick-walled yeast with broad-based budding strongly points to a thermally dimorphic environmental fungus causing primary pulmonary infection with secondary cutaneous spread.

hints.text: A 32-year-old previously healthy man presented to the emergency department with abrupt onset severe nausea and profuse non-bloody vomiting that began two hours after a friend's potluck dinner. He reported six episodes of vomiting over three hours and could not tolerate oral fluids. On arrival he was tachycardic at 110/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg with orthostasis, and had dry mucous membranes but no fever.

He had no chronic illnesses, took no regular medications, and had not received antibiotics recently. Two other attendees at the same dinner described similar rapid-onset nausea and vomiting. Over the next 12 hours he developed mild crampy abdominal discomfort and two watery bowel motions but remained primarily emetic.

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 145 g/L, white cell count 12.8 × 10^9/L, sodium 136 mmol/L and creatinine 95 μmol/L consistent with mild dehydration. A sample of vomitus was submitted for microscopy and culture; Gram stain showed large Gram-positive bacilli and aerobic culture produced beta-haemolytic, catalase-positive, spore-forming colonies within 18 hours.

A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT performed because of persistent pain showed no bowel wall thickening, no free air, and no focal intraperitoneal collection. The appearance argued against invasive enteritis or perforation and supported a noninflammatory, toxin-mediated process.

On further questioning the patient said the potluck included several rice dishes that had been cooked the previous day, left at ambient temperature for several hours, then briefly reheated before serving. Multiple guests who ate the rice had similarly rapid vomiting and recovered within 24 hours.

explanation: Rapid-onset predominant vomiting within a few hours of ingestion, isolation of an aerobic, catalase-positive, spore-forming, beta-haemolytic Gram-positive bacillus from vomitus, and a history of reheated rice left at room temperature indicate foodborne illness due to Bacillus cereus producing a preformed emetic toxin. Imaging showing no enteric inflammation supports a toxin-mediated rather than invasive infection.

hints.text: A 36-year-old schoolteacher presents with 3 weeks of progressive fatigue, intermittent low-grade fevers and migrating arthralgias. Over the last 5 days she developed a right-sided facial droop with inability to fully close the right eye; temperature 37.8 °C, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg. On exam there is an isolated right lower motor neuron seventh nerve palsy and a small, nontender effusion of the left knee that limits full extension.

Symptoms began several days after a late-May weekend away. She does not recall an obvious skin lesion at the time and denies recent upper respiratory infection. Past medical history only notable for mild asthma treated with inhaled corticosteroid. One week before presentation she had intermittent palpitations and a brief presyncopal episode; an ECG performed in the emergency department showed new first-degree atrioventricular delay.

Blood tests show leukocytes 6.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L and ESR 28 mm/h. Lumbar puncture demonstrated CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis 78 × 10^6/L, protein 1.1 g/L and glucose 3.0 mmol/L with paired serum glucose 5.2 mmol/L. PCR for common neurotropic viruses was negative and routine bacterial cultures showed no growth.

Contrast MRI of the brain shows enhancement of the right facial nerve along its intratemporal course and no parenchymal lesions. Plain radiograph of the left knee shows a moderate effusion without bony abnormality.

On further questioning she recalls a 10 cm, expanding, mildly erythematous rash with central clearing on the right thigh about 2 weeks after the outdoor trip; it was neither painful nor pruritic and resolved without treatment. The trip was to a heavily wooded area in the northeastern part of the country where she had removed an engorged tick from her calf several days before the rash appeared.

explanation: Progressive migratory arthralgia, new unilateral facial nerve palsy, conduction delay and lymphocytic CSF point to a disseminated spirochetal infection acquired after a tick exposure. The history of an expanding targetoid rash following a wooded outing supports the diagnosis of infection with Borrelia burgdorferi.

hints.text: A 47-year-old man presents to the respiratory clinic with an 8-week history of nonproductive cough, intermittent low-grade fevers, and progressive fatigue. He reports a 6-kg weight loss and a slowly enlarging crusted ulcer on his left forearm, temperature 37.8°C, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and decreased breath sounds over the right upper chest on auscultation.

He was previously well, without diabetes or use of immunosuppressive medications, and had a negative HIV test three months earlier. He received two courses of oral antibiotics for presumed community pneumonia without clinical improvement, is an occasional smoker, and reports no recent travel outside the country.

Blood tests show WBC 12.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 9.8 × 10^9/L and CRP 56 mg/L, renal and liver function within reference ranges. Sputum Gram stain and routine bacterial cultures are negative, PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis is negative, and a urine antigen test for Histoplasma returned negative. A punch biopsy of the forearm lesion was submitted for histology and fungal culture.

Chest radiograph shows a dense right upper lobe consolidation with a small cavitary component. Contrast CT of the chest demonstrates a 4.5 cm lobulated consolidation in the right upper lobe with adjacent satellite nodules and mildly enlarged mediastinal nodes. Plain radiograph of the left forearm shows cortical irregularity of the distal radius beneath the skin lesion suggesting focal bone involvement.

He reports spending the previous summer renovating an old wooden fishing pier along the Ohio River, repeatedly cutting into rotting logs and breathing dust without a mask. Culture of the forearm biopsy later grew a thermally dimorphic fungus with histology showing large, thick-walled yeasts demonstrating broad-based budding.

explanation: The patient has subacute nonresolving pulmonary consolidation with a cutaneous ulcer and contiguous bony lesion, features of disseminated dimorphic fungal infection rather than typical bacterial pneumonia. The occupational exposure to rotting wood along riverbanks in the Ohio River region and the biopsy culture showing large broad-based budding yeasts point to a thermally dimorphic organism known to cause pulmonary and cutaneous disease after inhalation of environmental conidia.

hints.text: A 29-year-old paediatric nurse presents to clinic with a 4-week history of cough. The cough occurs in intense paroxysms, worse at night, and occasionally ends with gagging and an episode of vomiting; she reports a 3 kg weight loss and severe sleep disruption. Temperature 36.7°C, heart rate 92/min, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air. Chest auscultation is clear without focal crackles or wheeze.

She is otherwise well, does not smoke and is not pregnant. She completed childhood immunizations but has not received an adult booster in over 10 years. Over the past month she has worked full time on a maternity ward. Primary care prescribed two short courses of amoxicillin with no clinical improvement.

Complete blood count shows WBC 18.6 × 10^9/L with absolute lymphocytes 11.4 × 10^9/L and neutrophils 6.2 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 6 mg/L. Multiplex respiratory PCR from a nasopharyngeal swab was negative for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, rhinovirus and common coronaviruses. Routine sputum culture grew only mixed oropharyngeal flora.
Chest radiograph demonstrates no lobar consolidation, only mild peribronchial cuffing and hyperinflation. There is no pleural effusion and cardiac silhouette is normal.

In the prior two weeks three neonates on her ward developed brief apnoea with bradycardia; one was admitted to the neonatal unit. A nasopharyngeal specimen from that infant returned positive on a targeted PCR for a small fastidious aerobic gram-negative coccobacillus transmitted by respiratory droplets, and epidemiologic investigation linked the cases to the nurse.

explanation: The occupational exposure and transmission to unprotected neonates who developed apnoea strongly support infection with Bordetella pertussis, confirmed by targeted PCR in the neonate.

hints.text: A 32-year-old primary school teacher presents with 3 weeks of worsening nocturnal paroxysmal cough that wakes her several times per night and limits her work ability. She is afebrile, pulse 102/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and chest auscultation shows intermittent expiratory wheeze without focal crackles or signs of consolidation.

Symptoms began after a mild coryzal illness. She reports no history of asthma, has not received a booster immunization since adolescence, and shares a household with a 3-month-old infant who developed brief apneic episodes last week. Several of her pupils have had prolonged coughs over the past month.

Full blood count shows WBC 15.6 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 9.8 × 10^9/L and neutrophils 4.8 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 6 mg/L. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for pathogen-specific PCR and routine bacterial culture of expectorated sputum showed no common respiratory pathogens.
Chest radiograph demonstrates mild peribronchial thickening and slight hyperinflation, with no lobar consolidation or effusion.

She was started on oral azithromycin; cough frequency and nocturnal awakenings fell markedly within 48 hours and she returned to work after 5 days. The nasopharyngeal PCR returned positive for a small Gram-negative coccobacillus, and local public health confirmed identical PCR results in symptomatic children from her school.

explanation: Prolonged paroxysmal cough in an adult with relative lymphocytosis, peribronchial changes on radiograph, a classroom outbreak including infants, and rapid clinical response to a macrolide point to infection by Bordetella pertussis. PCR confirmation from nasopharyngeal sampling supports this diagnosis.
