hints.text: A 58-year-old man on the oncology ward presented with 3 days of fever, rigors and light-headedness. On arrival he was febrile to 39.1°C, heart rate 110/min and blood pressure 98/58 mmHg, and had a right subclavian central venous port with mild surrounding erythema but no purulent drainage; oral mucosa appeared dry without white plaques.

He has metastatic oesophageal adenocarcinoma and received his most recent cycle of cytotoxic chemotherapy 8 days ago. He has had severe odynophagia requiring parenteral nutrition via the port for 4 weeks and has been on broad-spectrum intravenous cefepime for presumed bacterial pneumonia for 5 days.

Initial blood tests showed WBC 0.9 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 0.2 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 210 mg/L and lactate 3.2 mmol/L. Serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan was markedly elevated above the assay upper limit at presentation.

Contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple 5–12 mm hypodense lesions in the spleen and small hypodense foci in the liver, reported as microabscesses. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed no valvular vegetations.

Two sets of peripheral blood cultures later yielded budding yeast that produced germ tubes on incubation and showed pseudohyphal elements on wet mount. The port was removed, intravenous fluconazole was started, and the patient defervesced within 48 hours with subsequent clearance of blood cultures.

explanation: The combination of high beta-D-glucan, multifocal hepatic and splenic microabscesses, germ-tube positive budding yeast in blood culture and rapid clinical response after catheter removal and azole.

hints.text: A 34-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 6 days of fevers and crampy abdominal pain. Symptoms began with three to four loose stools per day that became more painful and localised to the right lower quadrant over 48 hours; maximum recorded temperature was 39.0°C and heart rate 110 beats per minute. On examination she had focal right lower quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs and was able to tolerate small oral fluids.

She returned 10 days earlier from a two-week volunteer placement in rural Southeast Asia. On the third day of the placement she had a brief self-limited bout of watery diarrhoea that resolved without treatment. She has no chronic gastrointestinal disease, takes no immunosuppressive medication, and has no family history of inflammatory bowel disease.

Admission bloods showed white cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L with 82% neutrophils and C-reactive protein 98 mg/L. Stool microscopy demonstrated numerous faecal leukocytes and positive faecal occult blood. Blood cultures were sterile and stool ova and parasite exam was negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen revealed segmental circumferential thickening of the terminal ileum over a 7 cm segment with adjacent mesenteric lymphadenopathy and mild fat stranding. The appendix was normal in calibre. The radiologist favoured infectious or inflammatory ileitis rather than acute appendicitis.

On directed questioning she remembered repeatedly eating grilled chicken skewers that were undercooked at a street vendor while abroad. Two days after admission the microbiology lab reported that stool culture grew a motile, curved gram-negative bacillus that was oxidase positive and grew under microaerophilic conditions at 42°C.

explanation: Acute post-travel ileitis with fever, faecal leukocytes and mesenteric lymphadenopathy, combined with exposure to undercooked poultry and a stool culture showing a motile, curved oxidase-positive organism that grows at 42°C, indicates infection with Campylobacter jejuni. The imaging can mimic Crohn disease but the acute onset, systemic inflammatory response and culture findings point to an enteric bacterial pathogen acquired from poultry.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to urgent care with three days of crampy abdominal pain and diarrhoea that became small-volume and bloody over the preceding 24 hours. He had fevers to 38.9 °C, lightheadedness when standing, dry mucous membranes, a pulse of 110 /min, and focal tenderness in the right lower quadrant without peritoneal signs.

He was previously well, on no regular medications, and had not taken antibiotics recently. He denied international travel, recent hospital contact, new sexual partners, or chronic gastrointestinal symptoms. Symptoms began abruptly with a single day of fever before diarrhoea developed.

Blood count showed white cell count 13.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 10.5 × 10^9/L, CRP 92 mg/L, serum creatinine 86 µmol/L. Stool microscopy demonstrated numerous polymorphonuclear leukocytes and occult blood. Routine stool culture was submitted and remained pending at presentation.

Contrast CT abdomen demonstrated segmental mural thickening and mucosal hyperenhancement of the terminal ileum and adjacent ascending colon with several enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. The appendix was normal and there was no free air or abscess.

He later reported eating lightly grilled poultry skewers at an outdoor food market 48 hours before symptom onset. Stool culture grew motile, oxidase-positive, gram-negative curved rods that grew preferentially at 42 °C and hydrolysed hippurate.

explanation: Acute febrile inflammatory bloody diarrhoea with right-sided ileocolitis and recent poultry exposure points to an invasive enteric bacterial pathogen. The culture phenotype described, together with the clinical picture, is diagnostic of Campylobacter jejuni.

hints.text: A 26-year-old woman presents to a sexual health clinic with three weeks of dull lower abdominal pain, new intermenstrual spotting, and deep dyspareunia. She reports increased purulent vaginal discharge. On examination she is afebrile at 37.2°C, has bilateral lower abdominal tenderness, and bimanual exam elicits cervical motion tenderness with mucopurulent endocervical discharge.

She is nulliparous and takes combined oral contraception. She started a new male partner two months ago and uses condoms inconsistently. She has not had STI screening in the past year and has no history of pelvic surgery.

Pregnancy test negative. C-reactive protein 22 mg/L, white cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L. Urine dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase and microscopy shows 25 leukocytes per high-power field, but routine urine culture shows no growth after 48 hours. Endocervical Gram stain shows many polymorphonuclear cells without gram-negative intracellular diplococci.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows bilateral tubular, fluid-filled adnexal structures up to 12 mm with thickened walls and small adjacent complex free fluid. Radiology report comments that findings are most consistent with acute salpingitis.

First-void urine nucleic acid amplification test detected DNA of a small obligate intracellular bacterium while culture on routine media remained negative. The recent male partner had urethral symptoms and tested positive on the same amplification assay.

explanation: Young sexually active woman with mucopurulent cervicitis, cervical motion tenderness, pyuria with negative routine culture, and sonographic salpingitis points to an STI causing upper genital tract infection. A positive nucleic acid amplification test from first-void urine that identifies an obligate intracellular organism confirms infection with Chlamydia trachomatis. Treating the patient and her partner is necessary to prevent reinfection and complications.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman admitted for induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia developed fever to 39.1°C and rigours on day 6 of treatment. She reported new pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath; exam showed tachycardia 112/min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, and a tender, erythematous area around her right internal jugular central venous catheter without frank purulence.

She received cytarabine and daunorubicin 6 days earlier and now has grade 3 oral mucositis. Her absolute neutrophil count fell below 0.2 × 10^9/L after chemotherapy. The tunneled central line was placed 3 weeks before admission and she has been eating packed meals from home because of intractable nausea.

Blood cultures drawn from the central line and a peripheral vein became positive at 18–24 hours. Gram stain reported large Gram-positive rods. Admission CRP was 188 mg/L, procalcitonin 4.2 µg/L, and repeat ANC 0.09 × 10^9/L.

Contrast CT chest showed multiple bilateral nodules 5–20 mm in diameter, several with central cavitation, and a small right pleural effusion. Transthoracic echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations.

The patient reported eating reheated rice porridge she brought from home daily. Culture of a retained portion of that porridge and swabs of her thermos grew the same organism as the blood isolate: large, motile, spore-forming, beta-haemolytic Gram-positive rods that were resistant to penicillin and third-generation cephalosporins and susceptible to vancomycin and gentamicin.

explanation: Neutropenic fever with central line involvement and septic pulmonary nodules points to catheter-related bacteraemia. Rapidly growing, beta-haemolytic, motile, spore-forming Gram-positive rods recovered from both blood and reheated rice strongly support Bacillus cereus as the source. The organism's resistance to beta-lactams and recovery from contaminated starchy food with matching isolates explains the clinical course.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with three days of intense vulvar itching and thick vaginal discharge. She reports mild dysuria and pain with intercourse; on speculum examination there is adherent white curd-like discharge and erythematous vulvovaginal mucosa, temperature 36.8°C and heart rate 78/min.

She completed a seven-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate for a sinus infection 10 days ago and started combined oral contraception six months prior. She has no known diabetes, no recent pregnancy, and no systemic corticosteroid use.
Vaginal pH is 4.0. KOH wet mount of the discharge demonstrates numerous budding yeast forms and pseudohyphae; saline wet mount shows no clue cells or motile trichomonads.
Transvaginal ultrasound performed because of pelvic discomfort shows normal uterus and adnexa with no fluid collections or abscess.
A single 150 mg oral dose of an azole agent was given and the patient reported marked improvement of pruritus and discharge within 48 hours, with complete resolution by one week.

explanation: Rapid clinical response to single-dose oral azole is consistent with an azole-susceptible mucosal Candida species. The most likely organism in this setting is Candida albicans.

hints.text: A 62-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with four days of profuse watery diarrhoea and crampy lower abdominal pain. She reported 8 to 10 loose stools per day, lightheadedness when standing, fever to 38.6°C, and on examination was tender in the left lower quadrant with mild abdominal distension.

Two weeks earlier she completed a 10-day course of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics for a complicated urinary tract infection. Her medical history includes gastro-oesophageal reflux disease treated with a proton pump inhibitor and osteoarthritis; she had no recent travel or unusual food exposures and lived independently prior to this illness.

Blood tests showed white cell count 21.3 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 110 g/L, creatinine 160 μmol/L (baseline approximately 75 μmol/L) and C-reactive protein 120 mg/L. Stool cultures for routine enteric bacteria and ova and parasites were negative, and stool microscopy showed fecal leukocytes.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated diffuse colonic wall thickening most pronounced in the ascending and transverse colon with pericolonic fat stranding and mild luminal dilation, without free air or focal perforation.

Infection‑control investigators noted a recent cluster of hospital-linked antibiotic-associated diarrhoea on the ward where she had been treated previously, and environmental sampling recovered resistant spores. Multiple affected patients had stool testing positive for toxin genes by PCR with matching clinical courses.

explanation: The combination of these features is most consistent with Clostridioides difficile infection.

hints.text: A 72-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with six days of profuse watery diarrhoea, diffuse cramping abdominal pain, and increasing weakness. She reported ten bowel motions per day, could not tolerate oral intake, and on arrival was febrile at 38.1°C, pulse 110/min, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg with dry mucous membranes.

Three weeks earlier she completed a 10-day course of oral broad-spectrum antibiotics after hospital admission for community-acquired pneumonia. She lives at home but returned from a two-week stay in a rehabilitation facility after a fall and takes a proton pump inhibitor for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. She has stage 3 chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes.

Admission bloods showed white blood cells 28 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, haemoglobin 110 g/L, platelets 320 × 10^9/L, creatinine 180 μmol/L (baseline 95 μmol/L), and albumin 28 g/L. Stool microscopy was negative for ova and parasites and routine stool culture for common enteric bacteria was pending.

Bedside flexible sigmoidoscopy performed because of ongoing high-volume diarrhoea revealed extensive raised yellowish plaques on an erythematous colonic mucosa, with no focal perforation on concurrent abdominal radiograph. CT abdomen performed earlier showed marked pancolonic wall thickening without free air.

She failed to improve after 48 hours of supportive care and an initial course of oral metronidazole, so oral vancomycin was started; diarrhoea frequency declined substantially within 72 hours. A stool nucleic acid amplification test for a toxin gene returned positive, confirming the diagnosis.

explanation: Endoscopic plaques consistent with pseudomembranous colitis plus a positive stool NAAT for a toxin gene and rapid clinical response to oral vancomycin make the diagnosis most likely.

hints.text: A 37-year-old woman presented to the neurology clinic with five days of progressive right-sided facial weakness and difficulty closing the right eye. She reported six weeks of intermittent migratory joint pains and two brief febrile episodes, and on examination she had a lower motor neuron facial palsy on the right with inability to wrinkle the forehead or fully close the eyelid.

She is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications, and is not immunosuppressed. She recalled a weekend camping trip in a temperate woodland region two months earlier and subsequently noted a single enlarging circular erythematous patch on her left thigh that expanded over several days then slowly faded without treatment.

Blood tests showed WBC 11.2 × 10^9/L and CRP 36 mg/L. Lumbar puncture produced clear CSF with WBC 180 × 10^6/L (≈90% lymphocytes), protein 1.2 g/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, Gram stain negative and no growth on routine bacterial culture.

Contrast MRI of the brain demonstrated enhancement of the intratemporal segment of the right facial nerve without parenchymal abnormality. Ultrasound of the right knee showed a 2.5 cm suprapatellar effusion with synovial thickening but no osteomyelitis.

On directed questioning she remembered removing an engorged tick from the left thigh about six weeks after the camping trip and the bite site developed an expanding annular erythematous lesion with central clearing. Two-tier serology was performed and returned positive with a reactive screening assay and confirmatory immunoblot bands that meet laboratory criteria for infection.

explanation: The combination of a prior expanding annular rash at a bite site, weeks of migratory arthralgia, and new peripheral facial nerve palsy indicates disseminated infection from a tick-borne spirochete. CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and MRI facial nerve enhancement support neuroinvasion. Positive two-tier serology with confirmatory immunoblot establishes infection by Borrelia burgdorferi.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man on postoperative day 2 after emergency laparotomy for perforated diverticulitis presents with 24 hours of escalating pain and swelling at the lower midline incision. He reports severe, localized pain that feels much worse than the appearance of the wound. On arrival he is febrile at 38.9°C, heart rate 120/min, blood pressure 86/50 mmHg. The incision edge is dusky with mild tense swelling but no frank purulent discharge.

His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes and peripheral vascular disease. Intraoperative notes recorded gross fecal contamination and some devitalized tissue at the incision. Perioperative broad-spectrum antibiotics were given but the surgeon noted substantial soft-tissue contamination and left a subcutaneous drain.

Hemoglobin fell from 130 g/L preoperatively to 78 g/L. Total bilirubin is 68 μmol/L and plasma LDH is 1 200 U/L. Haptoglobin is undetectable. White blood cell count is 18.5 × 10^9/L and the urine is dark with positive blood on dipstick but few red cells on microscopy.

Contrast CT of the abdomen and anterior abdominal wall shows extensive gas within the subcutaneous tissues and underlying rectus muscle on the left lower abdominal wall, tracking along the fascial plane without a discrete fluid collection.

The patient underwent immediate radical surgical debridement and was started on high-dose intravenous penicillin plus clindamycin. Intraoperative tissue sent for anaerobic culture produced heavy growth within 12 hours. The colonies showed rapid gas production in culture and a characteristic double zone of hemolysis on blood agar. After source control and ongoing antibiotics the hemolysis stabilized and hemodynamics improved.

explanation: Rapidly progressive postoperative soft-tissue infection with soft-tissue gas, profound intravascular hemolysis, and an anaerobic culture showing fast growth with a double zone of hemolysis indicate clostridial myonecrosis due to Clostridium perfringens. Urgent debridement plus high-dose penicillin and an agent that suppresses toxin production are the appropriate immediate measures, which in this case halted ongoing hemolysis.

hints.text: A 36-year-old woman presented after 48 hours of progressive blurred vision, slurred speech, dry mouth and difficulty swallowing. She reports new binocular diplopia and progressive neck weakness, is afebrile, respiratory rate 18/min, SaO2 96% on room air, and has bilateral ptosis with impaired extraocular movements but preserved facial sensation.

No chronic illness or regular medications, no recent antibiotics or anaesthetic exposure. Symptoms began about one day after a shared community dinner; two other attendees had brief diarrhoea but no neurologic complaints. She has no prior neuromuscular disease.

Full blood count 7.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 3 mg/L, electrolytes within reference limits. Lumbar puncture: opening pressure normal, CSF protein 0.35 g/L, cells 1 × 10^6/L. Serum acetylcholine-receptor and MuSK antibodies were negative.

MRI brain with angiography showed no acute infarct or structural lesion to explain cranial neuropathies. Contrast chest CT performed to evaluate myasthenia returned without thymic enlargement or mediastinal mass.

Leftover food from the community dinner included home-preserved jarred vegetables she ate three days before onset. Public health testing of the jar detected a neuroparalytic toxin by bioassay and an anaerobic, spore-forming organism was cultured from residue on the jar lid.

explanation: The acute, descending cranial nerve dysfunction with autonomic dry mouth, preserved sensation, normal CSF, negative neuromuscular antibodies and absence of thymoma point away from central causes and myasthenia. The link to home-preserved food with detection of a neuroparalytic toxin and an anaerobic spore-former supports foodborne botulism due to Clostridium botulinum.

hints.text: A 67-year-old man presented to the emergency department 48 hours after an elective right hemicolectomy with sudden worsening of diffuse abdominal pain and new confusion. He was febrile 39.0°C, hypotensive 86/52 mmHg, heart rate 118 min−1, and visibly jaundiced with dark urine.

His medical history included type 2 diabetes and coronary artery disease. The surgical report noted heavy contamination of the peritoneal cavity from a recently perforated tumour and prolonged operative time, but no obvious retained foreign body; postoperative course until this morning had been unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed a precipitous fall in haemoglobin from 130 g/L preoperatively to 62 g/L, total bilirubin 240 µmol/L with predominantly indirect fraction, lactate dehydrogenase 2,850 U/L, and undetectable haptoglobin. Direct antiglobulin test was negative and peripheral blood film demonstrated numerous ghost cells and spherocytes. Two sets of blood culture bottles flagged positive overnight in the anaerobic bottles.

Contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple gas-containing foci in the right hepatic lobe adjacent to the surgical anastomosis and portal venous gas, with no clear thin-walled abscess cavity on early imaging.

He underwent urgent reoperation with debridement of necrotic tissue and was started on high-dose intravenous penicillin plus clindamycin. Hemodynamic collapse and ongoing intravascular haemolysis slowed within 12 hours. Anaerobic cultures from blood and a hepatic aspirate later grew a rapidly growing, spore-forming, non-motile gram-positive bacillus producing lecithinase and a characteristic double-zone haemolysis on blood agar.

explanation: Postoperative sepsis with abrupt intravascular haemolysis, gas-forming hepatic lesions and portal venous gas points to an anaerobic pyogenic process seeded from the gut. The culture phenotype of a rapidly growing, spore-forming, non-motile gram-positive bacillus with lecithinase activity and double-zone haemolysis identifies the causative bacterium. Rapid source control and high-dose penicillin plus clindamycin arrested the haemolytic process, supporting the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 30-year-old man presents to the rheumatology clinic with three weeks of progressive asymmetric joint pain. He reports a swollen, painful right knee and aching left ankle with morning stiffness of about 45 minutes, difficulty bearing weight, subjective low-grade fever to 37.8°C, and new gritty sensation and mild redness in his right eye; exam shows a tense right knee effusion with reduced range of motion.

Six weeks before onset he had one week of dysuria and a clear urethral discharge after unprotected vaginal sex with a new partner. He sought care at a walk-in clinic and received a five-day course of oral ciprofloxacin with only partial symptom relief. He denies recent diarrhoea, recent travel, or prior rheumatologic disease.

Peripheral blood tests show WBC 9.2 × 10^9/L, ESR 48 mm/h, CRP 62 mg/L. Right knee aspirate is cloudy with WBC 60 × 10^9/L, 85% neutrophils; Gram stain shows no organisms and routine bacterial cultures remain sterile at 48 hours. HLA-B27 is positive.

Ultrasound of the right knee confirms a large complex effusion with synovial thickening and increased Doppler signal. MRI of the pelvis demonstrates bone marrow oedema and erosive change at the right sacroiliac joint compatible with an inflammatory sacroiliitis.

First-void urine nucleic acid amplification returns positive for an organism that does not grow on routine culture and is known to be obligately intracellular. The patient was started on oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and had resolution of urethral symptoms within days and gradual improvement in joint pain and eye symptoms over weeks.

explanation: The sequence of recent untreated urethritis after new sexual exposure followed by sterile asymmetric oligoarthritis, new ocular symptoms, HLA-B27 positivity, and a positive urine NAAT for a non-cultivable obligate intracellular bacterium treated successfully with doxycycline points to Chlamydia trachomatis as the trigger for postinfectious reactive arthritis.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented after 48 h of progressive blurred vision and dry mouth. Afebrile, HR 96/min, bilateral ptosis and soft-palate weakness with preserved limb strength.
No respiratory prodrome or new meds. Dental extraction 10 days earlier treated briefly with oral antibiotics.
WBC 7.8 × 10^9/L. CSF 1 × 10^6/L cells, protein 0.35 g/L.
Brain MRI including diffusion sequences normal.
He shared home‑preserved smoked fish at a family meal three days before symptoms; culture from the fish grew an anaerobic toxin‑producing bacillus.

explanation: Acute afebrile bulbar palsy with normal CSF and imaging plus a linked contaminated home‑preserved food that yielded an anaerobic toxin producer indicates foodborne neurotoxin-mediated bacterial infection.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously healthy man presented to the emergency clinic with 72 hours of fever, myalgias and new central chest discomfort that worsened with exertion. He was febrile to 38.3°C, heart rate 112 bpm, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, and on auscultation had a soft S3 and no murmurs; he reported reduced exercise tolerance and mild dyspnoea on minimal exertion.

He works as a childcare assistant and three days before his symptoms began a 2-year-old in his care developed fever, multiple small painful oral ulcers and scattered vesicles on the palms; the child remained febrile for two days and recovered without antibiotics. He has no travel, illicit drug use, or recent vaccinations and takes no regular medications.

High-sensitivity cardiac troponin I was 1 800 ng/L (reference < 14 ng/L). CRP was 48 mg/L, white blood cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L with relative lymphocyte predominance. Serial ECGs showed diffuse ST-segment elevations less concave than expected for pericarditis and mild PR depressions in several leads.

Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated global left ventricular hypokinesia with estimated ejection fraction 35%. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging performed on day 4 showed myocardial oedema on T2-weighted imaging and non-ischaemic late gadolinium enhancement in the lateral wall, consistent with acute myocarditis.

Reverse-transcription PCR from the patient blood and a throat swab from the symptomatic child detected identical viral RNA sequences matching strains previously reported in outbreaks of childhood febrile oral-and-palm vesicular illness and in cases of viral myocarditis.

explanation: Acute myocarditis after exposure to a young child with febrile oral and hand vesicles points to a small non-polio RNA virus that causes both hand-foot-and-mouth or herpangina-like illness and myocarditis. Elevated troponin, inflammatory markers, and cardiac MRI features confirm viral myocarditis. Identical viral RNA sequences in patient and child support transmission of that pathogen as the cause of his myocardial inflammation.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously healthy man presented with a 3-week history of persistent dry cough, right-sided pleuritic chest pain and progressive fatigue. He also noticed several painful red nodules on the anterior shins that developed over the past week and now limit his walking. On arrival temperature 38.1°C, pulse 94/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Lung examination shows decreased breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right lower lung field.

He is a construction worker, a non-smoker and takes no regular medications. He has no diabetes, no known immunosuppression and a negative HIV test six months ago. Primary care had treated him empirically with a 7-day course of amoxicillin without clinical improvement.

Full blood count shows WBC 12.3 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.4 × 10^9/L. C reactive protein is 48 mg/L. Sputum bacterial cultures were sterile and fungal serology returned positive for IgM with a rising complement-fixing antibody directed at a dimorphic environmental mould.

Chest radiograph demonstrates a right lower lobe consolidation with a 2.5 cm thin-walled cavitary area. CT chest confirms focal nodular consolidation in the posterior right lower lobe with adjacent small cavitation and mild ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

Two weeks before symptom onset he spent five days on a volunteer demolition project in rural southern Arizona. There was extensive soil disturbance and a high dust load during a wind event. Several co-workers reported similar respiratory symptoms.

explanation: Subacute pulmonary illness with erythema nodosum, peripheral eosinophilia, a cavitary right lower lobe lesion, and a rising complement-fixing antibody after heavy dust exposure in southern Arizona points to infection with Coccidioides species. The patient is immunocompetent and the serology pattern with clinical cavitation supports active primary pulmonary infection.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 5 days of progressive sore throat, odynophagia and muffled speech. He reported a low-grade fever and increasing difficulty breathing when supine; temperature 38.1°C, heart rate 102/min, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and exam showed tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy and an adherent white-gray coating over both tonsils and the posterior pharynx that limited visualization of the larynx.

He arrived in the country as a refugee three weeks earlier after living in a region with recent disruption of routine childhood immunisation programmes. He had no reliable childhood records and said he had not received any adult boosters. Household members include a school-age nephew who developed a sore throat two days earlier.

Blood tests showed WBC 15.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and CRP 112 mg/L, creatinine 78 μmol/L. A throat swab Gram stain demonstrated pleomorphic Gram-positive bacilli among squamous epithelial cells. Blood cultures were obtained and pending.

Contrast CT of the neck performed for progressive dysphagia demonstrated marked mucosal irregularity of the oropharynx with circumferential soft-tissue thickening and near-complete narrowing of the supraglottic airway. There was no discrete abscess but substantial adjacent oedema of submandibular and parapharyngeal soft tissues.

Public health investigation identified two additional symptomatic household contacts who were unimmunised. Oropharyngeal cultures from the proband grew a pleomorphic, club-shaped Gram-positive bacillus in characteristic palisading arrangement and in vitro toxin production testing was positive.

explanation: The combination of incomplete immunisation and an adherent oropharyngeal membrane with airway narrowing, pleomorphic Gram-positive bacilli on throat culture, and a positive toxin assay identifies toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae as the cause.

hints.text: A 35-year-old man presents with a three-week history of progressive dry cough, pleuritic right-sided chest pain and increasing fatigue after missing several days of work. On initial examination he is afebrile, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air and has reduced breath sounds at the right lower lung field.

He has treated type 2 diabetes mellitus with metformin, last measured HbA1c 8.2%. He is a non-smoker, has no known immunosuppression and reports symptoms began subacutely without preceding antibiotic use.

Full blood count shows WBC 13.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.6 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 48 mg/L. Serology from a local mycology service returned positive specific IgM and a complement fixation titre of 1:16.

Chest radiograph shows a right lower zone airspace opacity. CT thorax demonstrates a 2.8 cm thick-walled cavitating nodule in the right lower lobe with surrounding nodular ground glass changes and several subcentimetre satellite nodules.

Two weeks before symptom onset he had worked on an earth-moving crew in the Sonoran Desert near Phoenix where heavy dust plumes were generated during grading. Several co-workers reported transient respiratory illnesses at the same time.

explanation: Subacute pulmonary illness with a cavitating nodule, peripheral eosinophilia and positive specific IgM with moderate complement fixation titre, in the setting of heavy dust exposure in the Sonoran Desert, is most consistent with infection by Coccidioides species. The imaging and serology together support a fungal pulmonary infection acquired after inhalation of environmental spores.

hints.text: A 26-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 72 hours of pleuritic central chest pain and progressive exertional dyspnoea. He reports high fevers at home and is febrile 38.8°C and tachycardic 118 bpm on arrival, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, with clear lungs on auscultation and reproducible left anterior chest wall tenderness on palpation.

He was previously well, works as a software engineer, and has no cardiovascular risk factors. One week before presentation he had a brief febrile illness with sore throat and two days of small painful mouth ulcers, and he cared for his 2-year-old niece who had a recent febrile illness with vesicles on her hands and feet.

Blood tests show troponin T 2 100 ng/L (reference < 14 ng/L), C-reactive protein 92 mg/L, and white cell count 7.8 × 10^9/L. Blood cultures remain sterile at 48 hours and a nasopharyngeal viral PCR panel returned without a respiratory viral pathogen.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates global left ventricular hypokinesia with estimated ejection fraction 35% and a small pericardial effusion. Cardiac magnetic resonance shows myocardial oedema and subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement of the lateral wall consistent with acute myocarditis.

Public health follow-up revealed the child in the household had hand and mouth lesions the week before. PCR testing detected the same non-polio enterovirus RNA in the patient's serum and stool and in the child's throat swab, with sequence matching an enterovirus lineage known to cause both febrile herpangina/hand-foot lesions in children and sporadic myocarditis in adults.

explanation: The sequence of a preceding oropharyngeal febrile illness, household child with hand and foot vesicles, markedly elevated troponin with reduced LVEF, and enteroviral RNA detected in both patients points to a non-polio enterovirus causing viral myocarditis. Taken together these findings are most consistent with coxsackievirus infection causing acute myocarditis in the adult and a concurrent hand‑mouth illness in the child.

hints.text: A 36-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a three-week history of progressive, bifrontal headache, intermittent low-grade fevers, and increasing confusion. On examination he is febrile to 37.9°C, disoriented to time, and has moderate nuchal rigidity but no focal motor deficit.
He has known HIV infection but stopped antiretroviral therapy 18 months ago because of work instability. Recent outpatient testing recorded a CD4 lymphocyte count of 40 × 10^6/L.

Lumbar puncture shows opening pressure 32 cm H2O, CSF WBC 120 × 10^6/L with lymphocytic predominance, protein 1.2 g/L, and glucose 1.8 mmol/L while concurrent serum glucose is 6.8 mmol/L. Routine CSF Gram stain and bacterial cultures are negative.

Contrast MRI brain demonstrates leptomeningeal enhancement most pronounced at the basal cisterns and multiple small, well demarcated cystic lesions within the basal ganglia and perivascular spaces, without a large mass or acute infarct.
On further questioning he reports cleaning pigeon nests on the apartment roof most weekends and often breathing dust from dried bird droppings while working.

explanation: Subacute meningoencephalitis in a patient with profound CD4 lymphopenia, markedly elevated CSF opening pressure, lymphocytic CSF, and MRI showing basal meningeal involvement and dilated perivascular spaces is most consistent with an encapsulated environmental yeast acquired from bird droppings that causes meningitis in advanced immunosuppression.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents to the clinic with two weeks of profuse watery diarrhea. He reports 8 to 12 loose, non-bloody stools per day, progressive fatigue, a 4 kg weight loss, and lightheadedness on standing; on exam his pulse is 110 beats/min and orthostatic changes are present.

He is three months status post kidney transplant and takes tacrolimus and mycophenolate. His surgical recovery was uncomplicated and he lives in a shared apartment. He has no recent antibiotic use and receives routine prophylaxis for cytomegalovirus.

Blood tests show potassium 2.9 mmol/L, creatinine 140 μmol/L (baseline 110 μmol/L), white blood cell count 10.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 38 mg/L. Multiplex stool PCR panel for common bacterial enteropathogens and toxin testing for Clostridioides difficile are negative.
Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen demonstrates diffuse small-bowel wall thickening with mild mesenteric lymphadenopathy and no focal obstructing lesion or colonic wall thickening. There is no ascites.

He reports swimming daily in a chlorinated hotel lap pool the week before symptoms began and several other swimmers later complained of diarrhoea. Public health testing of his stool by concentrated modified acid-fast stain and PCR detected 4–6 μm oocysts consistent with a coccidian protozoan.

explanation: A kidney transplant recipient on immunosuppression with prolonged watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, small-bowel mucosal thickening, and exposure to a recreational pool raises concern for an enteric coccidian infection. Identification of small, acid-fast oocysts in stool with supportive PCR confirms the specific protozoan cause in this patient.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presents with six weeks of progressive non-productive cough and fatigue, and three weeks of intermittent bifrontal headache with short episodes of confusion and recent difficulty remembering names. On arrival he is afebrile at 37.9°C, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, chest auscultation reveals diminished breath sounds and faint crackles over the right upper zone, and bedside cognitive testing shows impaired short-term recall.

He has a 10-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with weekly methotrexate and intermittent oral prednisone, recently 10–15 mg daily for three months for a disease flare. He has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, no known HIV infection, negative HIV test two years ago, and no recent travel or known tuberculosis exposure.

Peripheral blood white cell count 8.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 36 mg/L. Lumbar puncture opening pressure 32 cm H2O, cerebrospinal fluid WBC 95 × 10^6/L with 80% lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, glucose 2.2 mmol/L while concurrent serum glucose is 6.4 mmol/L. Gram stain and acid-fast stain of CSF are reported as no organisms seen.

Contrast brain MRI shows multiple small T2 hyperintense lesions clustered in the basal ganglia and along perivascular spaces, with scant leptomeningeal enhancement and no large ring-enhancing abscess. Chest CT demonstrates a solitary 2.5 cm right upper lobe nodule with surrounding ground-glass change and no significant hilar lymphadenopathy.
He reports weekly maintenance work on his apartment building roof where he has routinely swept dried bird droppings from pigeon nests for the past five years, often without a mask.

explanation: Subacute pulmonary and meningeal disease in a patient receiving chronic immunosuppression, together with elevated CSF opening pressure, lymphocytic CSF with low glucose, basal ganglia and perivascular cystic lesions on MRI, and prolonged exposure to pigeon droppings point to infection with Cryptococcus neoformans. The combination of inhalational exposure, solitary pulmonary focus and characteristic CNS imaging helps distinguish this diagnosis from tuberculosis or toxoplasmosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 35-year-old warehouse worker presented to the emergency department after five days of worsening sore throat, progressive dysphagia and increasing neck tightness. He reported hoarseness and now had audible inspiratory stridor, temperature 38.2°C and heart rate 112/min with firm anterior cervical swelling on exam.

He recently arrived from a region with low adult immunisation coverage and lives in crowded employer-provided dormitories. He had no chronic illnesses, no recent antibiotics, and several roommates had similar mild sore throats earlier in the week.

Blood tests showed WBC 18.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and CRP 142 mg/L. Serum troponin I was 0.18 µg/L and 12-lead ECG showed intermittent first-degree atrioventricular block. Throat swab culture was pending.

Lateral neck radiograph demonstrated marked prevertebral soft tissue thickening with narrowing of the oropharyngeal and upper tracheal air column. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mildly reduced left ventricular function compared with prior normal study.

After administration of an equine-derived antitoxin and intravenous penicillin the patient's airway swelling stopped progressing and conduction abnormality resolved over 48 hours. Throat culture grew small grey colonies; microscopy showed club-shaped, pleomorphic gram-positive bacilli with metachromatic granules and PCR detected a gene encoding an exotoxin that inhibits eukaryotic protein synthesis.

explanation: Upper-airway obstruction with regional swelling and concurrent myocarditis in an unimmunised adult suggests a toxigenic respiratory bacillus. The culture morphology and detection of an exotoxin gene that halts host protein synthesis identify a toxigenic, club-shaped gram-positive bacillus as the cause.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to the antenatal clinic with 10 days of low-grade fever, profound fatigue, and sore throat. She has tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy on examination, a temperature of 38.4°C, and a palpable spleen 3 cm below the costal margin.

She is 20 weeks pregnant, previously healthy, and takes no regular medications. She reports no recent travel, no history of immunosuppression, and no known sick contacts other than children in her workplace.

Full blood count shows a WBC 6.5 × 10^9/L with 15% atypical lymphocytes. Liver enzymes are elevated with ALT 165 U/L and AST 140 U/L. A heterophile antibody test is negative and EBV serology is not consistent with acute infection.
Abdominal ultrasound confirms mild hepatosplenomegaly without focal lesions. A dated fetal ultrasound performed the same day shows normal biometry and no structural abnormality.

She works as an assistant in a centre for infants and toddlers and frequently cleans pacifiers and handles children’s saliva and diapers. One toddler in her room recently had a prolonged febrile upper respiratory illness, and she is worried about maternal infection affecting the pregnancy.

explanation: A pregnant adult with a mononucleosis-like illness, negative heterophile test, atypical lymphocytosis, transaminitis, and daycare exposure points to maternal primary infection with cytomegalovirus. The occupational exposure to young children and pregnancy raise concern for vertical transmission and prompt pathogen-specific testing and obstetric counselling.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously well man presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of high fever, severe myalgias and retro-orbital headache. On arrival his temperature is 39.3°C, pulse 110 beats/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, and examination shows a diffuse blanching maculopapular rash, scattered petechiae on the forearms, and mild gum bleeding when asked to brush his teeth.

He returned 4 days ago from a 10-day visit to urban and peri-urban areas in Bangkok, Thailand. He reports numerous daytime mosquito bites, took no malaria chemoprophylaxis, has no chronic medical conditions, and had no similar illness in the past.

Complete blood count shows leukopenia with a white cell count 2.8 × 10^9/L and thrombocytopenia with platelets 60 × 10^9/L. Hematocrit is 0.52 L/L. Alanine aminotransferase is 140 U/L and creatinine is within reference range.

Point of care ultrasound demonstrates small bilateral pleural effusions and a thickened gallbladder wall measuring 6 mm with trace free fluid in the right upper quadrant. Chest radiograph is otherwise unremarkable.

Acute serum real-time PCR detected a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus known to be transmitted by daytime-biting mosquitoes in the region he visited. Paired serology shows a rise in virus-specific IgM between day 3 and day 10 of illness.

explanation: The combination of high fever with severe myalgia and retro-orbital pain, rash and mucosal bleeding, leukopenia and marked thrombocytopenia with hemoconcentration, ultrasound evidence of plasma leakage, recent travel to Southeast Asia, and positive PCR for a mosquito-borne positive-sense RNA virus supports a diagnosis of dengue virus infection.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 4 days of high fever, diffuse myalgia and persistent vomiting. On arrival he was febrile 39.5°C, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, and had mild right upper quadrant tenderness without hepatomegaly.

He is otherwise healthy and returned 7 days ago from a two-week trip to Southeast Asia where he spent time in both urban and peri-urban neighbourhoods. Six years earlier he had an undiagnosed febrile illness with a transient rash while living in the same region.

Initial blood tests showed leukopenia 2.0 × 10^9/L, platelet count 28 × 10^9/L, and haemoconcentration with haematocrit 0.56 L/L. Alanine aminotransferase was 145 U/L and creatinine was within reference limits.

Point of care abdominal ultrasound demonstrated gallbladder wall thickening with a small volume of pericholecystic fluid and a small right-sided pleural effusion on the subcostal view. No biliary dilatation or stones were seen.

Local public health alerted clinicians to a surge of an arboviral febrile illness transmitted by daytime-biting Aedes mosquitoes in the area he visited, associated with marked platelet drops and plasma leakage. His acute serum returned positive on the outbreak-targeted acute-phase antigen assay.

explanation: Travel to an area with an Aedes-transmitted arboviral outbreak, a prior compatible febrile episode suggesting possible secondary exposure, pronounced thrombocytopenia with haemoconcentration and ultrasound evidence of plasma leakage are most consistent with dengue virus infection. The positive acute-phase antigen test directed at the outbreak agent supports this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presents to the hepatology clinic with six months of dull right upper quadrant discomfort and early satiety. She has had an intermittent dry cough on exertion, denies fever or jaundice, and on examination has a smooth, non-tender hepatic margin palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin.

Her medical history is notable only for well controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin and a routine abdominal ultrasound 12 months ago that reported a small, indeterminate hepatic lesion that was observed. She has not received immunosuppressive medications and has no history of recent travel or hepatotoxic exposures.

Full blood count shows WBC 8.2 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.3 × 10^9/L (15%), hemoglobin 130 g/L. Liver tests are near normal with ALT 48 U/L, AST 42 U/L, ALP 310 U/L, bilirubin 12 μmol/L. Serum IgG directed against a cyst-forming helminth antigen returns strongly positive.

Contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrates a 9.5 cm well circumscribed multiloculated cystic lesion in the right hepatic lobe containing several internal, rounded daughter cysts of varying sizes and focal peripheral wall calcification. There is no free intraperitoneal fluid or obvious biliary obstruction.

On further questioning she reports lifelong residence in a rural sheep-farming community, frequent participation in home slaughter of sheep, and two working farm dogs that sleep in the house and are infrequently dewormed; household members have occasionally noticed small rice-grain like segments in dog faeces.

explanation: A large multiloculated hepatic cyst with internal daughter cysts and peripheral calcification, together with eosinophilia and strongly positive cyst-specific IgG, points to a cyst-producing cestode infection of the liver.

hints.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the transplant clinic 6 weeks after deceased-donor renal transplantation with 10 days of low-grade fever, progressive malaise, and frequent watery diarrhoea. He is febrile to 38.2°C, pulse 96/min, blood pressure 130/78 mmHg, and abdominal examination shows mild diffuse tenderness without peritonism; urine output has fallen compared with his immediate post‑operative baseline.

Induction therapy included anti-thymocyte globulin followed by maintenance tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil; he is on a prednisone taper. The donor was seropositive for a common herpesvirus while the recipient was seronegative before transplant, and there were no early post‑op complications.

Blood tests show leucopenia 2.1 × 10^9/L, thrombocytopenia 95 × 10^9/L, ALT 265 U/L and AST 180 U/L. Stool studies are negative for bacterial pathogens and C. difficile. Mucosal biopsy from the rectosigmoid shows markedly enlarged cells with single large basophilic intranuclear inclusions surrounded by a clear halo.
Contrast CT abdomen demonstrates circumferential thickening of the distal colon and rectum with pericolonic fat stranding, greater on the left side, consistent with segmental colitis.

Quantitative plasma viral PCR returns at 2.4 × 10^6 IU/mL. Intravenous antiviral therapy is started and over 7 days the patient defervesces, diarrhoea improves, and viral load falls to 1.1 × 10^3 IU/mL.

explanation: A seronegative recipient of a seropositive donor with post‑transplant fever, colitis, cytopenias, and biopsy showing large cells with intranuclear inclusions points to cytomegalovirus disease.

hints.text: A 25-year-old previously healthy man presents to the emergency department with 5 days of crampy right lower quadrant abdominal pain and anorexia. He has had intermittent perianal discomfort for about 8 weeks that he calls 'itching' and reports worse sleep; on exam he is afebrile, pulse 92/min, and has focal tenderness at McBurney's point without peritoneal signs.

He lives in shared student housing and works part time at a café. Two housemates and his 6-year-old sister have recently complained of nocturnal perianal itching. He had two brief courses of oral antibiotics in the past month for presumed urinary symptoms.

Complete blood count shows WBC 8.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 5.9 × 10^9/L and eosinophils 0.8 × 10^9/L. CRP is 6 mg/L. A single random stool microscopy submitted the previous week was reported as negative for ova and cysts.

Contrast CT abdomen to evaluate the right lower quadrant pain demonstrates mild appendiceal wall thickening without fat stranding and a short linear filling defect within the appendiceal lumen. The intraluminal defect shifts position slightly between prone and supine reconstructions.

A housemate observed the patient at night and noted small white threadlike creatures emerging from the perianal region. Early-morning perianal adhesive tape applied at home showed numerous ovoid, slightly flattened eggs on light microscopy measuring roughly 50 µm by 30 µm and occasional slender white adult nematodes on direct inspection.

explanation: The combination of chronic nocturnal perianal pruritus with household spread, mild peripheral eosinophilia, an intraluminal mobile tubular filling defect in the appendix, and positive early-morning tape test with characteristic ovoid flattened eggs indicates infection with Enterobius vermicularis. The organism can lodge in the appendix causing intermittent RLQ pain and may be missed on routine stool microscopy.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presented with three weeks of intermittent fevers, progressive right upper quadrant pain and anorexia. He lost 5 kg, had a temperature of 38.6°C on arrival and examination revealed a tender enlarged liver palpated 3 cm below the right costal margin.

He was previously healthy, not on regular medication and had a negative HIV test two months earlier. Ten weeks before presentation he spent three weeks in rural Bangladesh where he drank unboiled well water and experienced a self-limited five-day episode of loose stools that resolved without treatment.

Blood tests showed WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, CRP 155 mg/L, ALP 410 U/L, AST 72 U/L, ALT 54 U/L and total bilirubin 12 µmol/L. Two sets of blood cultures were sterile at 48 hours and an initial stool bacterial culture was negative.

Contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrated a solitary 9 cm low-attenuation lesion in the posterior right hepatic lobe with a thin enhancing rim and no biliary tract obstruction. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous aspiration was performed for diagnostic and symptomatic relief.

Aspiration yielded about 60 mL of thick, brown odourless material described as 'anchovy-paste'; Gram stain and routine bacterial cultures of the fluid were sterile. Microscopy of the aspirate and repeat stool wet mount identified motile trophozoite forms that contained ingested erythrocytes, and the patient defervesced within 48 hours after starting a nitroimidazole agent.

explanation: These findings distinguish it from pyogenic bacterial abscesses which usually yield positive cultures and purulent, foul-smelling aspirate.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man developed fever and rigors 48 hours after urinary catheterisation for acute urinary retention due to benign prostatic hyperplasia. He is confused on arrival, temperature 38.9°C, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 105/60 mmHg, and has suprapubic tenderness with cloudy catheter effluent.

His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease stage 3. Two weeks earlier he completed a 7-day course of a second-generation cephalosporin for community-acquired pneumonia and he reports prior brief episodes of lower urinary tract symptoms but no recent dental procedures or intravenous drug use.

Blood tests show leukocytosis 14.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 182 mg/L. Urine dipstick is leukocyte esterase positive and nitrite negative, microscopy shows >50 WBC/HPF. A Gram stain of the urine shows Gram-positive cocci in short chains; blood cultures were obtained.
Because the patient remained bacteremic after 24 hours, a transesophageal echocardiogram was performed and demonstrated a 6 mm mobile vegetation on the mitral valve with no significant regurgitation.

Blood and urine cultures grew the same catalase-negative coccus that was PYR positive, hydrolysed esculin in the presence of bile and grew in 6.5% NaCl; the isolate was resistant to the earlier cephalosporin but susceptible to ampicillin. Bacteremia persisted on initial cephalosporin therapy and cleared within 48 hours after switching to intravenous ampicillin plus gentamicin, with sustained clinical improvement.

explanation: Urinary instrumentation followed by fever, Gram-positive cocci in short chains from urine and blood, a mitral valve vegetation, bile-esculin hydrolysis, growth in 6.5% NaCl and PYR positivity identify Enterococcus faecalis. The isolate's resistance to cephalosporins and prompt clearance with ampicillin plus gentamicin support this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to the outpatient clinic with 3 weeks of crampy lower abdominal pain and frequent loose stools that became bloody over the past 5 days. He has lost 6 kg, has intermittent fever with Tmax 37.9°C, pulse 102/min, and focal tenderness in the right upper quadrant with mild hepatomegaly on palpation.

He is otherwise fit, no chronic medications, and a rapid HIV test last month was negative. Two months earlier he spent 3 weeks doing relief work in rural Guatemala; during that time he drank untreated surface water and had a brief self-limited watery diarrhoea episode.
Bloods show leukocytosis 13.6 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 95 g/L, CRP 68 mg/L. Stool bacterial culture is negative and fecal occult blood is positive, ova and parasite microscopy pending.

Contrast CT of the abdomen shows a solitary 6.0 cm low-attenuation lesion in the posterior right hepatic lobe with smooth walls and no gas locules. Radiology reports findings most consistent with a unilocular liver abscess.

He confirms repeated consumption of untreated river water while in the region and recent casual oral–anal contact. Percutaneous aspiration produced 35 mL of thick brown odourless fluid; Gram stain and bacterial cultures remained sterile and stool PCR detected DNA from a nonflagellated intestinal protozoan.

explanation: Subacute dysentery followed by a solitary right‑lobe liver abscess with sterile brown aspirate and positive stool PCR for a nonflagellated intestinal protozoan points to Entamoeba histolytica. The travel and untreated water exposure provide the likely transmission route, and negative bacterial cultures with this clinical pattern confirm the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to a rural clinic with three months of progressive right upper quadrant fullness and dull pain and recent early satiety. She reports intermittent low-grade fevers and fatigue; on exam the liver is palpably smooth and extends 4 cm below the right costal margin, temperature 37.8°C, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg.

She has no chronic medical conditions, is not taking immunosuppressive medications, and has no history of viral hepatitis or prior abdominal surgery. She does not drink alcohol and has had normal general health until the current symptoms began.
Full blood count shows WBC 9.4 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.2 × 10^9/L. Liver tests show ALT 45 U/L and alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L. Serum IgG is positive by ELISA to a cestode larval antigen.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates an 8.5 cm well circumscribed cystic lesion in the right hepatic lobe containing multiple smaller internal daughter cysts and detached internal membranes. Non-contrast CT shows a thin peripheral calcified rim around the lesion.
She grew up and currently lives on a small sheep farm; she reports frequent close contact with farm dogs and that dogs are sometimes fed raw sheep viscera during seasonal slaughtering.

explanation: Chronic RUQ fullness with palpable hepatomegaly, peripheral eosinophilia, positive cestode larval antigen serology, and imaging showing a large hepatic cyst with daughter cysts and laminated membranes are diagnostic of a cystic hepatic infection caused by Echinococcus granulosus. The history of lifelong sheep farming with close contact between dogs and sheep offal provides a plausible exposure pathway.

hints.text: A 72-year-old man presented with 10 days of low-grade fevers, increasing fatigue, and new exertional breathlessness. On exam he was 38.1°C, heart rate 96/min, and had a new grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur at the apex with bibasal crackles and mild peripheral oedema.

Three weeks earlier he underwent transurethral resection of the prostate and required a urinary catheter for 48 hours during that admission. He has hypertension and a remote colorectal resection, no recent dental procedures and no history of intravenous drug use.

Three sets of blood cultures collected on admission grew gram-positive cocci in short chains and pairs after 48 hours. Peripheral blood count showed WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L and serum creatinine 118 µmol/L.

Transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrated a 7 mm mobile vegetation on the mitral valve with new moderate regurgitation. Contrast CT of the abdomen revealed two small wedge-shaped splenic infarcts consistent with embolic phenomena.

Empiric ceftriaxone and vancomycin were started but fevers and positive blood cultures persisted after 72 hours. Microbiology reported growth in 6.5% NaCl and positive bile-esculin hydrolysis; the team switched to intravenous ampicillin plus gentamicin and cultures cleared within 48 hours with clinical defervescence.

explanation: Subacute mitral valve endocarditis after recent urological instrumentation fits this presentation. Blood cultures showing gram-positive cocci in short chains plus bile-esculin positivity and growth in 6.5% NaCl identify an enterococcal species. Rapid clearance of bacteremia after switching to ampicillin with gentamicin synergy further supports Enterococcus faecalis as the cause.

hints.text: A 34-year-old previously well man presents to the emergency department with three days of crampy abdominal pain and progressively bloody diarrhoea. He reports 6 to 8 large-volume loose stools daily, minimal vomiting, a heart rate of 102 beats per minute and diffuse abdominal tenderness on examination without guarding or rebound.

Symptoms began abruptly after a brief prodrome of malaise and low-grade myalgia, there is no recent international travel, he is not immunosuppressed and he has not taken antibiotics before presentation. He gave himself an over-the-counter antimotility agent on day two with transient reduction in stool frequency but worsening abdominal pain.

Admission blood tests show haemoglobin 96 g/L, platelets 82 × 10^9/L and leukocytes 12 × 10^9/L. Creatinine is 180 µmol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 720 U/L and a peripheral blood film demonstrates fragmented red cells.

Contrast CT abdomen performed for persistent pain shows marked thickening and mucosal hyperenhancement of the descending and sigmoid colon consistent with colitis, no perforation or free gas is identified.

On targeted questioning he recalls eating undercooked minced beef burgers at a village barbecue two days before symptom onset, several other attendees reported bloody diarrhoea and local public health was notified after a child developed acute renal failure.

explanation: The combination of bloody diarrhoea following consumption of undercooked minced beef, radiologic colitis and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia and rising creatinine points to enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli producing a cytotoxin and causing haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

hints.text: A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with three weeks of profuse watery diarrhoea and progressive weakness. She reports 10 to 12 watery bowel movements per day including nocturnal episodes, a 5 kg weight loss, lightheadedness on standing, and no visible blood or tenesmus; on arrival her pulse is 110/min and she has an orthostatic fall in systolic blood pressure of 25 mmHg.

She received a kidney transplant 10 months ago and takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and low-dose prednisone. Two months ago she received a pulse of intravenous methylprednisolone for acute cellular rejection and she denies recent antibiotic use, international travel, or sick contacts.

Blood tests show sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 2.9 mmol/L, creatinine 140 μmol/L from a baseline of 95 μmol/L, and white cell count 7.2 × 10^9/L. Serial stool studies for routine bacterial culture and C. difficile PCR are negative, stool fecal leukocytes are absent, and calculated stool osmotic gap is low consistent with a secretory diarrhoea.

Contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrates diffuse small-bowel wall thickening and mesenteric fat stranding without frank obstruction, and there is mild intrahepatic biliary ductal dilation with periductal biliary wall enhancement. No abscess or focal hepatic lesion is seen.

After three weeks of persistent symptoms despite empirical ciprofloxacin and fluid rehydration, a concentrated stool specimen examined with a modified acid-fast stain showed round acid-fast oocysts measuring about 4 to 6 μm; the team reduced immunosuppression and started targeted antiparasitic therapy with partial clinical improvement over two weeks.

explanation: An immunosuppressed renal transplant patient with prolonged secretory watery diarrhoea, small-bowel mucosal change and biliary duct dilation, and identification of 4 to 6 μm acid-fast oocysts in stool points to an intestinal coccidian protozoan infection that also causes biliary disease.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously healthy man presented to the emergency department with three days of profuse watery diarrhoea and crampy abdominal pain. He reported 8 to 10 watery stools per day, light-headedness on standing, and a 3% weight loss. On examination he was tachycardic at 108 min−1, blood pressure 105/66 mmHg, mucous membranes dry and capillary refill slightly delayed, with a soft, non-tender abdomen and no fever.

He returned five days earlier from a two-week trip along coastal Peru where he stayed in small guesthouses and frequently ate food from street vendors. He remembered drinking bottled water but also drank from a sealed-looking vendor bottle once. He denied bloody stools, high fevers, recent antibiotics, or chronic medical problems.

Complete blood count showed white blood cells 7.5 × 10^9/L. Serum creatinine 120 μmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L. Stool microscopy showed no fecal leukocytes and no ova or parasites. Routine stool culture grew lactose-fermenting gram-negative bacilli reported as a non-invasive coliform by the local laboratory. Tests for norovirus and Giardia by PCR were negative.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed moderate small-bowel luminal fluid and mild jejunal wall thickening. There was no colonic wall thickening, no mesenteric stranding, and no focal abscess or obstruction.

Local public health screening of isolates from several travellers who ate at the same coastal market identified the same coliform from multiple patients. Molecular testing demonstrated plasmid-borne genes encoding both heat-stable and heat-labile enterotoxins in those isolates.

explanation: The patient has traveller's watery diarrhoea with volume depletion and no fecal leukocytes or colonic inflammation, pointing to a small-bowel secretory process. Detection of a coliform carrying plasmid-encoded heat-stable and heat-labile enterotoxin genes confirms Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli as the cause in this outbreak.

hints.text: A 22-year-old university student presents to the outpatient clinic with a 12-day history of sore throat, progressive fatigue, and low-grade fevers that have limited his attendance at exams. On examination his temperature is 38.3°C, he has prominent tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy and bilateral tonsillar exudates, and he reports difficulty swallowing solid foods.

He is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications, and lives in a shared student flat. He denies recent travel, intravenous drug use, and new medications before symptom onset, and he reports that several flatmates have had self-limited upper respiratory illnesses this term.

Complete blood count shows leucocytosis 13.6 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 48% and 18% atypical forms on the peripheral smear. Alanine aminotransferase is 156 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase is 142 U/L, while C-reactive protein is 6 mg/L.

Right upper quadrant ultrasound performed for persistent abdominal discomfort demonstrates an enlarged spleen measuring 15.5 cm with preserved architecture and no focal lesions. Chest radiograph is normal.

On further questioning he recalls a new romantic partner three weeks before symptom onset who had a similar febrile sore throat; the partner's primary care record documents a positive heterophile antibody test at that time.

explanation: Young adult with prolonged pharyngitis, tender cervical lymphadenopathy, marked fatigue, atypical lymphocytosis, splenomegaly, and mild transaminitis points to infectious mononucleosis. The epidemiologic link to a contact with a heterophile-positive illness largely confirms the most likely viral cause in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously well woman presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of crampy lower abdominal pain and profuse diarrhoea. She reports that stools were watery at onset but over the last 12 hours have become looser with visible bright red blood. On arrival T 37.8°C, HR 102/min, BP 108/66 mmHg; she appears pale and reports dizziness on standing. Abdominal examination reveals moderate left lower quadrant tenderness without peritoneal signs.

She has no chronic medical conditions and has not taken antibiotics recently. Three days before presentation she attended a neighbourhood summer barbecue where she ate a lightly charred ground‑beef burger and a raw sprout salad. Several other attendees developed diarrhoea over the next 24–72 hours. She works as a childcare assistant and has no recent travel.

CBC: haemoglobin 76 g/L, MCV 86 fL, platelets 48 × 10^9/L, reticulocytosis present. Peripheral smear shows fragmented erythrocytes and schistocytes. Serum creatinine 312 μmol/L (baseline documented at 68 μmol/L), LDH 1 200 U/L, total bilirubin 45 μmol/L. Stool microscopy positive for fecal leukocytes and gross blood. Blood cultures remain negative.

Contrast CT abdomen demonstrates continuous circumferential thickening of the descending colon and sigmoid consistent with active colitis, without perforation or abscess. Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys and no obstruction.

Public-health investigation traced an outbreak to the same barbecue. Culture of leftover burger yielded lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rods that produced colourless colonies on sorbitol‑MacConkey agar. PCR on the isolates detected a gene encoding a ribosome‑inactivating cytotoxin that has been implicated in bloody diarrhoea and post‑diarrhoeal microangiopathic renal injury; isolates from multiple affected guests had identical profiles.

explanation: The combination of a diarrhoeal illness after undercooked ground beef, frank bloody stools, colitis on imaging, and the triad of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury indicates post‑diarrhoeal haemolytic uraemic syndrome. The food isolates that fail sorbitol fermentation on selective agar and carry a ribosome‑inactivating toxin gene point to an enterohaemorrhagic strain of Escherichia coli as the causative pathogen.

hints.text: A 31-year-old previously well man presents to primary care after 11 days of progressive fatigue, sore throat and early satiety. He reports intermittent low-grade fevers and noticed a fullness under his left ribs; on exam temperature 37.9 °C, multiple tender cervical lymph nodes 2–3 cm and a spleen palpable 4 cm below the costal margin.

He takes no regular medications, does not smoke and has no recent travel. He works as a schoolteacher and recalls several pupils with recent upper respiratory illnesses, and he has a new monogamous partner whom he met about three weeks before symptom onset.

Blood tests show WBC 12.8 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 8.5 × 10^9/L and 18% atypical lymphocytes, haemoglobin 142 g/L, platelets 210 × 10^9/L. Liver tests are abnormal with ALT 156 U/L, AST 98 U/L and bilirubin 34 μmol/L. Rapid streptococcal antigen and fourth-generation HIV test are negative and a heterophile antibody test performed on day 11 is non-reactive.

Contrast CT of the abdomen performed for persistent left upper-quadrant pain shows an enlarged spleen measuring 15 cm and a peripheral wedge-shaped hypodense area in the lower pole consistent with infarction. There is no intra-abdominal free fluid or portal vein thrombosis.

Three days into his illness a local clinician prescribed oral amoxicillin for presumed bacterial pharyngitis; within 48 hours of starting the drug he developed a widespread pruritic maculopapular eruption over his trunk and limbs and the antibiotic was stopped.

explanation: The combination of prolonged pharyngitis with marked lymphocytosis and atypical lymphocytes, splenomegaly with a splenic infarct, elevated transaminases and the development of a diffuse rash after amoxicillin is most consistent with infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. A non-reactive heterophile test early in illness can occur, so EBV-specific serology or PCR would confirm the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of itching around the anus and intermittent crampy lower abdominal pain that wakes her from sleep two to three nights per week. She works part time at a community daycare; on examination she is afebrile, pulse 72/min, and the perianal skin is erythematous with superficial linear excoriations but no purulent discharge.

She reports that two of the preschool children in her care developed similar itching around the same time and that her 3-year-old daughter has been restless at night. She has not travelled recently, takes no regular medications, has no history of immunosuppression, and denies new sexual partners or recent antibiotic use.
Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 134 g/L, white cells 6.8 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 0.6 × 10^9/L. Two separate stool microscopy examinations for ova and parasites were negative.
Because of intermittent abdominal pain an abdominal and pelvic ultrasound was performed and showed no bowel wall thickening, free fluid, abscess, or appendiceal abnormality.
A morning perianal adhesive tape swab obtained before bathing yielded numerous flattened-sided, oval eggs and a 10 mm slender white nematode on microscopic inspection.

explanation: Nocturnal perianal pruritus with household clustering and restless children suggests a transmissible enteric helminth. Negative stool microscopy is common for this infection because eggs are deposited perianally. The positive morning tape test showing flattened-sided oval eggs and a short slender worm confirms Enterobius vermicularis infection.

hints.text: A 32-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 36 hours of profuse watery diarrhoea and crampy lower abdominal pain. He reports 10 to 12 watery stools per day, feels lightheaded when standing, heart rate 112 bpm, blood pressure 95/58 mmHg, dry mucous membranes and reduced urine output.

He returned five days ago from a two-week trip to rural coastal areas of South Asia where he frequently drank untreated well or tap water and ate salads and food from street vendors. He has no chronic illnesses, has not taken antibiotics recently, did not receive pre-travel antibiotic prophylaxis, and denies fever or bloody stools.

Serum tests show WBC 7.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 9 mg/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L and creatinine 120 µmol/L consistent with volume depletion. Stool dipstick negative for blood, microscopy shows no fecal leukocytes or ova/parasites, and routine stool culture is pending.

Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen performed to exclude focal intra-abdominal pathology demonstrates fluid-filled, non-dilated small bowel loops without segmental colonic wall thickening, mucosal hyperenhancement or mesenteric fat stranding. No abscess or obstruction is identified.

Multiplex stool PCR returned positive for plasmid-encoded heat-stable and heat-labile enterotoxin genes; cultured isolates showed non-invasive growth on selective media and retained susceptibility to ciprofloxacin and azithromycin. The patient received oral rehydration and a single-dose oral azithromycin with marked reduction in stool frequency within 48 hours.

explanation: The patient has an acute secretory watery diarrhoea after travel with absent fecal leukocytes, CT without colitis, and detection of plasmid-borne heat-stable and heat-labile enterotoxin genes in stool.

hints.text: A 62-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of fever, rigors, right-sided flank pain and dysuria. At presentation she was febrile to 39.1°C, heart rate 112/min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg and had marked right costovertebral angle tenderness on examination.

She has long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with oral agents and reports poor glycaemic control. Six months earlier a right renal calculus was diagnosed and managed conservatively; she denies recent urinary instrumentation or hospital admission.

Contrast CT of the abdomen showed multiple gas locules within the right renal parenchyma and perinephric space with adjacent inflammatory stranding, findings interpreted as a gas-forming renal infection.

She was started on empiric intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and underwent percutaneous drainage of the right collection. Fever and hemodynamics improved only slowly and blood cultures became positive for Gram-negative bacilli on hospital day 2.

Urine and blood cultures grew >10^5 CFU/mL of non-mucoid, lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli that were oxidase-negative and indole-positive and produced a green metallic sheen on eosin-methylene blue agar; isolates were susceptible to ceftriaxone.

explanation: A diabetic patient with gas within the renal parenchyma and perinephric space meets the picture of emphysematous pyelonephritis. The culture phenotype of a lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative, indole-positive bacillus with a green metallic sheen on EMB is characteristic of Escherichia coli among Enterobacteriaceae.

hints.text: A 45-year-old man presented to clinic with six months of intermittent epigastric burning and early satiety. He reports a 5 kg weight loss and increasing fatigue. On examination he is afebrile, pulse 76/min, and pale with mild epigastric tenderness to palpation.

He has no regular nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug or aspirin use and takes antacids intermittently. He smokes five cigarettes per day and drinks alcohol rarely. There is no recent travel and no family history of peptic ulcer complications.

Haemoglobin 96 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL. Iron studies consistent with iron deficiency: serum ferritin 8 µg/L, serum iron low, TIBC elevated. Faecal occult blood test positive on two separate samples.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a solitary 1.8 cm ulcer on the gastric antrum with a clean base and surrounding erythema. Multiple biopsies were taken from the ulcer edge and adjacent mucosa and no mass lesion was seen.

A biopsy-based rapid urease test returned strongly positive. He received a 14-day regimen combining a proton-pump inhibitor and two antibiotics, with complete resolution of dyspepsia and a rise in haemoglobin to 118 g/L at 8 weeks; a 13C-urea breath test at that time was negative.

explanation: Antral gastric ulcer with iron deficiency anaemia in a patient without NSAID exposure suggests an infective cause of chronic gastritis and ulceration.

hints.text: A 64-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of fever, progressive left flank pain, and increasing confusion. She was febrile to 39.4°C, heart rate 118 bpm, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, and had marked left costovertebral angle tenderness on examination.

Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes and recent functional decline after a hip fracture. She had a urinary catheter placed at a rehabilitation facility three days before the fever began and reports poor glycaemic control, most recent HbA1c 84 mmol/mol. She had a short oral antibiotic course for dysuria one month earlier.

Blood tests showed white cell count 19.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, CRP 320 mg/L, serum creatinine 268 µmol/L and lactate 4.1 mmol/L. Urine dipstick was positive for nitrite and leukocyte esterase and microscopy demonstrated marked pyuria.

Contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated gas within the left renal parenchyma and collecting system with perinephric fluid and stranding, consistent with emphysematous pyelonephritis. A 6 mm calculus was seen in the proximal left ureter with upstream dilatation.

She underwent urgent percutaneous drainage and started empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics with haemodynamic support, with gradual clinical improvement over 72 hours.
