Blood and urine cultures grew lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative Gram-negative rods that produced a green metallic sheen on eosin-methylene blue agar and were indole positive, resistant to ampicillin but susceptible to third-generation cephalosporins.

explanation: A diabetic patient with recent catheterisation and obstructing ureteric stone developed gas-forming renal infection and septic physiology, features typical of emphysematous pyelonephritis. The microbiology profile of a lactose-fermenting, indole-positive, oxidase-negative Gram-negative rod with a metallic sheen on EMB identifies the causative organism.

hints.text: A 68-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with five days of productive cough, fever and progressive dyspnoea. She reported purulent green sputum and right-sided pleuritic chest pain, had temperature 38.7°C, respiratory rate 24/min and oxygen saturation 90% on room air, with diminished breath sounds and coarse crackles over the right mid and lower lung.

She has COPD managed with inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting bronchodilator, is a former smoker with a 40 pack-year history, and began a short taper of oral prednisone three days before presentation for an outpatient flare. She underwent splenectomy after trauma 8 months ago and has not received adult pneumococcal or other post-splenectomy vaccines.

Blood tests showed leukocytosis 15.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 178 mg/L. Two sets of blood cultures and a sputum specimen both showed many neutrophils and small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli, and blood culture bottles flagged positive at 18 hours.

Chest radiograph demonstrated right middle and lower zone consolidation with mild blunting of the right costophrenic sulcus. CT chest confirmed focal lobar consolidation of the right middle lobe, peribronchial thickening with underlying bronchiectatic change, and a small parapneumonic effusion.

She lives with her two-year-old grandson who attends daycare and recently had purulent otitis media and conjunctivitis, and who missed routine infant immunisations. The clinical laboratory reported that the blood isolate failed to grow on standard blood agar unless the medium was supplemented with both haemin and NAD, and that the isolate produced a plasmid-mediated beta-lactamase resulting in ampicillin resistance.

explanation: Small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli from respiratory and blood cultures that require haemin and NAD for growth identify Haemophilus influenzae. The household toddler with purulent otitis media provides a plausible transmission source, the patientÕs splenectomy increases risk of invasive infection by encapsulated strains, and beta-lactamase production explains ampicillin resistance and the need for a beta-lactamase stable agent.

hints.text: A 14-month-old boy presented to the emergency department with 72 hours of fever and progressive left ear pain. He is irritable, pulling at the left ear, and his parents report decreased responsiveness to sound on that side. On arrival T 39.2°C, heart rate 136/min, and pneumatic otoscopy shows a markedly bulging, erythematous left tympanic membrane with absent mobility.

The child attends full-time daycare. He has no chronic medical conditions but missed the 12-month dose of the conjugate capsule vaccine following a recent family move. Ten days ago he had a brief viral upper respiratory illness treated conservatively and was given 48 hours of oral amoxicillin by the primary care clinician for persistent cough.

Blood tests show leukocytosis 18.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and C-reactive protein 86 mg/L. Tympanostomy produced purulent middle ear fluid. Gram stain demonstrated small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli and initial culture produced growth only on chocolate agar and heated blood-extract medium.

Contrast CT scan of the temporal bones demonstrates left mastoid air cell opacification with loss of septations and soft tissue density in the mastoid antrum. There is no evidence of intracranial extension or abscess.

Household contacts included an older sibling recently treated for conjunctivitis acquired at the same daycare. Microbiology later reported the middle ear isolate required both factor X and factor V for growth and produced a beta-lactamase. Antibiotic therapy was changed to a third-generation cephalosporin with rapid clinical improvement.

explanation: A toddler with daycare exposure, incomplete conjugate capsule vaccination, and otitis media complicated by mastoiditis suggests an encapsulated respiratory Gram-negative coccobacillus. Isolation of a fastidious organism that needs factors X and V and that can produce beta-lactamase fits this pathogen and explains failure of initial amoxicillin and response to a cephalosporin.

hints.text: A 47-year-old woman presented to clinic with progressive fatigue and exertional breathlessness over 5 months. She also describes intermittent early satiety and a vague gnawing epigastric discomfort after meals; on examination she is pale with a heart rate of 96 min^-1 and a single positive faecal occult blood test.

She has received two prior courses of oral iron with minimal improvement and a diagnostic colonoscopy two months earlier that was normal to the terminal ileum. She denies regular nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug use, reports no overt haematemesis, and has no recent travel or antibiotic courses.
Haemoglobin 84 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL, ferritin 6 µg/L and C-reactive protein 7 mg/L. Tissue transglutaminase IgA and stool ova and parasites were negative.

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed erythematous antral mucosa with a 6 mm superficial ulcer on the lesser curvature of the antrum; multiple biopsies taken from the antrum and body showed chronic active gastritis on routine histology but no immediate diagnostic organisms on the initial report.

A rapid urease test performed on the antral biopsy returned positive and the patient was treated with a proton-pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics according to local eradication guidelines; her epigastric symptoms resolved, faecal occult blood became negative, haemoglobin rose to 120 g/L at 12 weeks and a urea breath test at 8 weeks post-treatment was negative.

explanation: The sequence of negative colonoscopy, poor oral iron response, and eradication-confirmed cure makes other causes of chronic gastritis less likely.

hints.text: A 24-year-old previously healthy man presents to primary care with 10 days of malaise and anorexia followed by dark urine and three days of jaundice. He is afebrile, pulse 84/min, blood pressure 120/76 mmHg; examination shows scleral icterus and a tender liver edge palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin, without asterixis or stigmata of chronic liver disease.

He reports unprotected sexual intercourse with a new partner about 10 weeks before symptom onset. He denies intravenous drug use, recent blood transfusion, or travel, and says he has never been vaccinated against hepatitis viruses.

Serum transaminases are markedly elevated with alanine aminotransferase 1 540 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 1 020 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 180 U/L, total bilirubin 120 µmol/L, INR 1.1. Viral serology demonstrates a circulating hepatitis surface antigen with a positive IgM antibody directed against the viral core protein.

Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows a diffusely enlarged liver without intrahepatic or extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation, no gallstones, and normal portal and hepatic vein flow. There is no focal hepatic lesion or ascites.

He confirms his new partner had previously been told they had a long-standing liver infection and that condoms were not used during their encounters. He remains unvaccinated and has not had prior serologic testing for viral hepatitis.

explanation: Marked hepatocellular enzyme elevation with jaundice and ultrasound excluding obstructive causes indicates acute viral hepatitis. The combination of a circulating hepatitis surface antigen and IgM antibody to the viral core protein identifies acute infection with the blood-borne, sexually transmissible hepatitis virus. Recent unprotected sexual exposure and lack of vaccination provide a plausible route of acquisition.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to urgent care with 7 days of progressive fatigue, anorexia, nausea and low-grade fever, and 3 days of yellowing of the eyes and dark urine. He works in finance, is normally fit, and on exam has T 37.8°C, pulse 92/min, marked scleral icterus and a tender liver edge 3 cm below the right costal margin, with no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease and no encephalopathy.

He returned 5 weeks ago from a week-long trip to a coastal region in southern Europe to attend a friend's wedding. He drinks alcohol only socially, denies intravenous drug use and blood transfusions, and reports he did not receive any travel vaccinations before the trip. He has no prior liver disease and takes no regular medications.

Blood tests show ALT 1 950 U/L, AST 1 200 U/L, total bilirubin 85 µmol/L with conjugated bilirubin 60 µmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 220 U/L, INR 1.0 and platelets 220 × 10^9/L. Acute viral hepatitis panels were sent and an IgM antibody indicating recent infection with a hepatitis virus was pending at the time of presentation.

Abdominal ultrasound shows a mildly enlarged liver without focal lesions, a normal-calibre common bile duct and no gallstones. Doppler flow in the portal and hepatic veins is normal, supporting a hepatocellular pattern of injury rather than obstructive biliary disease.

Public health follow-up revealed several other wedding guests developed similar jaundice. The patient recalls eating several raw oysters at the seaside buffet about four weeks before his symptoms started. Convalescent testing returned positive for IgM antibody to the enterically transmitted hepatitis virus implicated in foodborne shellfish outbreaks, confirming the diagnosis.

explanation: The subacute onset of constitutional symptoms followed by jaundice, very high ALT greater than AST, normal INR and ultrasound excluding obstruction indicate acute hepatocellular injury. The epidemiologic link to raw shellfish eaten about four weeks before illness and a positive IgM for an enterically transmitted hepatitis agent are diagnostic of an acute, foodborne viral hepatitis infection acquired on travel.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man presents to an outpatient hepatology clinic with 6 months of progressive fatigue, intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, and new yellowing of his eyes. On examination he is afebrile, has scleral icterus and a liver edge palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, and no peripheral oedema.

Past medical history includes type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and well controlled hypertension. He drinks alcohol socially, denies heavy use, takes no herbal supplements, and has no recent travel; he recalls a prolonged period of incarceration in the early 1990s but no current high-risk behaviour.

Blood tests show ALT 156 U/L, AST 98 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, total bilirubin 28 µmol/L, albumin 39 g/L, INR 1.0 and platelets 140 × 10^9/L. Autoimmune hepatitis panel and iron studies are unremarkable and fasting lipids and glucose reflect his known metabolic disease.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a small nodular-appearing liver and mild splenomegaly (spleen length 14 cm) without focal hepatic lesions. Transient elastography measures liver stiffness 18.5 kPa, consistent with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis.

He reports remote injecting drug use for a few years in the late 1980s and a blood transfusion after a road traffic accident in 1989, both before routine donor screening for a blood-borne RNA hepatitis virus was in place.

explanation: Chronic mild to moderate transaminitis with imaging evidence of advanced fibrosis, plus remote blood exposures in the pre-screening era and prior injecting drug use, point to a chronic blood-borne RNA hepatitis infection acquired decades earlier. The clinical picture and exposure history make this the most likely diagnosis given the absence of alternative autoimmune or metabolic causes.

hints.text: A 52-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 10 days of anorexia and malaise followed by 3 days of progressive confusion and new jaundice. On arrival she is somnolent but arousable, temperature 37.9°C, has scleral icterus, asterixis on bedside testing, and a tender liver palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin.

Her medical history is notable for diffuse large B cell lymphoma treated with a rituximab-containing chemotherapy regimen completed 4 months ago. She denies heavy alcohol use, reports no recent acetaminophen overdose, and has no known prior diagnosis of liver disease; vaccination records for viral hepatitis are incomplete.

Admission blood tests show ALT 4,120 U/L, AST 3,800 U/L, total bilirubin 270 µmol/L, INR 3.2, ammonia 140 µmol/L, and platelet count 95 × 10^9/L. Serum PCR returns high-level viral DNA at 1.4 × 10^8 IU/mL, reported as consistent with a hepatotropic DNA virus.

Abdominal ultrasound and non-contrast CT demonstrate a small nodular liver contour with surface irregularity and moderate ascites, without biliary dilatation or focal hepatic mass. Radiology impression cites underlying chronic liver disease with superimposed acute hepatic injury.

Review of past records shows she was born in rural eastern Asia in 1973 before routine neonatal immunisation against common hepatitis agents; her mother had long-standing 'yellow eyes' and died of liver disease. Archived screening samples from 2000 and 2010 repeatedly documented a persistent viral surface antigen in her blood.

explanation: Longstanding surface antigen positivity and birth in an endemic area indicate chronic carriage likely acquired perinatally. These features point to reactivation of hepatitis B virus precipitated by immunosuppression.

hints.text: A 48-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 72 hours of fever and progressive confusion. Family noted new difficulty finding words and intermittent brief episodes of right-hand automatisms; temperature was 38.7°C and she was disoriented to time on examination.

She was previously healthy, took no regular medications, and had no recent travel. She reported occasional recurrent small painful blisters at the lip margin over the past decade, the last flare occurring about one week before admission after a long flight.

Blood count showed leukocyte count 12.4 × 10^9/L. Lumbar puncture produced clear CSF with opening pressure 18 cmH2O, WBC 140 × 10^6/L (lymphocyte predominant), RBC 320 × 10^6/L, protein 1.2 g/L, and glucose 3.8 mmol/L (serum glucose 5.0 mmol/L).

MRI brain with contrast revealed asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and mild swelling of the left medial temporal lobe and insular cortex with patchy restricted diffusion, without a large-vessel infarct pattern.

A swab from a crusted lip vesicle collected on admission returned PCR detection of viral DNA that matched the sequence recovered from the CSF. The virus detected is one commonly implicated in recurrent perioral vesicular disease.

explanation: Focal temporal lobe dysfunction with fever and new focal seizures suggests viral encephalitis. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with red blood cells and elevated protein, and MRI localises the process to the medial temporal lobe. The presence of the same viral DNA in a perioral lesion and CSF implicates the agent that causes recurrent lip vesicles as the cause of her encephalitis.

hints.text: A 48-year-old woman presented to the outpatient hepatology clinic with 3 months of progressive fatigue and intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort. She noted visible scleral icterus and new yellowing of the skin for 2 weeks, she was afebrile, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, heart rate 86 bpm, and examination revealed mild hepatomegaly 2 cm below the right costal margin without peripheral oedema or encephalopathy.

She drinks alcohol only on social occasions and reports no history of injecting drug use or recent travel. Her past medical history includes well controlled type 2 diabetes and a previous outpatient result of mildly elevated liver enzymes two years earlier that was not pursued; she received childhood immunisation that included the vaccine available for one common hepatotropic virus.

Serum liver tests showed ALT 312 U/L, AST 210 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 115 U/L, total bilirubin 45 µmol/L, albumin 42 g/L and INR 1.0. Full blood count WBC 5.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 178 × 10^9/L. Serologic screening demonstrated protective surface antibodies to the vaccine-preventable hepatotropic virus and absence of its surface antigen.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a mildly enlarged liver with coarse echotexture, no focal hepatic lesions and no biliary dilatation or ascites. Transient elastography measured liver stiffness 10.8 kPa, consistent with significant fibrosis but without definite imaging signs of decompensated cirrhosis.

On directed questioning she recalled receiving multiple blood transfusions after a motor vehicle collision in 1994. Subsequent testing returned a positive antibody to the non-vaccine-preventable chronic hepatotropic virus and nucleic-acid amplification detected viral RNA at 1.2 × 10^6 IU/mL.

explanation: The combination of remote transfusion before routine donor screening, months of mild transaminitis, imaging evidence of chronic liver disease and a positive antibody with detectable viral RNA points to a blood-borne RNA virus that causes chronic hepatitis and fibrosis. Vaccination against the vaccine-preventable hepatotropic virus and absence of its surface antigen make that pathogen unlikely, supporting the diagnosis of the non-vaccine-preventable chronic viral cause.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of worsening holocephalic headache, photophobia and neck stiffness. She reported subjective fever with a recorded temperature of 38.4°C on arrival, appeared mildly confused, and had marked nuchal rigidity on examination but no focal neurological deficits.

She is otherwise healthy, takes combined oral contraception, and has no chronic medical conditions or immunosuppressive medications. She denied recent travel or antibiotic use, and she described a new sexual partner beginning two weeks earlier.

Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 18 cm H2O, CSF white cell count 150 × 10^6/L with 85% lymphocytes, protein 0.9 g/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L (serum glucose 5.2 mmol/L). CSF Gram stain and routine bacterial cultures were negative. Peripheral blood white cell count was 8.1 × 10^9/L.

Non-contrast CT head was normal. MRI brain with contrast showed mild leptomeningeal enhancement over the basal cisterns and posterior fossa, without focal temporal lobe signal abnormality or diffusion-restricted lesions.

On directed questioning the patient recalled that her new partner developed painful grouped lesions on the genitals several days after they met; she also noted a brief episode of vulvar tingling followed by a few small grouped vesicles about one week before her headache, which resolved without treatment.

explanation: Aseptic meningitis with lymphocytic CSF, leptomeningeal enhancement, and recent genital vesicles after a new sexual exposure strongly suggest herpes simplex virus type 2 as the cause. The clinical pattern here fits primary or early recurrent genital infection complicated by meningitis.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department with three days of progressive headache and confusion. He developed intermittent visual hallucinations and difficulty finding words, his temperature was 38.4°C, and on examination he was disoriented to time with impaired short-term memory and a subtle left-sided naming deficit.

He is independent at baseline and has well controlled type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He had a dental extraction under local anaesthetic 10 days before presentation and a self-limited upper respiratory illness one week earlier, and he takes no immunosuppressive medications.

Lumbar puncture showed opening pressure 18 cmH2O, cerebrospinal fluid WBC 110 × 10^6/L with 85% lymphocytes, RBC 250 × 10^6/L, protein 1.1 g/L, and glucose 3.0 mmol/L (serum glucose 6.0 mmol/L). Peripheral blood WBC was 12.0 × 10^9/L. Routine bacterial cultures were sterile and routine bacterial antigen tests were negative.

Brain MRI with contrast demonstrated asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and restricted diffusion involving the left medial temporal lobe and insula, with small foci of susceptibility consistent with petechial haemorrhage, and no ring-enhancing collection.

On further questioning he recalled kissing his partner several times in the week before illness, and she had a painful grouped vesicular eruption on her lower lip during that period. He noted a small perioral blister of his own 48 hours before onset of his neurologic symptoms.

explanation: The combination of acute focal temporal lobe syndrome, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with red cells, asymmetric medial temporal lobe MRI changes with petechial haemorrhage, and recent exposure to perioral vesicular lesions points to a reactivation viral encephalitis from an orolabial pathogen. These features most strongly support infection by an alphaherpesvirus commonly acquired via oral contact.

hints.text: A 24-year-old man presents to the outpatient clinic with three weeks of progressive dry cough, intermittent fevers to 38.5°C and 4 kg weight loss. He reports reduced exercise tolerance and persistent pleuritic chest discomfort; examination shows a temperature of 38.2°C, respiratory rate 20/min and bilateral fine inspiratory crackles at the bases.

He is previously well, takes no regular medications and has no known immunodeficiency. Two weeks before symptom onset he spent a long weekend exploring limestone caves and crawling through sections with heavy bat guano; he has not travelled outside the region and has no household contacts with respiratory illness.
Blood tests show WBC 5.0 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L and platelets 190 × 10^9/L. Sputum cytology with special fungal stain demonstrates small ovoid budding yeast forms clustered within macrophages.
Chest CT shows multiple small centrilobular nodules in both lungs and prominent bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy without cavitation. No pleural effusion is present.

On further questioning he recalls disturbing deep guano deposits while squeezing through a narrow, poorly ventilated cave chamber inhabited by a large bat colony. Local public health had previously advised about cave-associated fungal exposures in that river valley.

explanation: The subacute febrile respiratory illness with hilar adenopathy, small intracellular yeasts on macrophage cytology and recent heavy exposure to bat guano in caves supports a diagnosis of pulmonary infection due to Histoplasma capsulatum. The imaging and exposure history together clarify the likely environmental source and organism.

hints.text: A 29-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of progressive perineal numbness, severe low back pain, and inability to void. She reported fever to 38.2°C and required urinary catheterisation; on examination she had diminished anal sphincter tone and a saddle sensory deficit with preserved lower limb strength.

She was otherwise healthy and not immunocompromised. Two months earlier she had a self-limited episode of painful vulvar blisters that resolved over one week without treatment; she has a new sexual partner since that episode and had received no prior care for the lesions.

Lumbar puncture showed CSF WBC 220 × 10^6/L with 92% lymphocytes, protein 1.10 g/L, and glucose 3.2 mmol/L (serum 4.8 mmol/L). CSF bacterial cultures and Gram stain were negative; nucleic-acid amplification detected viral DNA consistent with a neurotropic DNA virus known to establish latency in dorsal root ganglia.

MRI lumbosacral spine with contrast demonstrated T2 hyperintensity and enhancement of the S2–S4 nerve roots and mild conus medullaris swelling without compressive lesion, findings interpreted as acute inflammatory polyradiculitis.

She received intravenous aciclovir and within 48 hours her fever and pain improved; bladder function began to recover over the next five days. PCR from a swab of the earlier vulvar lesion amplified the same viral DNA sequence as the CSF sample.

explanation: Acute sacral radiculitis with lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, recent painful genital vesicles, concordant viral DNA in CSF and genital lesion, and prompt response to aciclovir indicate infection with Herpes simplex virus 2. The organism commonly establishes latency in sacral sensory ganglia and can reactivate to cause recurrent genital lesions and radiculitis.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents with six weeks of intermittent fevers, drenching night sweats, progressive fatigue, and a 6 kg weight loss. He reports a dry cough and increasing abdominal fullness; on exam he is febrile at 38.3 °C, has pallor, and a palpable spleen 3 cm below the costal margin.

He has seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated with a tumour necrosis factor blocker for the past eight months and takes low-dose prednisone during flares. He works as a maintenance electrician, denies tobacco or illicit drug use, and has no known recent contact with active tuberculosis.

Laboratory testing shows haemoglobin 88 g/L, white blood cells 3.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 110 × 10^9/L. CRP is 58 mg/L, ferritin 950 µg/L, and liver enzymes are mildly elevated with AST 98 U/L, ALT 76 U/L and alkaline phosphatase 210 U/L. Blood cultures remain sterile after 5 days.

Contrast chest CT demonstrates bilateral small peribronchovascular nodules and prominent right hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy; a 1.2 cm calcified nodule is present in the right lower lobe. Abdominal ultrasound confirms splenomegaly with several tiny hypoechoic splenic lesions.

On further questioning he describes two weekends of recreational spelunking three months earlier in limestone caves along a North American river valley where heavy bat guano accumulated, and he later helped clean an old poultry coop on a family property.

explanation: Subacute febrile illness with hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia in a patient receiving a TNF blocker, together with mediastinal lymphadenopathy, calcified pulmonary nodules, and clear recent exposure to bat guano in river-valley caves, points to disseminated infection by an endemic dimorphic fungus acquired from cave or bird/bat guano exposure.

hints.text: A 24-year-old woman presents to primary care with 6 days of progressive jaundice, anorexia, nausea, and dark urine. She reports marked fatigue that forced her to miss work, is afebrile at 37.8°C, has scleral icterus, and mild right upper quadrant tenderness on palpation.

She returned three weeks earlier from a two-week trip to a Caribbean coastal town. She has no chronic liver disease, does not drink alcohol, denies intravenous drug use, and did not receive vaccination against travel-related hepatotropic viruses before travel.
Serum ALT 1,420 U/L, AST 980 U/L, total bilirubin 85 μmol/L with predominantly conjugated fraction, alkaline phosphatase 150 U/L, INR 1.0.
Right upper quadrant ultrasound shows mild hepatomegaly, homogeneous liver echotexture, a common bile duct measuring 4 mm, and no gallstones or biliary dilatation to explain obstructive jaundice.

On further questioning she recalls eating raw oysters and other shellfish at a crowded beachfront festival about four weeks before presentation, and two dining companions developed similar febrile jaundice. Serology returned positive for IgM antibodies directed against the vaccine-preventable faecal-oral hepatotropic virus.

explanation: Acute symptomatic jaundice with very high transaminases and cholestatic bilirubin after ingestion of raw shellfish in an unvaccinated traveler, absence of biliary obstruction on ultrasound, and positive IgM to a vaccine-preventable faecal-oral hepatotropic virus support acute infection with that agent.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to the sexual health clinic with six weeks of progressive fatigue, night sweats, and a 6 kg weight loss. He reports painful swallowing for two weeks; on examination he is afebrile, pulse 92/min, has white adherent plaques on the tongue that scrape off and palpable 2 cm cervical and inguinal lymph nodes.

He is otherwise well, takes no regular medication, and remembers treatment for gonorrhoea two years ago. He reports condomless receptive anal intercourse with multiple male partners over the past year and intermittent non-injecting methamphetamine use. He denies recent travel or blood transfusion.

Full blood count shows leukocytes 3.4 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 115 g/L, platelets 180 × 10^9/L and absolute lymphocytes 0.8 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 18 mg/L. Rapid throat swab microscopy consistent with Candida species; oropharyngeal symptoms improved with topical nystatin.

High-resolution CT thorax performed for persistent exertional dyspnoea shows bilateral perihilar and diffuse ground-glass opacities without focal lobar consolidation. No pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy identified on the scan.

He acknowledges a recent partner who told him their screening assay for a human retrovirus was reactive. Repeat testing in clinic found a reactive fourth-generation antigen/antibody screening assay, confirmatory plasma nucleic acid testing detected 1.2 × 10^8 viral RNA copies per litre, and CD4 lymphocyte count was 120 × 10^6/L.

explanation: Subacute constitutional symptoms, oropharyngeal candidiasis and generalized lymphadenopathy with lymphopenia and diffuse ground-glass changes suggest opportunistic infection from advanced immunosuppression. Reactive fourth-generation antigen/antibody screening with high plasma viral RNA and low CD4 count confirms infection with Human immunodeficiency virus 1.

hints.text: A 34-year-old primary school teacher presented in mid-winter with 48 hours of abrupt fever, diffuse myalgias, frontal headache and a dry cough. She says symptoms began suddenly and left her unable to work yesterday. On examination T 39.2 °C, pulse 110/min, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, chest auscultation clear, no focal lymphadenopathy.

She is otherwise well, takes no regular medications, and is not pregnant. She did not receive this season's respiratory virus vaccine. Two children from her class were sent home last week with high fevers and reported skeletal muscle aches.

Complete blood count shows WBC 3.8 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 35 mg/L. Creatine kinase 420 U/L. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for multiplex respiratory PCR on day 2 of illness.
Chest radiograph performed because of tachycardia and subjective dyspnoea shows no lobar consolidation. There is mild peribronchial cuffing and increased perihilar markings, without pleural effusion.

Local public health notified the clinic of a small school cluster traced to a single respiratory pathogen. Multiplex PCR returned positive for a segmented negative-sense RNA virus that carries haemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface glycoproteins. The patient was started on a neuraminidase-targeted antiviral within 36 hours of symptom onset with rapid symptomatic improvement over 48 hours.

explanation: Abrupt onset febrile illness with prominent myalgias, relative lymphopenia, elevated CK and peribronchial radiographic changes in the setting of a school outbreak point to a seasonal human orthomyxovirus. Detection by PCR of a segmented negative-sense RNA virus with haemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface proteins and clinical response to a neuraminidase inhibitor confirm infection with Influenza A virus.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of worsening productive cough, pleuritic right-sided chest pain and increasing breathlessness. He is febrile to 39.0°C, heart rate 112/min, SpO2 88% on room air, and examination shows bronchial breath sounds with dullness to percussion over the right upper chest.

He has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and a long history of heavy alcohol use. Three weeks earlier he was hospitalised for a urinary tract infection and completed an oral antibiotic course; he has no recent travel and lives at home independently.

Peripheral blood tests show leukocytosis 17.8 × 10^9/L and CRP 172 mg/L. Peripheral blood cultures flagged positive for Gram-negative bacilli, and sputum microscopy demonstrated numerous neutrophils with abundant Gram-negative rods.

Chest radiograph and contrast CT show dense lobar consolidation of the right upper lobe with bulging of the horizontal fissure and a small right pleural effusion; early cavitary change is noted within the consolidation.

Sputum and blood cultures grew very mucoid, lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar with a glossy, capsule-like appearance; isolates were non-motile and resistant to ampicillin but susceptible to third-generation cephalosporins.

explanation: Severe lobar pneumonia in a patient with diabetes and heavy alcohol use, radiographic bulging fissure and bacteremia point to an encapsulated Gram-negative enteric bacillus. The combination of mucoid, lactose-fermenting, non-motile colonies with intrinsic ampicillin resistance is most consistent with Klebsiella pneumoniae.

hints.text: A 68-year-old woman presented from home to the emergency department with 72 hours of progressive dyspnoea, nonproductive cough, and new confusion after a week of malaise. On arrival she was febrile 39.2°C, tachypnoeic at 26/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air requiring 3 L/min supplemental oxygen, and chest auscultation revealed bilateral coarse crackles.

Her past medical history includes type 2 diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease treated with inhaled bronchodilators; she received the seasonal inactivated respiratory vaccine five months earlier. She lives with her daughter and two school-age grandchildren who had abrupt febrile respiratory illnesses the week before her symptoms; she reported no recent travel, no poultry or swine contact, and no known immunosuppressive medications.

Admission bloods showed leukocytes 3.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.7 × 10^9/L, CRP 120 mg/L, and creatinine 95 μmol/L. Two sets of blood cultures remained sterile at 48 hours and sputum culture grew only mixed oral flora.

Chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral patchy air-space opacities greatest centrally and at the bases. A CT pulmonary angiogram excluded embolus and showed multifocal ground-glass change with areas of consolidation in a peribronchovascular distribution.

She received empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics without clinical improvement, then clinicians started a neuraminidase inhibitor on hospital day 4. Within 48 hours she defervesced and oxygenation improved markedly, and subsequently a nasopharyngeal multiplex PCR detected a seasonal respiratory virus known to be susceptible to neuraminidase inhibitors.

explanation: An older patient with acute febrile respiratory illness during a household outbreak, lymphopenia, bilateral peribronchovascular ground-glass change, and rapid clinical improvement after a neuraminidase inhibitor, with PCR confirmation of a neuraminidase-inhibitor–susceptible seasonal respiratory virus, supports infection with Influenza A virus.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presented to the emergency department with five days of fever and progressive right upper-quadrant pain. He was febrile to 39.2°C, heart rate 110/min, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, and on examination had tender hepatomegaly and mild scleral icterus.

He has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus with recent HbA1c 10.8% and receives oral agents only. He reported no prior hepatobiliary disease, no recent abdominal procedures, no alcohol excess, and no intravenous drug use.

Blood tests showed WBC 18.6 × 10^9/L, CRP 212 mg/L, ALT 96 U/L, ALP 420 U/L, total bilirubin 45 µmol/L. Two sets of blood cultures flagged positive at about 18 hours and percutaneous aspiration produced thick, viscous purulent material.

Contrast CT of the abdomen demonstrated a 6.5 cm multiloculated low attenuation lesion in the right hepatic lobe consistent with a pyogenic abscess and no intrahepatic biliary dilatation. Chest CT showed several small peripheral nodular opacities in both lungs suggestive of septic emboli.

Three weeks before symptom onset he returned from a four-week visit to Taiwan where he stayed with family and ate street food regularly. Several relatives in the region had recently recovered from brief febrile gastrointestinal illnesses.

explanation: Poorly controlled diabetes, a solitary cryptogenic right-lobe liver abscess with bacteremia and metastatic pulmonary nodules after recent travel to East Asia fits hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae. The clinical picture of monomicrobial Gram-negative bacillary sepsis with viscous pus and metastatic spread is most consistent with that diagnosis.

hints.text: A 36-year-old previously well man presented to primary care with 6 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnoea, nonproductive cough, drenching night sweats and an 8 kg unintentional weight loss. On arrival his respiratory rate was 20 breaths/min and oxygen saturation 92% on room air. Examination showed scattered inspiratory crackles and white plaques on the buccal mucosa that scraped off.

Symptoms began after a brief febrile illness treated as bronchitis; he received two courses of oral antibiotics over three months with only transient improvement. He has no known chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications and received no systemic immunosuppressive therapy. He recalled an episode of shingles at age 33 that resolved without complication.

Haemoglobin 95 g/L, white blood cell count 3.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.5 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 28 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase 520 U/L. Sputum microscopy and nucleic acid amplification test for acid fast bacilli were negative. Oropharyngeal swab grew Candida species.

High-resolution computed tomography of the chest demonstrated diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities with perihilar predominance and mild interlobular septal thickening; there was no focal lobar consolidation or cavitation. Small bilateral axillary and mediastinal lymph nodes were present.

On directed questioning he admitted several new sexual partners over the past year and inconsistent condom use. A fourth-generation antigen and antibody screening assay returned reactive and confirmatory testing by nucleic acid amplification detected high-level plasma viral RNA, establishing the infective agent.

explanation: Subacute constitutional symptoms, mucosal candidiasis and lymphopenia indicate impaired cellular immunity with susceptibility to opportunistic infections. Diffuse ground-glass change on CT and elevated LDH point to an opportunistic pneumonia in that immunocompromised setting. A reactive fourth-generation antigen and antibody screen with detectable plasma viral RNA confirms infection with the virus that produces progressive CD4 T-cell depletion and explains the clinical picture.

hints.text: A 57-year-old man presents to the emergency department with five days of fever, dry cough, and progressive breathlessness. He reports new confusion and markedly reduced exercise tolerance, has had poor oral intake, is febrile to 39.1°C, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 89% on room air, and has bronchial breath sounds with crackles at the right base on auscultation.

Medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease after 40 pack-years of smoking, stable ischemic heart disease with a coronary stent, and gastro-oesophageal reflux managed with a proton pump inhibitor. He was seen by his primary clinician three days earlier and started on oral amoxicillin with no improvement, and he notes mild loose stools over the last two days.

Blood tests show white blood cell count 14.2 × 10^9/L, sodium 125 mmol/L, CRP 220 mg/L and AST 78 U/L. Two sets of blood cultures are sterile at 48 hours and sputum Gram stain shows many neutrophils with few visible organisms.

Chest radiograph demonstrates dense consolidation of the right lower lobe with patchy bilateral peripheral air-space opacities and a small right pleural effusion. CT chest performed to characterise the extent confirms lobar consolidation with adjacent ground-glass change but no pulmonary embolus.

He had returned from a four-day stay at a city hotel one week before admission during which he used the communal hot tub and took prolonged hot showers. Bronchoalveolar lavage cultured small grey-white colonies after 72 hours on buffered charcoal yeast extract supplemented with L-cysteine and iron, and the isolate would not grow on routine blood agar without those supplements.

explanation: This presentation is a community-acquired pneumonia that failed to. Recent exposure to warm water sources and recovery of a fastidious organism that requires buffered charcoal yeast extract with L-cysteine and iron for growth point to the causative pathogen. These features together make the waterborne, fastidious Gram-negative bacillus the most likely diagnosis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old male presented to the outpatient clinic with a 10-week history of intermittent low-grade fevers, night sweats, progressive fatigue and increasing abdominal fullness. He reports a 6 kg weight loss and now has exercise intolerance; on examination he is pale and the spleen is palpable about 9 cm below the left costal margin with mild hepatomegaly.

Symptoms evolved gradually over several months and have not responded to two courses of oral antibiotics prescribed in primary care. He has no known chronic illnesses, is not on immunosuppressive medication, and a rapid HIV test performed four weeks ago was negative.

Full blood count shows Hb 72 g/L, WBC 1.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 1.0 × 10^9/L, platelets 58 × 10^9/L. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrates polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia. Bone marrow aspirate shows macrophages that contain numerous small 2–4 μm oval intracellular organisms with a rod-shaped kinetoplast.
Abdominal ultrasound confirms marked splenomegaly with spleen length 18 cm and mild hepatomegaly. No focal splenic lesions are identified and chest radiograph is unremarkable.

He returned three months ago after a six-month work placement in rural houses with mud walls and thatched roofs. He slept outdoors many nights, recalled frequent small dusk-biting flies and close contact with neighbourhood dogs that had chronic skin sores.

explanation: Progressive fever, marked splenomegaly, pancytopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia point to a chronic intracellular infection of the reticuloendothelial system. The bone marrow finding of small intracellular organisms with a kinetoplast plus exposure to nocturnal, phlebotomine-type flies and canine reservoir strongly supports infection with Leishmania species causing visceral disease.

hints.text: A 58-year-old woman presented to the emergency department after 5 days of progressive fever, nonproductive cough and increasing fatigue. She reported two days of nausea and one episode of vomiting, was febrile to 39.1 C on arrival, respiratory rate 22/min, oxygen saturation 92% on room air and had coarse crackles at the right base on chest auscultation.

Her past medical history was notable only for well controlled type 2 diabetes and long-standing gastro-oesophageal reflux treated with a proton-pump inhibitor. She was not immunosuppressed and had not been hospitalized recently. Ten days before presentation she attended a three-night international conference and returned home seven days before symptoms began.

Blood tests showed white blood cell count 12.3 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance, C-reactive protein 210 mg/L, sodium 123 mmol/L and alanine aminotransferase 92 U/L. Blood cultures remained negative at 48 hours and a sputum Gram stain showed many neutrophils but no organisms identified.

Chest radiograph and subsequent CT demonstrated dense consolidation of the right lower lobe with a small right pleural effusion and patchy ground-glass changes in the left lower lobe. There was no cavitation or large bilateral alveolar flooding.

On further questioning she reported frequent use of the hotel hot tub during the conference and learnt that several other attendees later developed febrile respiratory illness. Hotel maintenance acknowledged intermittent problems with the spa water treatment while she was staying there.

explanation: The combination of community-onset lobar pneumonia with prominent systemic features, gastrointestinal symptoms, hyponatraemia and a cluster linked to a hotel spa points to a waterborne, fastidious intracellular gram-negative bacillus transmitted in aerosolized warm water. Negative Gram stain of sputum and recent proton-pump inhibitor use increase suspicion.

hints.text: A 72-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 36 hours of fever, headache and progressively slurred speech. He had a temperature of 38.8°C, marked confusion with disorientation to time, and a stiff neck on examination; cranial nerve testing was limited by agitation.

He has type 2 diabetes and has been taking prednisone 10 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for the past 3 months. He recalled two days of watery diarrhoea that began four days before presentation and resolved, and he lives independently without recent hospital admission.

Lumbar puncture showed CSF white cell count 1.2 × 10^9/L with 85% neutrophils, protein 1.8 g/L, and glucose 1.0 mmol/L (concurrent serum glucose 6.5 mmol/L). Blood cultures flagged positive at 36 hours and Gram stain demonstrated small Gram-positive rods.
MRI brain with contrast demonstrated diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement and a focal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the dorsal pons with mild surrounding oedema, without a large abscess.
On directed questioning he reported eating unpasteurised soft cheese and cold‑smoked salmon from a farmers' market five days before symptom onset; his wife ate the same foods and remained well.

explanation: Elderly, mildly immunosuppressed patient with neutrophilic CSF meningitis, blood cultures growing small Gram-positive rods, and pontine (rhombencephalic) involvement following ingestion of high‑risk refrigerated ready-to-eat dairy/seafood points to Listeria monocytogenes. The timeline and exposure support foodborne acquisition and the organism often causes bloodstream seeding with CNS tropism in this host group.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presents with 3 months of intermittent low-grade fevers, progressive fatigue, night sweats and an 8 kg weight loss. He reports increasing abdominal fullness; on examination he is pale and cachectic, temperature 37.8°C, and spleen palpable 8 cm below the left costal margin; there is a solitary 1.2 cm painless crusted papule on the left forearm that began as a small nodule months earlier.

He was previously well, not on chronic medications and denied known immunosuppression; a rapid HIV test performed two weeks prior was negative. Primary care treated the forearm lesion with two courses of oral antibiotics without improvement and arranged referral for progressive cytopenias noted on routine testing.

Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L, leukocytes 2.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 46 × 10^9/L. Inflammatory markers are modestly elevated, CRP 68 mg/L. Serum albumin 24 g/L with total protein 92 g/L and a polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia on electrophoresis. Blood cultures and malaria smears are negative. Bone marrow core showed macrophage hyperplasia without malignant infiltration.

Abdominal ultrasound shows marked splenomegaly with spleen length 22 cm and mild hepatomegaly, no focal hepatic lesions. Nasal endoscopy for intermittent crusting shows an ulcerated area of the anterior septum with submucosal induration but no septal perforation on maxillofacial CT.

He recently relocated after living for several years in a poor rural district where he slept outdoors and worked nights catching small crepuscular flies; he recalls numerous nocturnal bites and a single painless papule at a bite site about 6 months before systemic symptoms. Local hospital performed a diagnostic splenic aspirate and reported numerous small intracellular organisms within macrophages consistent with kinetoplast-containing amastigote forms.

explanation: The combination of months-long fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia points to an intracellular protozoal infection of the reticuloendothelial system. Night-time exposure to small sandfly-like flies in an endemic rural area together with visualization of intracellular kinetoplast-containing amastigotes on splenic aspirate supports a diagnosis of visceral infection by Leishmania species.

hints.text: A 72-year-old retired grocer presented with 9 days of low-grade fever, progressive headache, and increasing unsteadiness. He developed slurred speech and two falls at home; on arrival temperature 38.3°C, heart rate 92/min, neurologic exam showed gaze-evoked horizontal nystagmus, dysarthria, and a broad-based ataxic gait requiring assistance.

He has seropositive rheumatoid arthritis treated for 3 years with methotrexate and a biologic anti-TNF agent. He lives independently, had no recent travel, no diarrhoeal illness, and reports no recent dental or neurosurgical procedures.

Admission bloods showed leukocytes 13.5 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 72 mg/L. Lumbar puncture produced clear fluid with opening pressure 18 cm H2O, white cell count 180 × 10^6/L (60% neutrophils), protein 1.2 g/L and CSF glucose 3.2 mmol/L with concurrent serum glucose 6.4 mmol/L. CSF Gram stain was negative and routine viral PCR panel was pending.

MRI brain with contrast demonstrated multiple small T2 hyperintense foci in the cerebellar hemispheres and dorsal pons with several 5–10 mm ring-enhancing lesions and surrounding vasogenic oedema. Findings were felt most consistent with multifocal cerebellar and brainstem microabscesses.

On detailed questioning he recalled eating several varieties of unpasteurised soft cheeses and refrigerated smoked salmon purchased at a local farmers' market, plus multiple cold deli meat sandwiches in the 10 days before symptom onset.

explanation: The exposure and clinical pattern together narrow the diagnosis to that pathogen.

hints.text: A 19-year-old man presented to the student health clinic with three days of fever, headache, and progressive swelling over the left cheek and jaw. He reported pain with chewing and difficulty opening his mouth, temperature 38.7°C, tender swelling at the angle of the mandible with mild overlying erythema, and reduced salivary flow from the left Stensen region.

He is a first-year university resident who shares a dorm kitchen. Past medical history is notable only for childhood asthma. He remembers receiving a single childhood dose of a combined childhood vaccine but is unsure about later boosters, and he denied recent dental procedures, facial trauma, or alcohol misuse.

Complete blood count shows leukopenia with lymphocyte predominance, white blood cell count 3.8 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 12 mg/L. Serum amylase is elevated at 280 U/L. Two sets of blood cultures obtained on admission remained sterile at 48 hours.

Ultrasound of the swollen gland demonstrates an enlarged, heterogeneous parotid with increased vascular flow and no focal fluid collection to suggest abscess. No cervical lymphadenopathy beyond mild reactive nodes is seen.

Local public health was alerted after three other students in his dorm developed acute parotid swelling during the same week; one later had severe unilateral testicular pain and another transient meningeal irritation that required observation. Several affected students reported incomplete vaccination histories.

explanation: The combination of acute parotid swelling with fever, elevated amylase, sterile cultures and lymphopenia, plus a dorm outbreak with subsequent orchitis and aseptic meningitis in incompletely vaccinated young adults points to infection with the mumps virus. Ultrasound findings support viral parotitis rather than bacterial abscess. The vaccination history and clustering of typical complications make this diagnosis most likely.

hints.text: A 38-year-old freelance singer presents with four months of progressive hoarseness and intermittent noisy breathing. He reports reduced vocal range and exertional dyspnea, and on examination he has a hoarse, breathy voice with inspiratory stridor at rest.

He is otherwise well and HIV-negative. As a teenager he had multiple small 'mouth warts' removed by cryotherapy. He has had several sexual partners and did not receive adolescent vaccination against common mucosal viral infections.

Flexible nasendoscopy shows multiple sessile and pedunculated mucosal nodules along both true vocal folds and the anterior commissure, reducing the glottic aperture by roughly 60 percent. Contrast CT of the neck demonstrates well defined intraluminal soft tissue nodules confined to the laryngeal mucosa without deep tissue invasion.

He underwent microlaryngoscopic CO2 laser excision for airway compromise. Symptoms recurred within six weeks and he required three additional debulking procedures over four months despite smoking cessation and voice therapy.

Histopathology of excised tissue shows exophytic squamous epithelial proliferation with surface hyperkeratosis and characteristic vacuolated superficial keratinocytes. Molecular testing of the lesion detects viral DNA consistent with a small, circular, double stranded DNA virus known to cause epithelial wart like proliferations.

explanation: Recurrent exophytic lesions of the larynx with rapid regrowth after excision and a history of mucosal warts point to a wart forming mucosal virus. The histology shows koilocytic change and molecular detection of circular double stranded DNA in lesion tissue, which together support infection with human papillomavirus causing recurrent respiratory papillomatous disease.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 3-day history of worsening frontal headache, photophobia and nausea. He had fever 38.6 °C and marked neck stiffness on examination, with no focal neurological deficit and no facial or parotid swelling on arrival.

He is a previously healthy graduate student living in shared university accommodation and working part time as a teaching assistant at a primary school. He reported routine childhood immunisations but no adult boosters, no known immunodeficiency, no recent travel, and denied sick household contacts at initial presentation.

Lumbar puncture yielded opening pressure 18 cm H2O, CSF WBC 180 × 10^6/L with 85% lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, glucose 3.6 mmol/L while simultaneous serum glucose was 5.4 mmol/L. Gram stain and routine bacterial cultures of CSF were negative, PCR for enteroviruses was negative, and peripheral blood count was 7.2 × 10^9/L.

Contrast MRI brain was unremarkable with no parenchymal lesions and no abnormal meningeal enhancement. Scrotal ultrasound performed when scrotal pain developed showed increased testicular blood flow and swelling consistent with orchitis.

Headache and neck stiffness improved with supportive care over 48 hours, but on hospital day 3 he developed a tender unilateral parotid swelling and on day 5 an acutely painful swollen left testis. A buccal swab PCR detected viral RNA consistent with the agent causing parotitis and paired sera demonstrated a rising pathogen-specific IgM, after which symptoms resolved over the next 10 days with analgesia and scrotal support.

explanation: Aseptic meningitis followed by tender parotid swelling and subsequent orchitis in a young adult is most consistent with infection by mumps virus. Buccal swab PCR with rising IgM confirms the diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to a general clinic with a 9-month history of progressive numbness in his left hand and two pale patches on the same forearm. He reports difficulty buttoning clothes and numbness when he bathes, and examination shows two ill-defined hypopigmented macules on the volar forearm with markedly reduced pinprick and temperature sensation over the patches and mild weakness of left ulnar-innervated hand muscles.

He emigrated from a rural region of northeastern Brazil to the city 12 years ago and recalls several childhood neighbours who had chronic skin problems. He has no diabetes, is not taking immunosuppressants, and describes repeated burns on his feet over the past year because of diminished sensation.

Skin punch biopsy of a forearm lesion shows granulomatous inflammation with prominent involvement of cutaneous nerves. Modified acid-fast staining of the biopsy reveals numerous slender intracellular bacilli in nerve and dermal macrophages.

High-resolution ultrasound of the left ulnar nerve demonstrates focal diffuse enlargement with hypoechoic fascicles and loss of the normal fascicular pattern over the medial epicondyle. Nerve conduction studies show slowed ulnar sensory conduction velocities and conduction block across the elbow.

On further questioning he recalls spending childhood months trapping and preparing wild armadillos for family meals in his home village. Several family members there had similar long-standing skin lesions and progressive numbness.

explanation: Chronic hypopigmented anaesthetic skin patches with progressive peripheral neuropathy, granulomatous perineural inflammation, and numerous weakly acid-fast bacilli point to infection by a slow-growing, nerve-tropic mycobacterial species endemic in parts of South America. Focal nerve enlargement on ultrasound and the history of prolonged exposure in an endemic setting support that diagnosis.

hints.text: A 37-year-old male factory worker presents with 6 weeks of progressive cough, drenching night sweats, and an unintentional 6 kg weight loss. He describes intermittent low-grade fevers and new right-sided pleuritic chest pain; temperature 37.8°C, respiratory rate 18/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, and localized coarse crackles at the right apex on chest auscultation.

He emigrated from a country with a high burden of chronic pulmonary infection 3 years ago and lives in a crowded rented flat. Medical history is notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus with recent HbA1c 9.2% and a 15 pack-year smoking history; he takes metformin only and has no known HIV infection or immunosuppressive therapy.

Laboratory tests show haemoglobin 110 g/L, white cell count 8.5 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 1.0 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 35 mg/L and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 78 mm/h. Three sputum samples plated on routine bacterial media showed no growth at 48 hours.

Chest radiograph reveals a 4.5 cm cavitary opacity in the right upper zone with adjacent patchy consolidation. CT thorax demonstrates centrilobular nodules and a tree-in-bud pattern radiating from the cavity consistent with endobronchial spread.

He reports that his older brother returned 4 months earlier after two years in prison abroad with a chronic productive cough and episodes of haemoptysis and was not treated. The patient provided close daily care and slept in the same small room during that period.

explanation: Chronic constitutional symptoms with prolonged cough, weight loss, high inflammatory markers, an upper-lobe cavitary lesion and tree-in-bud nodularity indicate an active pulmonary infection with airway spread. Prolonged close household exposure to an untreated person with chronic cavitary pulmonary disease makes infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis the most likely diagnosis. sputum culture or nucleic acid amplification testing would confirm it.

hints.text: A 19-year-old university student presents to the campus health clinic with a 10-day history of dry cough, sore throat and progressive exertional dyspnoea. He reports low-grade fevers and malaise; examination shows T 38.1°C, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 95% on room air and scattered late inspiratory crackles at the left base.

Previously healthy and a non-smoker with no chronic medical conditions and no recent travel. Two classmates developed similar prolonged coughs the previous week and he completed a five-day course of amoxicillin from primary care with no clinical improvement.

Haemoglobin 112 g/L, white blood cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L, platelets 240 × 10^9/L. CRP 34 mg/L. Evidence of mild haemolysis with reticulocytes 140 × 10^9/L, bilirubin 46 µmol/L, low haptoglobin and a positive cold agglutinin test.

Frontal chest radiograph shows patchy peribronchial and reticulonodular opacities predominating in the left mid and lower zones. There is no dense lobar consolidation and no pleural effusion, favouring an interstitial or atypical pattern.

He had no clinical improvement on amoxicillin but after starting oral azithromycin he reported marked reduction in cough and fever within 48 hours. Convalescent serology later demonstrated a fourfold rise in organism-specific IgM and IgG titres.

explanation: Young adult with a subacute dry cough, normal white count, interstitial chest radiograph, and a dormitory cluster suggests an atypical respiratory pathogen. The presence of cold agglutinins with mild haemolysis, lack of response to a beta-lactam and rapid improvement with a macrolide point to Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Serologic rise in specific antibodies confirms the diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 19-year-old university student presents to the campus clinic with a 3-day history of high fever, dry cough, nasal congestion and increasing eye redness. Temperature is 39.3°C, pulse 108/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. On examination he has marked bilateral conjunctival injection with photophobia and tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy; there is no skin rash at this first assessment.

He was born and raised in a country with intermittent childhood vaccination programs and reports no written record of childhood immunisations. He returned from a 10-day family visit there 11 days before presentation and lives in a crowded dormitory; he attended a large student orientation 7 days before symptom onset. He has no chronic illnesses and had an HIV test that was negative three months ago.

Complete blood count shows leukopenia 2.9 × 10^9/L with lymphopenia 0.6 × 10^9/L. CRP is 22 mg/L and there is a mild transaminitis with ALT 72 U/L and AST 65 U/L. A nasopharyngeal viral PCR and paired acute and convalescent serology were sent.

Chest radiograph performed on day 4 of illness demonstrates bilateral perihilar peribronchial cuffing and patchy air-space consolidation in the right mid and lower zones, most consistent with viral pneumonitis; there is no lobar consolidation or pleural effusion.

Local public health reports several recent arrivals from the same region who attended the same event developed febrile illness with a maculopapular rash that began on the face and spread downward. One of those contacts had tiny white spots on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars one day before the rash and that contact's serum was IgM positive for the outbreak virus.

explanation: The constellation of high fever with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis followed by a descending maculopapular rash in an incompletely vaccinated person linked to an outbreak, plus lymphopenia and viral pneumonitis, points to infection with measles virus. Confirmation is by virus-specific IgM or RT-PCR from respiratory specimens, which were sent for this patient.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to an outpatient infectious-diseases clinic with three months of progressive midline lower thoracic back pain and increasing difficulty walking. The pain is worse at night and with movement, he has lost 6 kg, his temperature is 37.9°C, and there is focal tenderness over the T12–L1 region with limited trunk flexion.

He emigrated from a densely populated region in South Asia 12 years ago and works as a driver. Medical history includes poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin, no known immunosuppressive therapy, and no recent trauma or intravenous drug use.

Blood tests show haemoglobin 110 g/L, white blood cell count 9.8 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 95 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 92 mm/h. Percutaneous aspiration of a paravertebral collection produced purulent fluid with negative Gram stain and no growth on routine aerobic cultures after 72 hours.

MRI of the thoracolumbar spine demonstrates destructive lytic lesions of the T12 and L1 vertebral bodies with collapse of the T12 vertebral height and a large anterior paravertebral fluid collection that tracks along the psoas sheath, with thin rim enhancement and relative preservation of adjacent intervertebral disc height.

He reports prolonged household exposure in childhood to his father, who had a chronic productive cough and cavitary lung lesions on chest radiographs while they lived abroad; the father received intermittent short courses of unspecified antibiotics but no prolonged supervised therapy.

explanation: Chronic focal vertebral destruction with a large paravertebral abscess in a patient from a high-incidence region and prolonged household contact with someone who had chronic cavitary pulmonary disease strongly suggests reactivation pulmonary pathogen seeding the spine. The most likely pathogen is Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

hints.text: A 27-year-old previously well man presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of severe bifrontal headache, high fever, and progressive confusion. On arrival he was febrile to 39.2°C, heart rate 110/min, GCS 13, photophobic, had marked nuchal rigidity and a subtle right-sided pronator drift on neurological exam.

He had no chronic medical conditions and took no regular medications. He had spent the preceding long weekend camping and swimming, and reported several episodes of diving under water; he denied recent upper respiratory infection or ear symptoms and had not travelled abroad.

Bloods showed WBC 14.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and CRP 120 mg/L. Lumbar puncture had opening pressure 300 mmH2O, turbid CSF with leukocyte count 1 200 × 10^6/L (95% neutrophils), protein 3.5 g/L, glucose 0.8 mmol/L (concurrent serum glucose 5.2 mmol/L). Gram stain of CSF was reported as no organisms seen and bacterial cultures were pending.

Non-contrast CT showed diffuse cerebral oedema with early effacement of the frontal sulci. MRI brain demonstrated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and restricted diffusion most pronounced in the olfactory bulbs and medial frontal lobes with surrounding meningoencephalitic change.

On further questioning the patient said he had performed forceful dives and repeatedly inhaled water while swimming in a warm inland lake two days before symptom onset, and after returning home used a nasal irrigation device with unboiled tap water.

explanation: Rapidly progressive meningoencephalitis in a previously healthy young adult with neutrophilic, hypoglycorrhachic CSF and negative Gram stain points away from routine pyogenic bacteria. MRI changes focused on olfactory bulbs and frontal lobes plus recent forceful nasal exposure to warm freshwater strongly suggest a primary amoebic meningoencephalitis from a thermophilic free-living amoeba acquired via the nasal route.

hints.text: A 48-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of progressive frontal headache, fever and increasing confusion. He is febrile to 39.2°C, somnolent but arousable, has nuchal rigidity and a subtle left-sided pronator drift on neurologic exam.

He is previously healthy with no chronic illnesses and no immunosuppression. He reports intermittent saline nasal irrigation for chronic rhinosinusitis; he had a mild upper respiratory prodrome 3 days before the headache began and denies recent dental procedures or antibiotic use.

Peripheral blood leucocyte count 14.0 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance. Lumbar puncture shows opening pressure 300 mmH2O, CSF white cell count 2,300 × 10^6/L with 88% neutrophils, CSF protein 2.1 g/L and CSF glucose 0.9 mmol/L with concurrent serum glucose 5.6 mmol/L. Gram stain of CSF shows no bacteria and routine bacterial cultures remain negative after 24 hours.

MRI brain with contrast demonstrates confluent T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and patchy haemorrhagic change in the right frontal lobe with restricted diffusion. Abnormal enhancement tracks from the right cribriform region into the adjacent olfactory bulb and medial frontal cortex.

On re‑questioning the patient reports submerging his head while diving into a warm inland freshwater lake 5 days before presentation and that he last used his nasal irrigation device the day after that trip using untreated household well water. The CSF wet mount examined by the microbiology laboratory demonstrated rapidly motile, amoeboid organisms.

explanation: Fulminant meningoencephalitis with marked neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis, very low CSF glucose and haemorrhagic frontal lobe necrosis extending from the cribriform plate localises the process to the anterior cranial fossa. Recent head submersion in warm freshwater with subsequent nasal irrigation provides a plausible nasal route of entry. The combination of these findings and rapidly motile amoeboid forms on CSF wet mount indicates primary amebic meningoencephalitis caused by a thermophilic free-living amoeboid parasite.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man from a rural farming district presents with three months of progressive fatigue, exertional dyspnoea and intermittent crampy abdominal pain. He reports dizziness on standing and has reduced his work hours because of weakness. On examination he is pale with conjunctival pallor, pulse 98 min−1 and blood pressure 110/70 mmHg. There is no fever and chest auscultation is clear.

He is otherwise well, HIV test last year was negative and he has no history of liver disease or heavy alcohol use. He has tried oral iron supplements for six weeks with minimal improvement. He takes no nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and denies overt gastrointestinal bleeding such as melaena or haematemesis.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 68 fL and eosinophils 1.4 × 10^9/L. Ferritin is 9 µg/L and faecal occult blood is positive. Stool microscopy demonstrates numerous ovoid thin-shelled ova consistent with a hookworm-type nematode.

Chest radiograph obtained because of transient cough three weeks earlier shows a fleeting patchy peripheral infiltrate in the right lower zone that was not present on a radiograph taken two months before. Abdominal ultrasound is unremarkable.

He reports working barefoot in irrigated rice paddies during the planting season and notes recurrent intensely pruritic papules on the soles of his feet that coincide with fieldwork. During a recent community deworming survey adult worms recovered from several symptomatic neighbours were described on light microscopy as having a curved anterior end with semicircular cuticular cutting plates.

explanation: Chronic iron deficiency anaemia with peripheral eosinophilia, transient pulmonary infiltrate from larval migration, barefoot exposure to irrigated soil and recovery of adult worms with cuticular cutting plates identify Necator americanus as the cause of his chronic hookworm infection.

hints.text: A 38-year-old man presents to clinic with 4 months of progressive right-hand weakness and intermittent numbness, plus several painless skin plaques on both forearms. He reports difficulty with buttoning and a new clawing posture of the ring and little finger; temperature 36.7°C.

Symptoms evolved slowly over months despite topical steroid courses for presumed dermatitis. He has no diabetes, is HIV negative, and has spent recent years doing field ecological surveys in rural areas; no household febrile illnesses reported.

Routine bloods normal: haemoglobin 145 g/L, WBC 6.4 × 10^9/L, CRP <5 mg/L. Nerve conduction studies show focal slowing and conduction block of the right ulnar nerve at the elbow with preserved sural sensory potentials.
High-resolution ultrasound of the right ulnar nerve demonstrates a focally enlarged 9 mm segment with hypoechoic swelling and disrupted fascicular pattern, without a compressive lesion identified.
On detailed questioning he describes frequent direct contact with wild armadillos during fieldwork, including handling carcasses and trapping animals in rural regions where those mammals are common.

explanation: Chronic mononeuropathy with focal ulnar nerve enlargement, insidious skin plaques, and direct armadillo exposure point to infection with Mycobacterium leprae. Normal systemic inflammatory markers and negative HIV make inflammatory or diabetic neuropathy less likely. The exposure is a recognized zoonotic risk that helps distinguish this diagnosis.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department with five days of migratory joint pains and acute right knee swelling that began yesterday. He is febrile to 38.5°C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, the right knee is tense, erythematous and warm with markedly reduced range of motion, and he cannot bear weight.

He is otherwise healthy, takes no regular medications and has no history of joint disease or prosthetic joints. He reports unprotected receptive and insertive intercourse with a new partner two weeks before presentation and had a brief episode of mild urethral discomfort and scant discharge about 10 days ago that resolved without treatment.

Arthrocentesis yielded turbid yellow synovial fluid with leukocyte count 80 × 10^9/L, 95% neutrophils. Peripheral blood leukocyte count is 12.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein is 120 mg/L. Initial Gram stain of synovial fluid reported no organisms and blood cultures remain sterile at 48 hours.

Point-of-care ultrasound shows a large effusion of the right knee. MRI of the ipsilateral wrist performed for migratory hand pain demonstrates marked fluid within flexor tendon sheaths consistent with tenosynovitis.

A urethral swab from the patient is positive by nucleic acid amplification for the same organism subsequently visualized within polymorphonuclear cells on repeat Gram stain of synovial fluid as intracellular Gram-negative diplococci; culture from enriched media yielded oxidase-positive colonies.

explanation: The presentation of migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis and a purulent joint effusion in a sexually active young adult after recent unprotected intercourse points to a disseminated sexually acquired bacterial infection. Synovial fluid neutrophil predominance with initially negative blood cultures fits a pathogen that often produces culture-negative bacteremia and shows intracellular Gram-negative diplococci within neutrophils. Positive NAAT from a urethral swab and matching microscopy from the joint confirm the diagnosis in this patient.

hints.text: A 23-year-old woman presented to the student health clinic with a 10-day history of persistent dry cough, fatigue, and intermittent low-grade fevers. She lives in shared university accommodation and reports progressive exertional dyspnoea that now limits climbing a single flight of stairs; on examination T 38.1°C, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, and sparse fine crackles audible over the right lower lung field.

She completed a five-day course of oral amoxicillin prescribed for presumed bronchitis without clinical improvement. She has no chronic medical conditions, is a non-smoker, had several classmates with recent ‘cold’ illnesses three weeks earlier, and has not travelled or had animal exposures.

On day 10 blood tests showed Hb 106 g/L, WBC 6.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 34 mg/L, reticulocyte count 4%, LDH 420 U/L and haptoglobin 0.15 g/L; direct antiglobulin test was positive for complement only. Multiplex nasopharyngeal PCR was negative for influenza and SARS‑CoV‑2, and sputum Gram stain showed no predominant bacteria with routine culture remaining sterile at 48 hours.

Chest radiograph demonstrated patchy perihilar and peribronchial interstitial markings greater on the right without lobar consolidation. High-resolution CT performed because symptoms persisted showed bilateral patchy ground-glass opacities and bronchial wall thickening, most pronounced in peribronchovascular distribution.

Because symptoms failed to improve on a beta-lactam, oral doxycycline was started and fever resolved within 48 hours with marked improvement in cough and exercise tolerance over the following five days. Convalescent serology four weeks later demonstrated a fourfold rise in specific IgM and IgG to an atypical respiratory pathogen identified by the hospital laboratory.

explanation: Prolonged dry cough in a young adult with interstitial imaging changes, negative routine cultures and poor response to a beta-lactam suggests an atypical respiratory pathogen. Complement-positive direct antiglobulin test with hemolysis points to cold agglutinin mediated haemolysis, a recognised complication of Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection. Rapid clinical response to a tetracycline and a fourfold rise in specific antibodies confirm the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 19-year-old previously healthy university student presented to the emergency department with an 18-hour history of severe frontal headache, high fever and two episodes of projectile vomiting. He reported progressive neck stiffness and photophobia, on arrival T 39.3°C, HR 112/min and BP 105/65 mmHg, and he was alert but irritable with a positive Kernig sign.

He lives in a crowded on-campus dormitory and attended a packed orientation event 48 hours before symptom onset. He takes no regular medications, is a non-smoker and reports he did not receive the adolescent meningococcal conjugate vaccine offered by the university health service.

Peripheral blood showed WBC 18.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and CRP 156 mg/L. Lumbar puncture yielded turbid fluid with opening pressure 280 mmH2O, CSF leukocytes 2,800 × 10^6/L (95% neutrophils), CSF glucose 1.6 mmol/L with serum glucose 5.2 mmol/L, and CSF protein 2.1 g/L; Gram stain showed many neutrophils and no organisms visualised.

Non-contrast CT of the head was unremarkable without mass lesion or hydrocephalus, so empiric intravenous antibiotics and adjunctive corticosteroid were started and blood and CSF cultures were sent before therapy.

Public health follow-up identified two febrile classmates and nasopharyngeal swabs from several dormitory contacts grew an oxidase-positive, gram-negative diplococcus that fermented glucose and maltose; isolates from the patient’s blood and CSF matched those carriage strains on molecular typing.

explanation: Young adult with acute purulent meningitis, a dormitory cluster and nasopharyngeal carriage point to a meningitis-causing encapsulated diplococcus. The organism's oxidase positivity and ability to ferment both glucose and maltose identify Neisseria meningitidis as the cause in this epidemiologic setting.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 3 days of a progressively swollen, painful right knee that prevents him from bearing weight. He also reports 5 days of dysuria and urinary frequency, temperature 38.1°C, right knee visibly swollen with an obvious effusion and markedly reduced range of motion on examination.
