He is otherwise healthy, no chronic illnesses and no recent joint procedures. He reports unprotected sexual activity with two new partners over the past month and was treated for a different sexually transmitted infection 8 months ago, he denies intravenous drug use or recent travel.

Blood tests show WBC 12.6 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 112 mg/L. Arthrocentesis yields cloudy fluid with synovial WBC 85 × 10^9/L, 92% neutrophils, and the initial Gram stain reported no organisms. Peripheral blood cultures are pending.

Ultrasound of the knee confirms a large complex effusion with synovial thickening and internal echoes. MRI shows synovial enhancement consistent with septic arthritis and no bone marrow signal change to suggest osteomyelitis.

He reiterates recent unprotected intercourse and a urethral nucleic acid amplification test returned positive for a sexually transmitted bacterial pathogen. A later review of the joint fluid reported neutrophils containing intracellular gram-negative diplococci and parallel culture growth on selective medium matching the urethral NAAT result.

explanation: Acute monoarthritis following recent urethritis in a sexually active adult, together with intracellular gram-negative diplococci in synovial neutrophils and a positive urethral NAAT, indicates dissemination of a sexually transmitted gram-negative diplococcal bacterium. The clinical course and laboratory correlation support septic arthritis due to that organism rather than typical staphylococcal or streptococcal causes.

hints.text: A 72-year-old retired gardener presented with 10 days of fever, drenching night sweats and progressively worse midline lower back and lower abdominal pain. He now has difficulty walking because of pain and had a temperature of 38.4°C on arrival and a pulse of 100/min. Examination showed lumbar paraspinal tenderness and reduced forward flexion of the spine. No focal neurologic deficit was identified.

Medical history included an endovascular stent graft placed for an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm 18 months earlier, type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with metformin, and prior peripheral arterial disease. He denied recent hospital admissions, dental procedures, or indwelling catheters. He recalled a brief self-limited episode of loose stools three weeks before the current illness that lasted about 48 hours and resolved without treatment.

Initial blood tests showed WBC 15.8 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 13.5 × 10^9/L and CRP 210 mg/L. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures became positive within 24–36 hours for motile, oxidase-negative gram-negative bacilli. Urine dipstick was normal and renal function was stable.

Contrast CT angiography of the abdomen demonstrated a focal saccular pseudoaneurysm of the infrarenal aorta at the site of the endograft with surrounding soft tissue stranding and a small periaortic fluid collection consistent with an infected graft. There was no free intraperitoneal air.

On directed questioning the patient said his granddaughter had recently brought over a pet turtle that he handled and whose tank he cleaned with bare hands about three weeks before symptom onset; he also recalled eating a sandwich while the animal was on his lap that same day.

explanation: Bacteremia with a motile oxidase-negative gram-negative bacillus seeding a vascular endograft explains the subacute fever and focal aortic pseudoaneurysm. The preceding brief gastroenteritis and recent direct contact with a pet turtle point to non-typhoidal Salmonella as the pathogen.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of escalating right knee pain and fever. He had temperature 39.0°C, heart rate 112/min, was unable to weight-bear because of pain, and examination confirmed a tense, warm effusion with markedly reduced range of motion; there was no neck stiffness and no obvious skin rash on arrival.

He was previously well, a non-diabetic, and takes no regular medications. He reported a sore throat that began 5 days before knee symptoms after attending a crowded outdoor music event 10 days earlier, lives in a shared flat, is in a monogamous relationship and denied urethral symptoms or recent STI diagnosis; he had no record of prior meningococcal vaccination.

Arthrocentesis yielded turbid fluid with leukocyte count 82.0 × 10^9/L, neutrophil predominance. Gram stain of synovial fluid showed numerous neutrophils containing small gram-negative diplococci within their cytoplasm. Peripheral blood white cell count was 16.8 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 224 mg/L.

MRI of the knee demonstrated a large joint effusion, diffuse synovial enhancement and focal marrow oedema of the distal femoral epiphysis consistent with septic arthritis with early contiguous osteomyelitis. Chest radiograph showed no pulmonary consolidation.

Both synovial fluid and blood cultures grew a fastidious, oxidase-positive, small grey colony forming Gram-negative diplococci. Biochemical testing showed fermentation of glucose and maltose. On further questioning the patient recalled a housemate hospitalised with a febrile meningitic illness two weeks earlier.

explanation: Purulent monoarthritis with intracellular gram-negative diplococci indicates invasive infection by a meningotrophic diplococcus. The culture profile showing oxidation positive colonies that ferment both glucose and maltose plus recent household contact who had meningitic illness identifies the invasive diplococcus that commonly colonises the oropharynx and can produce both meningitis and bloodstream-seeding disease. The maltose fermentation distinguishes it from the sexually transmitted diplococcus that ferments glucose only.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with 6 months of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnoea that now limits walking two flights of stairs. She reports light-headedness and reduced work capacity, on examination she has conjunctival pallor and a pulse of 96 beats per minute at rest with an orthostatic rise to 112 beats per minute, and there is no visible melaena or anal bleeding.

She emigrated from a rural coastal province three years ago and made a 2-week visit back to her home village four months ago. She denies heavy menses, recent NSAID use, peptic symptoms, prior transfusions, or chronic diarrhoea, but recalls a brief itchy papular eruption on both feet while in the village and a self-limited dry cough for about two weeks after returning.

Haemoglobin 78 g/L, MCV 62 fL, ferritin 8 µg/L and transferrin saturation 8%. White cell count 8.4 × 10^9/L with eosinophils 1.4 × 10^9/L. Stool guaiac test is negative and peripheral smear shows hypochromic microcytic red cells without schistocytes.

Chest radiograph obtained during the cough episode three months ago showed a patchy right lower lobe airspace opacity that had cleared on repeat radiograph two weeks later. Abdominal ultrasound performed to evaluate anaemia was unremarkable with no masses or obvious sources of bleeding.

On targeted questioning she admits routinely walking barefoot through irrigated vegetable plots fertilised with untreated human faeces while visiting relatives in the village. Local public health workers in that community reported frequent chronic iron deficiency anaemia and noted that several villagers had stool microscopy showing oval thin-shelled eggs consistent with a soil-transmitted strongylid.

explanation: Chronic microcytic iron deficiency with marked eosinophilia, transient pulmonary infiltrate after a respiratory illness, and a history of barefoot exposure to faecally contaminated irrigated soil point to a soil-transmitted hookworm infection acquired by percutaneous larval penetration. The community stool findings of thin-shelled strongylid eggs and the clinical pattern of chronic intestinal blood loss support the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 42-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4 days of profuse watery diarrhoea and fever. He reports 8 to 12 loose stools daily with cramping abdominal pain and two episodes of near-syncope when standing. On arrival T 38.6°C, pulse 108/min, BP 100/60 mmHg, mucous membranes dry and capillary refill slightly delayed. He is alert but mildly confused and has diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritonism.

He has a history of type 2 diabetes treated with metformin and a 6-month history of gastro-oesophageal reflux treated with a proton pump inhibitor. He has not been hospitalized recently and takes no immunosuppressants. He ate at a family gathering 6 days ago and has no sick contacts he is aware of.

Blood tests show leukocytosis 14.2 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 180 mg/L and creatinine 118 µmol/L. Two sets of blood cultures drawn on admission flagged positive for gram-negative rods after 24 hours. Stool microscopy shows numerous neutrophils and red blood cells, and a stool culture has been submitted.

Contrast CT abdomen shows segmental thickening of the terminal ileum and adjacent mesenteric lymphadenopathy, without free air or large fluid collections. There is no biliary tract abnormality and no evidence of an intra-abdominal abscess on this study.

When asked again about exposures he says his niece gave his household a small pet turtle one week before his symptoms and he had cleaned the turtle's enclosure with bare hands. The same organism grew from both stool and blood cultures and laboratory typing showed concordant isolates.

explanation: Febrile diarrhoea with leukocytosis and identical growth from stool and blood indicates invasive enteric infection. Recent direct contact with a pet turtle is a classic exposure risk, and diabetes plus acid suppression increase susceptibility to invasive non-typhoidal enteric bacteria. These features point to a non-typhoidal Salmonella causing gastroenteritis complicated by bacteremia and ileocolitis.

hints.text: A 34-year-old female paediatric nurse presents with five days of progressive hoarseness and cough. Symptoms began with nasal congestion and low-grade fever up to 38.1°C and evolved to persistent dry cough and voice fatigue. On examination she has audible inspiratory stridor at rest, respiratory rate 22/min, O2 saturation 96% on room air and scattered expiratory wheeze. She reports nocturnal worsening and difficulty projecting her voice at work.

She has a history of mild intermittent asthma treated with a short-acting beta agonist as needed. She is otherwise immunocompetent and was not recently hospitalised. Her primary care clinician started a course of oral amoxicillin two days before presentation without clinical improvement. She does not smoke and takes no chronic steroids.

Complete blood count shows white cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 3.8 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 1.5 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein is 12 mg/L. Rapid tests for influenza and SARS-CoV-2 are negative. A nasopharyngeal swab was sent for a multiplex respiratory viral PCR panel.

A lateral neck radiograph demonstrates subglottic narrowing and increased prevertebral soft tissue density consistent with acute laryngotracheal narrowing. A chest radiograph shows no focal consolidation and no lobar collapse.

The multiplex PCR returned positive for an enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA virus in the same family as measles and mumps. Infection control reports a cluster of children on her ward with acute laryngotracheitis in the preceding week and sequence typing showed identical viral strains among the paediatric cases and hers.

explanation: The adult presentation with progressive hoarseness, inspiratory stridor and radiographic subglottic narrowing indicates laryngotracheitis. Negative influenza and SARS-CoV-2 testing with multiplex PCR identifying an enveloped negative-sense RNA virus related to measles and mumps in the context of a paediatric croup cluster points to human parainfluenza virus as the cause.

hints.text: A 52-year-old man receiving induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukaemia presented with 7 days of progressive dry cough, increasing dyspnea and low-grade fever. On arrival he was tachypnoeic at 24 breaths/min, peripheral oxygen saturation 90% on room air and had diffuse expiratory wheeze with fine crackles at both lung bases; he became breathless walking from stretcher to examination bed.

He completed his third cycle of cytarabine and anthracycline 12 days earlier and remained neutropenic. He has an implanted central venous catheter and takes prophylactic posaconazole and acyclovir. He lives with his adult daughter who works outside the home in childcare.

Full blood count showed WBC 0.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 0.3 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 0.2 × 10^9/L. CRP was 98 mg/L. Blood and sputum bacterial cultures were sterile. A nasopharyngeal swab was negative for influenza A/B and respiratory syncytial virus; bronchoalveolar lavage bacterial cultures and fungal tests were negative while a broad respiratory PCR panel detected a single viral target not accounted for by influenza or RSV.

High-resolution CT chest demonstrated diffuse peribronchial wall thickening, tree-in-bud centrilobular nodularity and patchy bilateral ground-glass opacities, greatest around the central airways. There was no focal lobar consolidation or pleural effusion.

Three days after the patient's symptoms began his daughter reported an outbreak of children at her daycare presenting with acute onset barking cough and inspiratory stridor diagnosed locally as laryngotracheitis. Nasopharyngeal PCR from one symptomatic toddler returned the same single viral target that had been identified in the patient’s BAL.

explanation: An immunocompromised adult with progressive bronchiolitis and tree-in-bud change, sterile bacterial studies and a single viral PCR signal suggests a viral lower respiratory infection. The temporal link to a paediatric outbreak of laryngotracheitis with identical molecular detection points to the same respiratory virus transmitted from young children as the cause of his severe bronchiolitis.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presented to the emergency department 18 hours after abrupt onset of nausea and profuse non-bloody vomiting. During the preceding 6 hours she had vomited more than 10 times and had several watery stools, felt lightheaded when standing, and was unable to tolerate oral fluids; temperature 37.8°C, blood pressure 96/62 mmHg, heart rate 110/min, mucous membranes dry.

She is previously healthy, takes no regular medications, and has no history of chronic gastrointestinal disease. She had not taken antibiotics recently and says two children in her class were sent home the previous day with a 'stomach bug' but she continued to work.

Serum sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, urea 16 mmol/L, creatinine 118 µmol/L consistent with moderate pre-renal dehydration. White cell count 8.2 × 10^9/L. Stool microscopy shows no fecal leukocytes and initial bacterial cultures and C. difficile toxin are negative.

Focused abdominal ultrasound performed to exclude biliary or surgical causes was unremarkable for gallbladder disease, without free intraperitoneal fluid, and showed non-specific fluid-filled small-bowel loops but no obstruction.

Over the next 24 hours 17 of 28 children and four of six staff in her class developed similarly abrupt vomiting and watery diarrhoea within 24 to 48 hours after a shared snack. Public health testing reported negative bacterial cultures and a positive reverse-transcription PCR for a small, non-enveloped single-stranded positive-sense RNA virus known to cause short-incubation vomiting-predominant outbreaks with rapid person-to-person spread.

explanation: The rapid onset of vomiting-predominant gastroenteritis, high attack rate among close contacts after a shared exposure, absence of fecal leukocytes, negative bacterial studies, and PCR confirmation for a small non-enveloped ssRNA virus point to norovirus.

hints.text: A 30-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation presented with 6 days of low-grade fever, malaise and new painful swelling of both hands. She reported morning stiffness lasting about 45 minutes, and on examination temperature was 38.1°C, there was symmetric tenderness and mild synovitis of the metacarpophalangeal joints, and a faint erythematous macular rash over both cheeks and the upper chest.

She is G2P1 with a prior uncomplicated pregnancy. She has no chronic medical conditions, takes no regular medications, and has no known immunodeficiency. She works as a teaching assistant in a preschool and has not travelled recently.

Full blood count showed haemoglobin 98 g/L, white cell count 6.0 × 10^9/L and platelets 235 × 10^9/L. Reticulocyte percentage was 0.5%. C reactive protein was 18 mg/L and liver transaminases were within reference range.
Obstetric ultrasound performed because of persistent maternal symptoms demonstrated new fetal ascites, scalp oedema and a small pericardial effusion, consistent with hydrops fetalis.

Clinic public-health follow-up revealed an outbreak at the preschool two weeks earlier in which multiple children had brief febrile illnesses with prominent facial flushing followed by a netlike rash on the trunk and limbs.

explanation: The combination of maternal febrile arthropathy with a transient reticulocytopenia and ultrasound evidence of fetal hydrops after exposure to an outbreak among young children points to maternal infection with parvovirus B19. The virus preferentially infects erythroid precursors, producing reticulocytopenia, and can cross the placenta causing fetal anaemia and hydrops.

hints.text: A 38-year-old woman presented to clinic with three weeks of progressive exertional dyspnoea and severe fatigue that limited her ability to climb a single flight of stairs. She denied bleeding, fever, or recent travel. On examination she was pale with a heart rate 108 min−1, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, and no peripheral lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

She is four months post deceased-donor renal transplant and takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and low-dose prednisone. Two weeks before symptom onset her 5-year-old nephew stayed in the household and developed a brief febrile illness with an erythematous facial rash; she recalls close contact but did not develop a rash herself.

Complete blood count showed haemoglobin 62 g/L, white cell count 5.8 × 10^9/L and platelets 212 × 10^9/L. Absolute reticulocyte count was 6 × 10^9/L. Direct antiglobulin test was negative and serum bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase were within reference ranges.
Chest radiograph was unremarkable. Focused abdominal ultrasound showed no hepatosplenomegaly and the transplanted kidney appeared satisfactory without perinephric collection.

Because bone marrow evaluation documented severe erythroid hypoplasia the team administered intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g·kg−1·day−1 for 5 days. Reticulocytes rose to 140 × 10^9/L and haemoglobin increased to 98 g/L within 10 days, and archived serum later returned positive by PCR for a small non-enveloped single-stranded DNA virus.

explanation: An immunosuppressed transplant recipient with isolated severe anaemia and very low reticulocyte count indicates pure red cell aplasia. Household contact with a child who had an erythematous facial rash and the rapid haematologic recovery after intravenous immunoglobulin with confirmatory serum PCR for a small non-enveloped single-stranded DNA virus support infection with Parvovirus B19 causing persistent aplasia.

hints.text: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of high fevers, drenching sweats, severe headache and increasing confusion. He reports rigors and dark urine, is febrile to 39.8°C, heart rate 120/min, blood pressure 95/60 mmHg, and appears jaundiced and somnolent on examination.

He was previously well with no chronic illnesses and no known hemoglobinopathy. Symptoms began as intermittent fevers and myalgias about 6 days ago then progressed to persistent high fevers and oliguria over the past 48 hours; he took paracetamol at home with minimal effect.

Hemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 45 × 10^9/L, total bilirubin 72 μmol/L, creatinine 210 μmol/L, lactate 5.1 mmol/L. Thick and thin peripheral blood films demonstrate intraerythrocytic parasites on microscopy.
Point of care abdominal ultrasound shows splenomegaly with spleen length 16 cm and mild hepatomegaly. Chest radiograph is clear and non-contributory.
He returned 12 days ago from a three-week visit to rural Ghana where he slept without mosquito netting. He did not take any malaria prophylaxis.

explanation: The laboratory and clinical severity indicate a high parasite burden and need for prompt species-directed antimalarial treatment.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presents to the emergency department with four days of fever, headache and progressive confusion. He is febrile at 39.4 °C, tachycardic at 120 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/60 mmHg, and examination shows jaundice and dark urine.

Two weeks before symptom onset he returned from a two-week work trip to coastal West Africa. His past history includes a childhood splenectomy after trauma and well controlled type 2 diabetes; he reports starting but then stopping a prescribed travel prophylactic tablet after the first dose because of nausea.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 68 g/L, platelets 28 × 10^9/L, white cell count 12.6 × 10^9/L. Chemistry shows creatinine 220 µmol/L, total bilirubin 95 µmol/L, lactate 6.2 mmol/L and blood glucose 2.9 mmol/L. Haemolysis markers are striking with undetectable haptoglobin and LDH 1,480 U/L. Blood cultures are pending.

Non-contrast CT brain is normal. Chest radiograph reveals bilateral interstitial infiltrates consistent with acute lung injury. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates post-splenectomy anatomy without residual splenic tissue and a small volume ascites.

Given concern for a fulminant erythrocytic protozoal infection, empiric intravenous artemisinin-class therapy was administered. Thick and thin blood films showed about 11% of erythrocytes infected, with multiple delicate ring forms within single red cells and characteristic crescent-shaped gametocytes. Fever and parasitaemia fell markedly within 24 hours of therapy.

explanation: Recent travel to West Africa with incomplete prophylaxis, profound haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury and very high percentage erythrocyte parasitaemia with multiple rings and crescent gametocytes indicate severe infection with Plasmodium falciparum.

hints.text: A 29-year-old previously healthy man presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of intermittent fevers, drenching night sweats and progressive fatigue. On arrival he is febrile at 38.9°C, pulse 110/min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, exam notable for scleral pallor and a spleen palpable 6 cm below the left costal margin.

He spent six weeks working in rural eastern India four months before presentation and recalls a brief febrile illness there that resolved after a few days following an oral antibiotic from a local clinic. He did not take formal malaria chemoprophylaxis, has no history of transfusion or intravenous drug use, and is not on immunosuppressive medication.

Laboratory tests show hemoglobin 95 g/L, leukocytes 4.2 × 10^9/L, platelets 90 × 10^9/L and a reticulocyte count 120 × 10^9/L. Peripheral blood thin film reveals low-level intraerythrocytic parasitaemia around 0.8% with pleomorphic ring forms and infected red cells that appear slightly enlarged.

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates an enlarged spleen measuring 18 cm in length with several small peripheral subcapsular hypoechoic areas consistent with recent small infarcts or areas of sequestration. Liver size and architecture are within normal limits.

Since admission the patient has had febrile paroxysms occurring every 48 hours and repeat thin films show fine Schuffner-type stippling of infected erythrocytes with parasites concentrated in larger, younger red cells; a relapse of the same pattern began about four months after his travel.

explanation: Relapsing tertian fevers months after travel, low parasitaemia with enlarged, stippled infected erythrocytes that prefer reticulocytes, and marked splenomegaly with small splenic infarcts point to Plasmodium vivax.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency department with progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough for 10 days. He reported low-grade fever and 8 kg weight loss over two months, and had oxygen saturation 88% on room air with fine bilateral inspiratory crackles on auscultation.

He has known HIV infection diagnosed two years earlier but stopped antiretroviral therapy six months ago after moving country. He has never taken prophylaxis for opportunistic infections and denies recent travel or sick contacts.
Blood tests showed WBC 5.6 × 10^9/L and lactate dehydrogenase 520 U/L. CD4 count was 80 × 10^6/L. Arterial blood gas on room air showed PaO2 7.6 kPa with an elevated alveolar-arterial gradient.

Chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral interstitial markings. High-resolution CT demonstrated widespread bilateral ground-glass opacities with perihilar predominance and relative subpleural sparing.

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage was performed and the patient was started on high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with adjunctive corticosteroids because of hypoxaemia. Oxygenation began to improve within 72 hours and silver staining of lavage fluid revealed thin-walled, cup-shaped cysts consistent with the causative organism.

explanation: Subacute dyspnea and hypoxaemia in a patient with advanced untreated HIV and CD4 80 × 10^6/L points to an opportunistic pulmonary infection. Elevated LDH and diffuse ground-glass change on CT support this impression. Confirmation came from bronchoalveolar lavage with characteristic cysts and clinical improvement after high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and steroids.

hints.text: A 24-year-old man presents to the outpatient clinic with 5 days of intermittent high fevers, rigors and drenching night sweats. He reports the fevers recur roughly every other day, feels markedly fatigued, and on examination is febrile to 38.7°C, tachycardic with pulse 110 beats per minute, pale, and has a spleen palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin.

He travelled to rural Uttar Pradesh, India, nine months ago and worked in flooded rice paddies where he slept without a mosquito net. At that time he had a similar febrile illness that was treated with a short course of blood-stage antimalarial agents but he did not receive any additional medication thereafter.

Complete blood count shows haemoglobin 86 g/L, leukocytes 3.5 × 10^9/L, platelets 78 × 10^9/L. Peripheral blood smear shows low-level parasitaemia estimated at 0.6% of erythrocytes with ring forms and amoeboid trophozoites predominantly within enlarged red cells that display fine stippling.
Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates isolated splenomegaly with splenic length 16 cm and no focal hepatic lesion or abscess.

He describes heavy nocturnal mosquito exposure during the India trip and notes that local clinicians warned the area has a high burden of relapsing malaria. He reports that his fevers resolved permanently only after receiving a course of an agent targeted at dormant hepatic stages.

explanation: Recurrent fevers every other day with splenomegaly, anaemia, low parasitaemia and enlarged red cells with fine stippling on smear point to a relapsing Plasmodium species that preferentially invades reticulocytes. The travel history to northern India and the need for a drug that clears dormant hepatic stages support Plasmodium vivax as the diagnosis.

hints.text: A 42-year-old woman presents to clinic with 3 weeks of progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. She reports low-grade fevers and now has resting oxygen saturation 89% on room air, respiratory rate 22/min, and fine bilateral crackles on auscultation; she remains ambulatory but is limited by breathlessness.

She has rheumatoid arthritis treated with weekly methotrexate and was started on oral prednisone 60 mg daily six weeks ago for a severe flare. She has no known HIV diagnosis, no recent travel, and no household sick contacts.

Blood tests show white cell count 6.8 × 10^9/L, CRP 18 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase 680 U/L, and serum 1,3-beta-D-glucan markedly elevated at 600 pg/mL. Arterial oxygen partial pressure is reduced on room air consistent with hypoxaemia.

High-resolution CT chest demonstrates bilateral, diffuse ground-glass opacities with a perihilar predominance and patchy areas of relative subpleural sparing. There is no lobar consolidation or pleural effusion.

Because of progressive hypoxaemia she underwent bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and was started empirically on high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus oral prednisone. Within 72 hours her oxygen requirement decreased and dyspnoea improved markedly. The lavage fluid appeared foamy and proteinaceous and a silver stain later demonstrated rounded and crescentic cystic structures.

explanation: Subacute hypoxaemic pneumonitis in a patient on prolonged high-dose corticosteroids with elevated LDH and markedly raised 1,3-beta-D-glucan, diffuse ground-glass CT changes, characteristic foamy BAL fluid with silver-stain cysts, and rapid improvement on high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole identify Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia in this case.

hints.text: A 62-year-old man on day 7 of mechanical ventilation in the ICU developed fever to 38.9 °C and increasing purulent secretions from his endotracheal tube. His fraction of inspired oxygen requirement rose from 0.35 to 0.6 over 12 hours and bedside auscultation revealed new coarse crackles on the right chest.

He was admitted 10 days ago with community-acquired aspiration and required intubation. Medical history includes COPD and type 2 diabetes. He received 5 days of ceftriaxone for a urinary tract infection during this admission and the ventilator circuit humidifier has been changed only intermittently.
Blood tests show a white cell count 16.8 × 10^9/L and CRP 220 mg/L. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain shows abundant polymorphonuclear leukocytes and frequent Gram-negative rods.
Portable chest radiograph demonstrates a new dense consolidation in the right upper lobe with a small adjacent pleural effusion, not present on the study performed three days earlier.

Infection control cultured the ICU sink and the ventilator humidifier. The same non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod grew from both sites and from the patient's tracheal aspirate, producing a blue-green pigment on agar and a distinctive sweet, grape-like odour. The isolate was resistant to ceftriaxone and levofloxacin but susceptible to an antipseudomonal cephalosporin.

explanation: A ventilated patient with new fever, increased secretions, new focal consolidation, and Gram-negative rods on aspirate fits ventilator-associated pneumonia. Environmental colonization of humidifiers and sinks with a blue-green pigmented, non-fermenting Gram-negative rod that has a characteristic odour points to Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Prior broad-spectrum beta-lactam exposure and prolonged ventilation increase risk and explain the typical resistance pattern.

hints.text: A 28-year-old man presented to the emergency department with 48 hours of worsening confusion, restlessness, and nocturnal agitation. He was febrile at 38.7 °C, tachycardic, intermittently disoriented to place, and had excessive drooling; staff noted brief episodes of forceful gagging when offered water.

He was previously healthy and had returned three weeks earlier from a six-week stay in a rural province in Southeast Asia where he handled stray animals while volunteering. He had not received any preexposure immunisations for zoonoses and remembered caring for an ill puppy but did not seek medical care for any skin wounds at the time.

Blood tests showed a white cell count of 11.8 × 10^9/L. Lumbar puncture produced clear cerebrospinal fluid with 80 × 10^6/L white cells (predominantly lymphocytes), protein 1.2 g/L, and glucose 3.8 mmol/L with concurrent serum glucose 5.2 mmol/L. Multiplex PCR panel for common herpesviruses and enteroviruses returned negative.

MRI brain demonstrated bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the hippocampi and dorsal brainstem with no focal cortical enhancement or abscess formation. There was mild diffuse cerebral cortical swelling but no restricted diffusion to suggest large territorial infarct.

On further questioning a family member reported the patient had sustained a puncture wound to his right hand from an unvaccinated stray dog three weeks before symptom onset. The wound was not cleaned and he did not receive postexposure immunoglobulin or vaccine.

explanation: This patient has subacute encephalitis with prominent autonomic and brainstem-related signs appearing weeks after a mammalian bite and no postexposure care. CSF shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis and MRI signal in hippocampi and brainstem, findings consistent with a neurotropic virus transmitted by animal bites. The exposure timing and absence of prophylaxis make a bite-transmitted viral encephalitis the most likely diagnosis.

hints.text: A 69-year-old man on day 9 of mechanical ventilation in an intensive care unit becomes febrile and more hypoxaemic. He developed a new fever to 38.9°C, copious purulent tracheal secretions, and his required FiO2 rose from 0.40 to 0.60 over 24 hours with new vasopressor support for borderline blood pressure.

He has long-standing COPD and insulin-treated type 2 diabetes mellitus and was intubated for an acute exacerbation two weeks earlier. On admission he received a five-day course of ceftriaxone and azithromycin; he remains with an endotracheal tube connected to a heated humidifier whose saline reservoir is changed on-ward by nursing staff.

Peripheral white cell count is 18.4 × 10^9/L with neutrophil predominance and procalcitonin 6.2 μg/L. Endotracheal aspirate Gram stain shows many polymorphonuclear cells and moderate numbers of Gram-negative rods. Aerobic culture on MacConkey agar produced colourless, mucoid colonies identified as a non-lactose fermenting Gram-negative bacillus; blood cultures remain sterile at 48 hours.

Chest radiograph and contrast CT show a new dense consolidation of the right lower lobe with small cavitations and peribronchial wall thickening adjacent to the airways. Prior imaging two months earlier showed only emphysematous change without focal consolidation.

Following an infection-control inspection, culture of the heated humidifier reservoir and the ICU sink drains grew the identical non-lactose fermenting Gram-negative bacillus found in the endotracheal aspirate. The colonies produced a blue-green diffusible pigment and a sweet, grape-like odour and shared an antibiogram showing resistance to many third-generation cephalosporins but susceptibility to ceftazidime and piperacillin-tazobactam.

explanation: The clinical isolates match organisms found in the ward water sources, and the blue-green pigment with a characteristic odour together with a non-lactose fermenting Gram-negative rod and the antibiogram point to a waterborne nosocomial Gram-negative bacillus as the causative pathogen.

hints.text: A 38-year-old previously well man presented with 6 days of fever, headache, and malaise followed by 48 hours of progressive confusion and intermittent agitation. On arrival he was febrile 38.6°C, heart rate 112/min, intermittently disoriented, and reported a focal burning sensation in his right forearm while motor strength remained normal.

He returned 6 weeks earlier from a three-week trip to rural communities in Southeast Asia where he walked through villages and agricultural areas. He has no chronic medical problems, takes no immunosuppressive medications, and reports no recent vaccinations for travel; family notes increasing insomnia and worsening photophobia over the last day.

Blood count showed leukocytes 9.8 × 10^9/L. Lumbar puncture produced clear cerebrospinal fluid with opening pressure 18 cm H2O, WBC 150 × 10^6/L with 90% lymphocytes, protein 1.2 g/L, and glucose 3.4 mmol/L with concurrent serum glucose 5.8 mmol/L. Routine bacterial cultures remained sterile after 48 hours.

MRI brain with T2/FLAIR sequences demonstrated bilateral hyperintense signal in the hippocampi and dorsal midbrain and medulla, without restricted diffusion or contrast enhancement. There was no focal abscess or large vessel infarction.

On targeted requestioning the patient recalled being bitten on the right forearm by a stray dog while walking through a village six weeks before presentation; the wound was not treated and he received no postexposure injections. While in hospital he developed increasing hypersalivation and painful laryngospasm triggered by attempts to drink water.

explanation: Progressive encephalitis with lymphocytic CSF and MRI signal in hippocampi and brainstem combined with an untreated dog bite and development of hypersalivation and painful spasms strongly point to infection with rabies virus. Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting viral RNA or antigen in saliva, nuchal skin biopsy, or by autopsy when available.

hints.text: A 27-year-old previously well man presented to a regional hospital with 36 hours of progressive weakness in his left leg and new difficulty walking. Symptoms began three days after a febrile prodrome with sore throat and myalgias. On examination temperature 38.1°C, left hip and knee flexion MRC 2/5, left ankle dorsiflexion 3/5, markedly reduced deep tendon reflexes on the left, intact light touch and vibration, and no cranial nerve deficits. Respiratory effort and oxygenation were normal.

He had returned 10 days earlier from a three-week volunteer placement at a crowded refugee camp abroad where routine childhood immunisation coverage had been disrupted. He reports incomplete childhood vaccinations and that he assisted at a community oral vaccine drive in the camp where a live attenuated viral preparation was administered to children. He denied recent injections, travel-associated arthropod exposures, and has no chronic medical conditions.

Lumbar puncture on hospital day 2: CSF white cell count 120 × 10^6/L with lymphocytic predominance, protein 0.9 g/L, glucose 3.4 mmol/L. Bacterial cultures were sterile. Nerve conduction studies showed preserved sensory amplitudes with markedly reduced motor amplitudes. Electromyography of affected muscles revealed active denervation with fibrillation potentials and reduced voluntary recruitment.

MRI of the spine with contrast demonstrated focal T2 hyperintensity confined to the anterior horn grey matter of the lumbar enlargement. There was no spinal cord compression and no nerve root enhancement on post-contrast sequences.

Local public health investigators reported that several recipients of the oral vaccine used in the camp later shed in stool an identical small non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus. Stool specimens from this patient tested positive for the same viral sequence, temporally linking his illness to transmission related to the live oral vaccination campaign.

explanation: Acute flaccid asymmetric motor weakness after a brief febrile prodrome with preserved sensation, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis, EMG motor neuronopathy, and MRI signal confined to anterior horn cells point to a viral anterior horn cell infection. Isolation of a small non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus linked epidemiologically to an oral live vaccine campaign confirms poliovirus as the cause, most consistent with transmission of an attenuated vaccine-related strain.

hints.text: A 72-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with 4 days of progressive dyspnoea, wheeze and productive cough following several days of nasal congestion. Her respiratory rate was 26 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 89% on room air, temperature 37.8°C, and chest examination showed diffuse expiratory wheeze with scattered inspiratory crackles; she required supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 >92%.

She has COPD treated with tiotropium and an inhaled corticosteroid, is a former smoker with a 30 pack-year history, and remains independent at baseline. She received the seasonal influenza vaccine this autumn, has no known immunosuppression, and reports no recent travel or antibiotic use.

Blood tests showed white cell count 8.2 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 0.9 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 28 mg/L and procalcitonin 0.05 µg/L. Blood cultures were sterile and a nasopharyngeal PCR panel was negative for influenza A/B and for SARS-CoV-2.
Chest radiograph demonstrated hyperinflation and peribronchial cuffing with patchy perihilar interstitial and air-space opacities, but no lobar consolidation or pleural effusion.

She reports her 2-year-old grandchild attends a local daycare and had a recent episode diagnosed as bronchiolitis during a small winter outbreak among the children. A targeted nasopharyngeal PCR returned positive for a single seasonal enveloped negative-sense RNA virus known to be a leading cause of bronchiolitis in infants and to cause similar winter outbreaks in older adults.

explanation: An older adult with COPD, hypoxaemia, wheeze and radiographic peribronchial changes in the setting of household exposure to a child with bronchiolitis suggests a viral lower respiratory infection. Negative tests for influenza and SARS-CoV-2, low procalcitonin, and PCR confirmation of the described seasonal virus point to respiratory syncytial virus as the cause in this case.

hints.text: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 48 hours of fever and malaise followed by 18 hours of progressive right leg weakness. He reports difficulty bearing weight; examination shows flaccid paresis of the right lower limb with decreased tone, absent deep tendon reflexes at the knee and ankle, and preserved light touch and pinprick sensation, temperature 38.5°C.

He is previously well with no chronic medical conditions and says he missed routine childhood vaccinations while moving between countries with limited access to care. One week before onset of weakness he had a 4-day watery diarrhoeal illness while volunteering for two weeks in a rural area with intermittent sanitation infrastructure; he returned home five days ago.

Blood count shows white blood cells 7.4 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L. Lumbar puncture on day 2 of weakness: opening pressure normal, CSF 120 × 10^6/L cells with lymphocytic predominance, protein 0.90 g/L, glucose 3.8 mmol/L with paired serum glucose 5.1 mmol/L, bacterial cultures negative.
MRI of the spine shows T2 hyperintensity confined to the anterior horn grey matter of the lumbar cord without significant gadolinium enhancement; the remainder of the cord and conus are unremarkable.

Local public health notified the hospital of several recent cases of acute flaccid paralysis in children from the rural community visited by the patient. Stool viral culture from this patient yielded a small non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus consistent with a fecal-oral enteric pathogen capable of targeting motor neuron cell bodies.

explanation: The combination of a prodromal febrile enteric illness, acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis with areflexia and preserved sensation, CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose, anterior horn T2 signal on MRI, and stool isolation of a small non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus in an unvaccinated traveller points to poliovirus infection.

hints.text: A 6-month-old previously well girl presented to the paediatric emergency department with three days of cough, progressive nasal congestion, and poor feeding. On arrival she was tachypnoeic at 64 breaths/min with intercostal retractions, scattered expiratory wheeze on auscultation, and pulse oximetry 90% on room air.

She was born at 39 weeks, has no chronic medical conditions, and received all routine immunisations. Parents report two older siblings who attend daycare developed runny noses and cough one week earlier, and the infant has had decreased breastfeeds and fewer wet nappies over 24 hours.

Capillary blood glucose and electrolytes were normal. Full blood count showed white cell count 7.6 × 10^9/L with neutrophils 3.2 × 10^9/L and lymphocytes 3.4 × 10^9/L, and C-reactive protein 5 mg/L. A nasopharyngeal swab for multiplex respiratory PCR was sent.
Frontal chest radiograph showed diffuse hyperinflation and peribronchial cuffing, without focal lobar consolidation to suggest bacterial pneumonia.

Household exposure to older siblings with winter upper respiratory illness was confirmed. A point-of-care nasopharyngeal antigen test returned positive for a single seasonal, enveloped, negative-sense RNA respiratory virus known to cause bronchiolitis in young infants.

explanation: This infant has classic bronchiolitis with tachypnoea, retractions, wheeze, hypoxaemia, low inflammatory markers, and radiographic small airway disease. The positive rapid antigen for a seasonal enveloped negative-sense RNA respiratory virus confirms respiratory syncytial virus as the cause of her illness.

hints.text: A 29-year-old man presents to an outpatient clinic three weeks after returning from a six-week backpacking trip in South America with a three-week history of intermittent watery diarrhoea, marked postprandial bloating and excessive flatulence. He has lost 4 kg, reports bulky, foul-smelling stools without visible blood or fever, and on examination appears thin with a heart rate of 102 min and mild orthostatic reduction in blood pressure.

He is previously healthy, HIV test 6 months ago was negative and he takes no regular medications. During travel he stayed in hostels, ate street food intermittently and sometimes relied on municipal tap water when bottled supplies ran out; he took a short course of oral doxycycline early in his trip for presumed traveller's diarrhoea without sustained improvement.

Abdominal ultrasound and non-contrast CT were unremarkable without biliary or high-grade inflammatory changes. A small-bowel follow-through showed mildly increased luminal fluid and a subtle blunting of proximal jejunal mucosal folds consistent with a malabsorptive process rather than an obstructing lesion.

Empirical courses of ciprofloxacin followed by azithromycin produced no symptomatic benefit, and loperamide worsened cramping. A brief, clinician-initiated five-day course of a nitroimidazole-class agent produced rapid reduction in watery diarrhoea but the patient continued to pass bulky, greasy stools and his weight loss plateaued without recovery.

Stool microscopy for ova and parasites demonstrated motile, pear-shaped trophozoites with two prominent anterior nuclei and a ventral adhesive disk; a stool enzyme immunoassay for an intestinal flagellated protozoan returned positive. Fecal fat testing was elevated on qualitative testing.

explanation: Post-travel chronic non-bloody diarrhoea with bulky, foul-smelling stools and weight loss suggests proximal small-bowel malabsorption. Identification of pear-shaped, flagellated trophozoites with a ventral adhesive disk and a positive stool antigen confirms an enteric protozoan causing malabsorption in this patient.

hints.text: A 28-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with 6 weeks of intermittent watery diarrhoea and postprandial bloating. She reports 4 to 6 bulky, foul-smelling bowel motions daily, a 3 kg unintentional weight loss, denies fever or night sweats, and is afebrile on exam with mild periumbilical tenderness and dry mucous membranes.

Symptoms began shortly after a 3-week volunteer trip to rural highland communities in South America two months ago. She took no antibiotics during or after travel, uses a proton pump inhibitor for reflux, has no chronic medical conditions and is not immunosuppressed.

Haemoglobin 135 g/L, white blood cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 3 mg/L. Stool cultures and tests for bacterial pathogens were negative, faecal leukocytes were absent, and 24-hour faecal fat measured 18 g (elevated).

CT enterography shows mild circumferential mucosal fold blunting and subtle hyperenhancement of the proximal jejunum without focal mass, lymphadenopathy, or obstruction. No biliary or pancreatic abnormality is identified.

While volunteering she frequently drank untreated mountain-stream water because bottled supplies were limited. A stool antigen assay returned positive for a single-celled intestinal protozoan known to adhere to proximal small-bowel mucosa and produce malabsorption.

explanation: Prolonged watery, bulky, foul-smelling diarrhoea with weight loss and elevated faecal fat indicates small-bowel malabsorption without inflammatory markers. Proximal small-bowel mucosal changes on imaging and a history of drinking untreated stream water point to an enteric protozoan acquired in fresh water. A positive stool antigen for a single-celled intestinal protozoan confirms the diagnosis in this clinical context.

hints.text: A 28-year-old previously well graduate student presents to the campus health clinic with 3 days of nasal congestion, watery rhinorrhoea, sneezing, sore throat, and a dry cough. He reports low-grade fever and new chest tightness on exertion, temperature 37.8°C, respiratory rate 14/min, exam shows erythematous nasal mucosa, clear posterior pharynx, and faint expiratory wheeze on auscultation.

He lives in a six-person dorm and says three housemates developed similar mild symptoms two days before his onset. He has intermittent childhood asthma well controlled with a short-acting beta-agonist, no recent antibiotic use, no travel, and no known immunodeficiency.

Complete blood count shows white cell count 6.2 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 3.8 × 10^9/L. C-reactive protein 3 mg/L. Nasopharyngeal swab sent for multiplex respiratory testing produced a positive result for an RNA respiratory virus. Viral culture produced cytopathic effect on epithelial cell monolayers incubated at 33°C but not at 37°C.

Chest radiograph is unremarkable with no focal consolidation or airspace opacity. Peak expiratory flow is reduced compared with his baseline, consistent with a mild obstructive change that improved after inhaled bronchodilator.

The illness began after attendance at a crowded, poorly ventilated indoor rehearsal in early autumn where many participants reported similar mild upper airway illnesses over the next 48 hours. Public-health sequencing of the cultured isolate identified a non-enveloped, positive-sense RNA virus that grows optimally at cooler upper-airway temperatures and has numerous serotypes implicated in community cold outbreaks.

explanation: The presentation is a viral upper respiratory infection with mild asthma exacerbation and an indoor outbreak among close contacts. Growth of a non-enveloped, positive-sense RNA virus at 33°C and the epidemiology point to rhinovirus. This pattern explains the predominant nasal symptoms, low systemic inflammatory markers, and triggering of bronchospasm in a patient with asthma.

hints.text: A 68-year-old man presented to the urgent clinic with five days of nasal congestion and sore throat followed by two days of progressive dyspnoea and wheezy cough. He was tachypnoeic at 24 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 88% on room air, and examination showed diffuse expiratory wheeze with prolonged expiratory phase and no focal crackles.

He has COPD treated with long-acting bronchodilator and inhaled corticosteroid, a 40 pack-year smoking history, and completed a short oral prednisolone taper two weeks ago for a previous exacerbation. He reports no recent travel, is not chronically immunosuppressed, and did not receive the seasonal influenza vaccine this year.
White blood cell count 7.8 × 10^9/L with lymphocytes 1.0 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 18 mg/L. Rapid influenza A/B test negative, blood cultures sterile, and sputum culture grew mixed oral flora.
Chest radiograph showed hyperinflation and prominent peribronchial cuffing without lobar consolidation or focal airspace opacity. No pleural effusion was present.

He reports close contact with two preschool grandchildren who had runny noses the week before his illness. A nasopharyngeal multiplex PCR returned a positive amplicon from assays targeting the 5' untranslated region; sequencing matched a small non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus that groups into A, B and C species and is the commonest viral finding in outpatient upper respiratory infections and in virus-triggered obstructive airway exacerbations.

explanation: An older patient with COPD developed an upper respiratory prodrome followed by bronchitic symptoms and hypoxaemia, with imaging showing peribronchial inflammation and minimal systemic inflammatory response. Multiplex PCR that targets the 5' untranslated region and the species A/B/C grouping points to the small non-enveloped positive-sense RNA virus most often recovered from common colds and implicated in asthma and COPD exacerbations, which explains the clinical course and negative bacterial workup.

hints.text: A 58-year-old man presents with 72 hours of rapidly progressive right-sided facial pain, nasal congestion, and a bitter taste in his mouth. He is febrile to 38.4°C, has right periorbital swelling with proptosis and restricted extraocular movements, and a dusky black area on the right hard palate.

He has long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus and was admitted five days earlier for diabetic ketoacidosis requiring intravenous insulin and fluids. He left hospital two days ago and reports missing several insulin doses since discharge.
Point-of-care glucose 28 mmol/L, venous bicarbonate 14 mmol/L and venous pH 7.28. White blood cell count 16.2 × 10^9/L and C-reactive protein 132 mg/L.

Contrast CT of the paranasal sinuses and orbits shows complete opacification of the right ethmoid and maxillary sinuses, erosion of the medial orbital wall, orbital fat stranding, and filling defect consistent with thrombosis of the right cavernous sinus.

Urgent endoscopic surgical debridement was performed because of progressive orbital involvement. Intraoperative tissue was extensively necrotic and direct microscopy and histology showed broad, non-septate ribbon-like hyphae with irregular right-angle branching and angioinvasion, and intravenous amphotericin B was started with early local clinical stabilization.

explanation: This is invasive rhinocerebral infection due to Rhizopus species. Recent diabetic ketoacidosis with poorly controlled glucose, rapid sinonasal and orbital spread with palatal necrosis and cavernous sinus thrombosis, and histology demonstrating broad non-septate hyphae with angioinvasion support the diagnosis and the need for urgent surgical debridement plus amphotericin B.

hints.text: A 34-year-old man presented to outpatient dermatology with an 8-month history of progressive scaling of both soles and thickening of several toenails. He reports increasing pruritus on plantar surfaces and pain under the right great toenail that limits running. On examination there is focal plantar hyperkeratosis, yellow-brown discoloration of the distal nail plates, and distal onycholysis of the right great toe. Vitals are normal.

His past medical history includes type 2 diabetes managed with metformin, most recent HbA1c 48 mmol/mol. He is not on systemic immunosuppression and has no history of peripheral vascular disease. Over the course of symptoms he intermittently used an over-the-counter topical antifungal with partial relief and was briefly prescribed a topical corticosteroid by his family clinician which seemed to reduce redness but the lesions then worsened.

Nail clippings and subungual debris were examined with a potassium hydroxide preparation and showed branching septate hyphae. Bacterial culture from a superficial swab was negative. A sample was submitted for fungal culture and microscopy.

Clinical photography and onychoscopy demonstrate distal subungual hyperkeratosis, longitudinal streaking of the nail plate, and lateral nail thickening without periungual pustules or erythema. No bone involvement was seen on plain radiograph of the toe.

He reports daily use of a communal gym shower and frequent wearing of tight occlusive work shoes. After 10 days on Sabouraud agar the fungus produced flat, suede-like colonies with a distinct red-brown pigment on the reverse. Lactophenol cotton blue mount showed numerous tear-shaped microconidia borne along the hyphae and occasional thin macroconidia.

explanation: Chronic plantar scaling with concurrent distal onycholysis suggests tinea pedis with secondary onychomycosis. KOH-positive septate hyphae confirm a dermatophyte infection. The culture phenotype of suede-like colonies with red-brown reverse pigment and abundant tear-shaped microconidia strongly points to the common anthropophilic dermatophyte responsible for chronic toe and nail infections in adults.

hints.text: A 72-year-old male resident of a long-term care facility presents with a 3-month history of progressive thick, yellowish crusting and scaling over both hands, interdigital spaces, soles and scalp. The lesions are fissured and painful with some serous discharge. He reports surprisingly little pruritus. Facility clinicians prescribed emollients and medium-potency topical corticosteroids without benefit. Low-grade fever to 37.8 °C and a 3 kg weight loss over 6 weeks are noted.

Past medical history includes chronic lymphocytic leukaemia treated with purine analogue chemotherapy 5 months ago and a prolonged oral corticosteroid taper for a drug reaction. He is bedbound and requires help for washing. Staff report that several other residents developed new nocturnal itch and superficial rash in the prior month. No recent travel or fresh water exposures.

Dermoscopic examination of palmar and interdigital regions shows numerous linear serpiginous tracks beneath adherent crust, each terminating in a small dark triangular focus. High-resolution clinical photographs document thick hyperkeratosis with fissuring and yellowish scale rather than isolated papules.

He failed empiric topical antifungal therapy and two courses of oral antibiotics. After a single supervised dose of oral ivermectin combined with mechanical keratolytic debridement of crusts, the thick scales began to slough and odour and serous discharge decreased within 7 days. Several symptomatic staff improved after application of a prescribed topical agent.

Mineral oil skin scrapings obtained from beneath the crust yielded numerous oval translucent arthropods approximately 0.3–0.4 mm in length with a stout rounded body and four pairs of short legs visible anteriorly, together with multiple ovoid eggs and dark faecal pellets on microscopy. Peripheral blood eosinophils were 1.6 × 10^9/L, CRP 22 mg/L.

explanation: Immunosuppressed, institutionalized patient with thick hyperkeratotic crusting, low itch, outbreak among contacts, dermoscopic linear burrows, rapid response to oral ivermectin plus keratolysis, and mineral oil scrapings showing numerous small oval arthropods with eggs identifies infection by Sarcoptes scabiei presenting as crusted (Norwegian) infestation.

hints.text: A 78-year-old woman from a residential care home presented to the emergency department with 24 hours of profuse vomiting and watery diarrhoea, marked reduction in oral intake, and new-onset confusion. On arrival she was orthostatic with blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, pulse 112/min, temperature 37.8°C, dry mucous membranes and diminished skin turgor.

Her medical history includes Alzheimer-type dementia, chronic heart failure and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. She had not received antibiotics in the prior month, takes a loop diuretic, and staff reported several other residents developed similar vomiting and diarrhoea beginning the previous morning after a shared communal meal.

Bloods showed WBC 9.6 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 14 mg/L, and acute kidney injury with creatinine 180 μmol/L from a baseline of 85 μmol/L. Stool culture and multiplex bacterial PCR were negative, toxin assay for Clostridioides difficile was negative, and stool microscopy showed no fecal leukocytes.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT demonstrated non-specific mild small-bowel wall thickening and prominent luminal fluid without focal colonic inflammation, obstruction or perforation, features felt most compatible with a diffuse enteric process.

Public-health follow-up revealed the residential home had recently hosted a visiting catering team; within 36 hours 32 of 50 residents and 10 of 18 staff developed a similar short-duration illness dominated by vomiting. Environmental and clinical specimens from multiple cases and from high-touch surfaces yielded the same small, non-enveloped single-stranded RNA virus by RT-PCR, with a very short incubation and high attack rate.

explanation: Acute onset vomiting-predominant gastroenteritis with rapid spread in a closed setting, high attack rate, environmental contamination, negative bacterial studies and detection of a small non-enveloped single-stranded RNA virus point to norovirus. The elderly patient's dehydration and pre-renal acute kidney injury explain the clinical severity despite the usually self-limited nature of the infection.
